<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigations into mechanics and the physics of levers, specifically how the distribution of weight and external factors like air resistance affect equilibrium. It follows the preceding analysis of balanced forces.</meta>

If a lever is equal and on one side supports a quantity of weight which is suspended from a single thread attached to the lever at one point, and from another point of the same lever multiple threads depart which support the same weight as the single one was meant to do, I ask if the force of the same lever is changed by hanging the weight from multiple threads or from only one, or not. And if it is changed, I say that it changes greatly, because the weight hanging from multiple threads is equal to the sum of multiple weights, each of which is attached to its own thread at that same point and at the points of the lever where said threads are fixed; from which it follows that if the attachment points of the threads are near or far from the center <note>original: "centro", referring to the fulcrum or pivot point</note> of the lever, the force <note>original: "forza", here meaning the mechanical advantage or effective weight</note> of the lever will be changed.

---

*Four diagrams of horizontal levers. The top-left shows a lever with a single vertical line supporting a weight. The top-right shows a lever where multiple lines originate from different points along the bar and converge to support a single weight. The middle-left shows a similar configuration with a wide spread of supporting lines. The middle-right shows a weight hanging from a single point on a tilted lever.*

---

If that which was spread across multiple points of the lever is gathered into a single point of the same, the force of the lever will be changed in proportion <unclear>...</unclear>

---

*Two diagrams of balances. The left one shows a beam with a central fulcrum and weights hanging from the ends, with a vertical support. The right one shows a similar balance but with a different suspension mechanism above the fulcrum, labeled with points and lines.*

You see that here one of the parts of the equal lever breaks the air only at a single point, which is **.m.**; the other breaks it at several points, namely at **.f. .n. .s. .e. .r. .m.** and therefore this side will be lighter than the other, because where there is more breaking of the air <note>original: "rōsura d’aria", a characteristic Leonardesque term for air resistance or friction</note> there is greater resistance <note>original: "fatica", literally "toil" or "effort"</note>. Hence, if the said weights are hung from the aforementioned points of the same lever and at an equal distance from the center of that lever, the one hanging from multiple points will become lighter for the said reason.

---

The path of the cord is the straight line that goes from the center of motion to the middle of the thickness of such a cord.

<margin>
Why the cord that supports the weight is weaker when it is more oblique, that is, when it is further from the line of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>the vertical line of gravity or plumb line</note>.
</margin>
The perpendicular cord will be more powerful than any other which is oblique; and it will be as much weaker as it is more oblique, which will be proven by the line of equality of weights in the arms of the balance.

Why the weight *m* hangs more by the cord *f d* than by the cord *a d*: it says that the weight *m* is pulled upward by the cord *d a* and by the cord *f d*; and because the motion <note>or path</note> *m d f* is shorter <note>meaning more direct or less angled</note> than the motion *m d a*, that cord *f d* will be more powerful than *m d a* <note>Leonardo likely refers to the tension/force exerted by cord *d a*</note>, and this is proven in the path *d f* and *d a*.

The difference of the weight *m n* from the counterweight *o p* will be as much as the difference of the path *d n* from *d p*. *m* will be as much less than *n* as *d f* is less than *d a*; and *n* will be as much greater than *m* as *d a* is greater than *d f*.

<meta>This page continues the geometric study of solids and their physical properties, specifically focusing on the center of gravity in triangles and pyramids, following the general principles of mechanics established in the previous section.</meta>

# Explanation of the triangular pyramid
## and of its gravity

All triangles, whether equilateral or with unequal sides, have their center of weight <term>center of gravity</term> <note>The point where the weight of an object is perfectly balanced in all directions.</note> on that line which is drawn from the angle to the middle of the opposite base, which is distant from the base by a third of its length. And the same occurs in every pyramid, which have their center of weight on the line that falls from the angle <note>Here referring to the apex or top point of the pyramid.</note> onto the center of the base, and it is distant from that base by the fourth part of that line.

<image-desc>A horizontal row of five geometrical and mechanical diagrams. From left to right: 1) A cone with a vertical line descending from the apex to the center of the base, ending in a small circular weight. 2) A zig-zag line connecting three circular weights. 3) A rhombus (two triangles joined at the base) with circular weights at each vertex. 4) A pyramid shown in profile with a central vertical axis line. 5) A mechanical device consisting of a rectangular block with a curved upright arm supporting a weight at its tip.</image-desc>

---

Every weight that hangs by an oblique <note>slanted or non-vertical</note> line pulls toward the perpendicular of its suspension. Therefore, the weight of the pyramid *b a c* pulls toward the perpendicular *a d*. Since the entire weight of the pyramid is concentrated in that point which is the center of its gravity. Therefore, by drawing the line *e f* through the center of the pyramid *g h i* parallel to the base *h i*, this line *e f* intersects the line *a d* at point *l*, which is the center of gravity of that pyramid. Thus, that point is the terminus of all the gravity of the pyramid, and that point is what pulls toward the perpendicular of its suspension.

If a pyramid were made of water or another liquid substance, its center of weight would be at the sixth degree <note>The author specifies a "sixth degree" here, though standard Euclidean and Archimedean geometry—and indeed other notes by this author—usually place a pyramid's center of gravity at one-fourth of its height. This may represent an experimental variation or a specific system of measurement.</note> of its height, and if it were made of lead <note>original: "pionbo"</note> it would be in the same degree, and so with every other heavy matter. Since gravity is nothing other than a desire to flee inequality <note>A poetic Renaissance way of describing the physical drive toward equilibrium and balance.</note>. And because the pyramid is unequal, it moves by its gravity toward the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the center of the Earth, which in the science of the time was believed to be the natural destination for all heavy objects seeking rest.</note>, and because the center of the world is equal in every part, it stops when it has reached its center, for there is no reason that would move it further in one direction than another.

<margin>
<image-desc>A vertical diagram in the right margin depicting a long vertical line with a central ring or pulley and small weights at the top and bottom terminals, labeled with characters 'a' and 'd'.</image-desc>
</margin>

<insert>
**The Royal Society of London**
**from the gift of Henry Howard**
**of Norfolk.**
<note>original Latin: "Soc. Reg. Lond. ex dono Henr. Howard Norfolciensis." This is a provenance mark indicating the manuscript was part of the Arundel collection given to the Royal Society in 1667.</note>
</insert>

<note>Technical vocabulary: pyramid (piramide), center of gravity (cientro della gravità), weight (peso), line (linia), perpendicular (perpendiculare), inequality (disugualità), sixth degree (sesto grado), lead (pionbo)</note>

<summary>This page explains the geometric location of the center of gravity in triangles and pyramids, asserting that the material (water or lead) does not change this point. It describes gravity as a natural drive for objects to seek balance at the center of the Earth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of gravity and mechanics. While the previous page focused on the static balance and center of gravity in pyramids and triangles, this page shifts to dynamics—specifically how the angle of a path (obliquity) affects the speed and impact of a falling weight.</meta>

<image-desc>At the top right, a diagram shows three vertical lines, each with a small circular weight attached at a different vertical position.</image-desc>

¶ The <term>impact</term> <note>original: "percussione"; refers to the force with which a moving body strikes another.</note> of a weight will be less in proportion as its motion is slower.

¶ And the motion will be slower in proportion as the descending weight has less <term>effective weight</term> <note>original: "pondo"; the weight of an object as it is modified by its position or the angle of its path.</note>, whether it is hindered by a counterweight, or by its slant, or by some other circumstance.

¶ Thus, the weight *m*, descending along the cord *am* to the position *n*, will have less weight than at *m*, as well as a lesser impact and a slower motion.

---

¶ The impact of the weight will be less in proportion as its slant is less.
Or you might say, the impact of the weight will be less in proportion as its motion is slower.

---

¶ The impact of a weight will be less in proportion as its descent is less.
And its descent will be less in proportion as its path is more slanted.
From this, it is concluded that the impact will be less as the line is more slanted; and it will be more slanted as the angle *n m o* is more <term>obtuse</term> <note>An angle greater than 90 degrees.</note>.

---

The weight *m* will have a greater slowness of motion as the line *m n* becomes more slanted.

<image-desc>A series of three diagrams illustrates a mechanical experiment. Each contains a quadrant within a square frame. A cord passes over a pulley at the top left corner (labeled 'o') and connects a hanging weight to a point (labeled 'm') on a rotating radial arm. The three diagrams show the arm at varying angles of descent.</image-desc>

The descending weight *m* will always have less effective weight as its line of descent is more slanted; and it will have less effective weight in proportion as the weight *n* is stronger in resisting it, preventing it from descending along the line *m n*. This is proven by the study of impacts.

<image-desc>Two additional diagrams on the right side of the lower page. The upper one shows a weight (m) on a lever arm connected to a pulley. The lower one depicts a rectangular weight on an inclined plane with geometric labels.</image-desc>

<insert>
¶ The weight *m*, descending through a circular motion *n m*, will have a greater slowness of motion the closer *m* is to the position *d*; and this arises because this weight *m* must have less effective weight the closer it is to *d*.
</insert>

<summary>Leonardo examines how the path of a falling object influences its force. He concludes that as a path becomes more slanted (oblique) and less vertical, the object's effective weight and speed decrease, resulting in a weaker impact.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, impact, effective weight, inclined plane, circular motion, gravity, obliquity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of dynamics—the study of bodies in motion. While the previous page examined how the slant of a path affects the impact of a falling weight, this page moves toward defining the proportional laws of motion, force, and the resistance of different media like air and water.</meta>

<term>Equality</term> <note>original: "equalita’"; in this context, it refers to a state of balance or the application of a force equal to the load.</note> will move beyond any opposing part; so that if it possessed its own <term>resistance</term> <note>The internal or external force acting against the movement.</note> within itself, the motion would be as fast as the weight of the <term>mover</term> <note>The active force or weight causing the movement.</note> is relative to the resistance of the object that resists.

<image-desc>A circular diagram featuring a horizontal diameter line. Along the line are labels for points designated by the letters 's', 'n', 'f', 'r', 'm', and 'A'. Small vertical strokes above the line suggest measurements of force or distance relative to a central balance point.</image-desc>

---

If the weight is as 1 and the force is as 1, the motion is as 1. 
If the force is 2 and the weight is 1, the motion is as 2. 
If the force is 1 and the weight is 1/2, the motion is 1, or rather 2. <note>Leonardo is calculating ratios; reducing the weight by half is equivalent to doubling the force.</note> 
If the weight is as 1 and the force is as 1/2, the motion will be <note>The manuscript leaves this unfinished; following his logic, the answer would be 1/2.</note>

---

The time occupied in the motion of every weight will be proportionately less for one than the other.

---

The force that pulls through the air in the same amount of time will be as much faster than that which pulls through the water as the weight of the air is less than that of the water. 
The space occupied will be greater for one than the other in the same proportion as one weight is less than the other.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of mechanics, transitioning from the proportional laws of motion (force and weight) to the geometric behavior of cords or strings under tension. He applies the principles of the balance (equilibrium) to understand how the angle of a cord affects its strength and resistance to weight. The British Museum stamp and mirror-script indicate this is part of his private notebooks, likely the Codex Arundel.</meta>

Let **c** be the center of a circular motion between the ends of a **chord** <note>original: "corda"; in geometry, a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note> **ab**. This chord is pulled by two weights, **p** and **q**, which are equal to each other; and the **perpendicular** <note>A line at a right angle (90°) to the chord.</note> from the center **c** shall be **d**, which falls in the middle of said chord **ab**.

[A geometric diagram of a circle with a vertical chord labeled 'a' at the top and 'b' at the bottom. The center is labeled 'c'. A horizontal line 'cd' meets the chord at its midpoint. Radii extend from the center 'c' to points 'a' and 'b'. A vertical line extends downwards from a point on the circle.]

But if **c** is the center and the chord is **ab**, between the ends of which there is circular motion moved by a weight **p**, which is equally distant from the center of said motion **c**: I say that the perpendicular from the center **c** above said chord is **d**, and that this perpendicular is shorter than any other line drawn from that center to the upper part of said chord. By the law of equilibrium, said weight will keep this chord equally distant from the center **c**, as appears at **f**, which is the center of the chord **ab**. This chord is pulled by two weights, **p** and **q**, which are equal to each other; these weights, by the principles of the balance, will remain on this chord at equal distances from the perpendicular **cd**. This perpendicular is shorter than any other line drawn from the center **c** to the chord **ab**. I say that the perpendicular **cd** is the shortest line that can be drawn from center **c** to chord **ab**; and the further these lines move away from the perpendicular **cd**, the longer they become, and consequently more **oblique** <note>Slanting or at an angle; not Steiner/perpendicular.</note>. Because they are more oblique, they move further away from the perpendicular of the weight, which is **p** when the chord is straight. Therefore, the chord, being oblique, will be weaker in resisting the weight **p**; and the weaker it is, the more it will be bent by that weight, and that weight will be lower than its opposing weight **q**.

---

->Since you are to give an imperfect knowledge of the thing for which it is given,<-
->by mixing other things together with it.<-
<meta>Small textual mark: ANP</meta>

[A geometric diagram showing a circle with a vertical chord ab and center c. Multiple lines are drawn from the center to various points on the chord. Two small circles representing weights p and q are suspended from different points on the chord, illustrating the tension and angle of the string.]

The more the chord **ab** is bent toward the center **c**, the less distant that chord will be from the center. The perpendicular of the center **c** is **cd**; and I say **cd** is shorter than any other line drawn from the center **c** to the chord **ab**. I say that the further these lines move from the perpendicular **cd**, the longer they are and consequently more oblique. Because they are more oblique, their resistance will be less; and because of this lack of resistance, the chord **ab** will be moved more quickly by circular motion than by perpendicular motion. Therefore, said chord is said to be weaker than the perpendicular; thus, the chord is said to be less capable of resisting the weight **p**, and the chord will be less bent by that weight **p**.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of a cord under tension, demonstrating through geometry that as a cord becomes more oblique (angled) relative to its center of motion, its resistance to weight decreases. He uses the concept of the perpendicular as the shortest and strongest point of resistance in a system of equilibrium.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, geometry, chord, perpendicular, equilibrium, weight, circular motion, resistance, physics of strings, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s study of mechanics and the behavior of suspended weights. While the previous page focused on the geometry of chords within a circular motion, here he moves toward the practical and theoretical physics of how weight is distributed along a cord and how weight can be used as a proxy for measuring length and volume. He continues to use the term "center of the world" to refer to the center of gravity or the center of the Earth.</meta>

### Why a cord, however it hangs

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the upper right showing a trapezoid with internal lines connecting vertices (labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd') and points on the sides, illustrating geometric relations of forces and gravity.</image-desc>

Every heavy body <note>original: "graue"; referring to an object with mass/weight.</note> that is suspended comes to rest above the center of the world <note>Leonardo’s term for the center of gravity or the center of the Earth.</note>. And that which is suspended by two ends will have so much less weight at one end than the other, as the one is shorter than the other. This occurs if the cord is of negligible weight. Because if it is of a weight that must be considered relative to the weight suspended upon it, the weight of the cord itself will be added to the weight suspended from it, and then the proportions vary, because the cord will be as much heavier as it is longer. And in whatever way a cord hangs, its weight will be above that center.

<image-desc>A perspective drawing of a truncated pyramid or a geometric solid with horizontal segments, marked with a central vertical line and letters, likely exploring the center of gravity in 3D shapes.</image-desc>

The weight that hangs suspended between the center of the world and its pole of suspension is always proportional to the cord from which it hangs, which is between the pole and the said weight. If one wishes to measure it, it must fall toward the center of the world. And if the cord is longer at one end than the other, the weight will create the same proportion from the pole to the cord as that of the cord from the pole to the center of the world. And if the cord is divided into two proportional parts, the center will be between those parts.

<image-desc>A diagram showing a horizontal beam from which several curved cords hang, all converging on a single central weight. Numerical values like 4, 8, and 10 are annotated along the cords and beam to show how weight is distributed.</image-desc>

->Why the weight does not change regardless of how the cord hangs<-

<margin>
The weight
always willingly 
moves toward the 
center of the 
world; that is 
to say, along 
the central line.
</margin>

<image-desc>A diagram of a simple lever or balance beam 'a-b' with a central support 'n' and a hanging weight '+' at point 'o'.</image-desc>

If you wish to see which part of the cord willingly <note>Leonardo often personifies physical forces, using "willingly" (uolentieri) to describe the natural path or tendency of an object.</note> supports the weight and which does not, place the cord upon a fixed straight line and place the weight in the middle of that cord. You will see that one end pulls more than the other, and you will arrive at the knowledge of the truth. This is because the strain on such cords changes from point to point, so that one is more strained than the other. And if you wish to see if this cord is more strained here than there, you will see by the angles of the cords which are more acute than others.

<image-desc>A composite diagram: On the left, a balance beam with multiple hanging cords forming a parabolic shape under a weight. On the right, a vertical diagram of a plumb line with a weight, labeled with points 'a', 'd', and 'n'.</image-desc>

• If you wish to find the length of a cord by weighing it, find the weight of 10 or more braccia <note>A 'braccio' (plural 'braccia') was a Florentine unit of measurement, literally meaning 'arm,' approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> of that cord. Then, by weighing the entire cord, you will know its length. 
• If 10 braccia weigh 1 pound <note>original: "libra"</note> and the whole cord weighs 10 pounds, then the cord is 100 braccia. And if it weighed 2 pounds, it would be 20 braccia. And if it weighed half a pound, it would be 5 braccia; and thus you will arrive at its full length. You shall do the same to find the weight of 10 braccia of a wall, to see how high the wall is. And likewise, you will see by weighing lead or another metal, of which you weigh a piece one finger in thickness; then by weighing a heavy body of the same metal, you would know its thickness. And if you weighed a piece of tin one square braccio in size, and then weighed another piece of one square braccio that weighed twice as much, you would say this one is double the thickness. And if it weighed triple, it would be of triple thickness. And if it weighed half, it would be of half thickness.

<summary>Leonardo explains how tension and weight are distributed in suspended cords based on their length and angle. He also describes a practical method for determining unknown lengths or thicknesses of materials (like walls or metal plates) by comparing the weight of a known sample to the total weight.</summary>
<keywords>center of gravity, tension, proportions, measurement, braccia, weight distribution, thickness, geometry of forces</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of mechanical advantage and the behavior of ropes and weights. Following the previous page's focus on the geometry of suspension, he now investigates the relationship between the distance a force moves ("the motor") and the distance a weight travels, establishing early principles of work and proportionality in pulley-like systems.</meta>

->of the old man, old age which does not feel its own harm at the end<-

---

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a weight 'm' suspended by a cord 'o-n-p' that passes through a system within a rectangular frame. Points are labeled with letters o, n, p, and m.</image-desc>

As much as weight **m** descends at **p**, so much will the force **o** rise at **n**; and the motion of weight **m** will be equal to that of weight **n**. That which descends is raised by the same amount, and this happens because the power <note>original: "uirtù"; referring here to the physical capacity or potential of the force.</note> of the motor <note>original: "motore"; Leonardo uses this term for the source of motion or the acting force.</note> extends through line **o-n-p**, which is of one and the same length, and such length does not vary by varying the position of that rope.

---

<image-desc>A diagram of a pulley-like system. Multiple lines descend from a horizontal bar, converging towards a central vertical line that terminates in a weight. Labels include a, b, c, d, m, n, p.</image-desc>

From the difference in the proportionality of the motor's motion, there will be a difference in the proportion of its power relative to its weight; and similarly, the difference in the proportionality of the weight compared to its heaviness <note>original: "graueçça"; the inherent gravity or weight of the object.</note> will result in a difference in the proportionality of the force of that motor.

---

<image-desc>A diagram showing a weight 'm' suspended from several ropes that fan out to different points on an arc above. Points are labeled with letters.</image-desc>

See, by the proportion of the motor's force to the weight moved, how much the motion of the motor will be compared to the motion of the weight moved. This will be verified by the line along which the motor moves compared with the line along which the weight moves, because weight **m** cannot descend except along line **c-d**, and the motor **a-b** cannot run except along the circular line **a-b**; it will not be pulled more by one rope than by the other.

---

<image-desc>A diagram of a horizontal beam 'a-g' from which many vertical ropes hang at equal intervals, all supporting a single weight 'm' below.</image-desc>

That rope will have greater force which is pulled by a motor of faster motion. Here it is proven by weight **m**, which, being suspended by the ropes **a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, l**, has the same heaviness in each of these ropes, even though they are of various lengths, since the motor **n** moves along a line of equal length and at an equal velocity.

<summary>This page explores the laws of motion and equilibrium in pulley systems, specifically how the distance traveled by a moving force (the 'motor') relates proportionally to the movement and weight of the load. Leonardo also includes a brief, unrelated philosophical note on the insensitivity of the elderly to their own decline.</summary>

<keywords>mechanics, pulleys, motor, force, weight, proportionality, motion, ropes, gravity, velocity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigation into the laws of equilibrium, moving from the study of ropes and pulleys on the previous page to the mechanics of the sliding weight, or "ring" (anello), on a balance arm. He is exploring how the shifting position of a weight along a lever changes the proportional forces required to maintain balance.</meta>

If the ring moves from **f** to **m**, the weight at the column **m-r** will decrease. It will remain of that weight of the <unclear>r</unclear> of the column <note>original: "con."; likely an abbreviation for "colonna" (column) or "contrappeso" (counterweight).</note> **m-r**, which shall be **m** and **r**. And if the ring moves in the arm of the balance **m-n** to **n**, it will remain of weight at the column **f-f**. If the ring moves in the arm **f** of the balance to **q**, <unclear>n</unclear> of the **f** shall be. 

If the ring moves in the arm **p** to **q**, it will remain of weight in **p**. <unclear>m-m-r</unclear> of the **f** shall be. If the ring moves in the arm **m-n** to **o**, it will <unclear>remain</unclear> of weight at the column **f-f**. <unclear>m-f-a-b</unclear> shall be. And if the ring moves in the arm of that balance **p-r** to **s**, it will remain at the column <note>original: "con."; likely "colonna".</note> **m-r** of the **f** shall be.

---

If it be balanced as **r-m** is, and if from it is taken the whole half **f-m-f-n**, leaving **f-n-a-p** with **f-n-p-q-f-q**, it will be balanced such that **m-f** shall be 2 and **f-n** shall be 1; and the ring in arm **f** shall be 4, and in arm **n** shall be 1; and the **r** shall be 8 <note>Leonardo is calculating the moments of force: Weight multiplied by Distance. Here he posits specific numerical values to demonstrate how the balance is maintained.</note>. Which, being taken from the balance, it will remain in itself in balance by the ring **f-n**.

---

The ring, or rather the ring <note>Leonardo often repeats words as he refines his thought.</note> that moves upon a balance—whether that balance by itself be in equilibrium or not in equilibrium—the ring will move toward that part where there is weight <note>meaning the heavier side.</note>, and it will never stop in any place except <unclear>where</unclear> the part where the ring rests is in balance <note>This describes the principle of a self-centering weight or the seeking of a center of gravity.</note>.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the movement of a sliding weight (ring) on a steelyard or balance, calculating the specific numerical proportions required to maintain equilibrium as the weight shifts. He concludes that a sliding weight will naturally move toward the heavier side of a scale until it reaches the point where the forces are perfectly balanced.</summary>

<meta>The previous page detailed Leonardo’s experiments with weights and rings on balance arms, calculating how shifting a weight's position alters the force required for equilibrium. This page transitions those mechanical principles to fluid dynamics, specifically how the motion of water—which he describes as "rolling"—affects its perceived weight relative to the center of the earth.</meta>

Water that moves atop other water of its same kind is lighter the further it is removed from its center. I am speaking of the center of the **rolling motion** <note>original: "moto rotolante"; Leonardo conceptualizes the movement of waves or surface currents as a series of rolling or rotating cylinders of water.</note> of the surface of the water rolled above said water.

---

Let the center of **d** be the weight of the water that moves above other water, and let the center **n** be the weight of an identical quantity of water that is at rest, and let **m** be the center of the earth.
I say that the water **d** will be lighter than the water **n** by as much as the line **d-m** is longer than the line **n-m**. For it is manifest that the further a weight is removed from the center of its rolling motion, the more lightness it acquires, because the circumference of the circle of that water—

---

How water that moves over other water of its very same kind is lighter the further it is removed from the center of the earth.

---

Let **a** be the center of a rolling mass of water, and let the other water **n** be at rest. I say that water **a** will be lighter than water **n** by as much as the line **a-n** is further removed from the line **m-n**, where **m** shall be the center of the earth; this is because the line **a-n** is the radius of the circumference of the circle of that water rolling above the radius **n-m**, which is the radius of the earth.

<column-break/>

Water that moves shall be so much lighter as it is further removed from its center.

Rolling water does not have the weight of still water, because the weight is resolved into the **circumscribing motion.** <term>circunscriptibile: motion that follows a circular or enclosed path, effectively "spending" its downward force as rotational energy.</term>

<summary>Leonardo argues that moving or "rolling" water possesses less weight than still water. He explains this by comparing the distance of moving water from the center of the earth to that of still water, suggesting that rotational motion offsets gravitational weight.</summary>

If the power be one pound <note>original: "libbra"; a contemporary unit of weight.</note> and the weight be 4 pounds <insert>②</insert>, this will be equal to such a weight at the position **m-p-n**, if the length of the motion **m-n** is 4 times as much as the depth <term>depth</term> <note>original: "bassezza"; literally the 'lowness' or the vertical distance the weight hangs below the horizontal line of the pulleys.</note> of the weight **m** below the cord **s-p-n**. <meta>Continuing from the previous page, Leonardo moves from the general principles of tension in cords to a specific demonstration of complex pulley systems. He is applying his rule that "movement" and "weight" are inversely proportional in mechanical systems to prove how multiple weights can reach equilibrium.</meta>

This other [arrangement] is of such a nature that the weight which is attached to these cords shall be equal to the weight that supports it; and weight **1** shall be equal to **3**, and weight **1** shall also be equal to weight **4**, or rather weight **4** shall be equal to **3**, and thus for every space they shall be equal among themselves.

Every segment of the cord weighs as much as the other, or rather one cord pulls as much as the other, as is demonstrated in weight **1**, weight **4**, and weight **3**, which are equal among themselves because their cords pull through an equal distance and with equal power <term>power</term> <note>original: "potenza"; in Leonardo's mechanics, this refers to the force or effort exerted to achieve balance.</note>.

Each of these two cords supports half <note>original: ".1. 1/2"; Leonardo's notation here likely signifies "1 [part of] 2" or "half," as the logic follows that two cords share the load of one weight.</note> of weight **3**, and each of the supports of said cord similarly supports half, and the supporting weight **3** shall be equal to weight **4** and to weights **2** and **1**; and weight **4** shall also be similar to **2** and **1** and similar to **3**, because the movement of cord **f-g-h** is similar to the movement of weight **3**, and the movement of cord **a-b-c-d** is similar to the movement of weight **4**, and the movement of weights **1** and **2** together is similar to the movement of weight **3** or **4**; from which it follows that weights **3** and **4** shall be equal to **2** and **1**, and because the two cords support two weights, namely **3** and **4**, these cords are loaded with the gravity <note>original: "gravità"; meaning the heaviness or downward force.</note> of said weights, and weight **1** supports half of it and weight **2** supports the other half.

Experience demonstrates and reason confirms that weights **3** and **4** are equal to weights **1** and **2**, because if you lower weight **3** and **4** by a certain distance <term>space</term> <note>original: "spatio"; Leonardo uses this to describe the distance or displacement of a weight.</note>, weights **1** and **2** will rise by the same distance, and by joining weight **3** to **4**, they will be equal to **2** and **1** joined together. Therefore, for the reason recorded, there shall be equal movement and consequently equal weight. And it could also be proven by saying: cord **d-c-b-a** supports weight **4** and gives half of it to pivot <term>pivot</term> <note>original: "polo"; literally "pole," here referring to the point of support or the axis of the pulley wheels.</note> **a** and the other half to pivot **d**; and the same shall be for cord **f-g-h** which supports weight **3** and gives half of it to pivot **h** and the other half to pivot **f**; and because pivot **a** and pivot **h** are loaded upon weight **2**, that weight **2** shall be equal to the two pivots **a-h** which are half of those weights **3** and **4**; and because the other two pivots **d** and **f** are loaded upon weight **1**, that weight **1** shall also be equal to them.

The endpoints **a** [and] **b**, because they move toward **b**, and **c** [and] **d**, because they move toward **d**, so **e**.

If **f**, the shaft <term>shaft</term> <note>original: "albero"; the central rotating axis or axle of a machine.</note> of a mill, were moved by a constant weight of such power <term>power</term> <note>original: "virtù"; in this context, Leonardo uses it to mean the force or energy that creates movement.</note> that it made the mill perform **l** revolutions <note>Leonardo uses the letter "l" as a variable for an unspecified number of turns.</note> in one minute of time, then the motion of this shaft would have **t** power <note>original: "virtù"; here referring to momentum or impetus.</note> that would keep it moving for 30 minutes of time. <meta>This page transitions from the kinematics of motion and motors discussed previously into the realm of optics and physics. Leonardo is now applying geometric principles to understand how the intensity (potency) of light and heat changes based on two variables: the size of the source and its distance from an object.</meta>

To know the proportion of the difference between light and shadow, it is necessary to measure the diameters of the bodies that create said shadow and the diameters of the light.

---

On the difference between doubling the length of a light or doubling its proximity to the object **f f**.

---

Every light or every heat source that is doubled by doubling its length <note>Leonardo refers to "length" here as the physical dimension or size of the light source, such as making a candle flame twice as long.</note> does not double its power; rather, in doubling that length, it doubles that power within the same distance. But if that light remains at its first length and its proximity to the object **h h** is doubled, then its power is doubled at **h h**; and this is proved because the light **f f f** doubled in length occupies the space **h h** as if it were doubled in proximity. 

But such light doubled in length occupies those pyramidal rays <term>pyramidal rays</term> <note>original: "ragi piramidali"; Leonardo conceived of light traveling in "pyramids" or cones from the source to the eye or object.</note>—one shall be doubled in length and the other in proximity. And to double such proximity, it will cover the space **a d** and **h b b**, and to double such length **f f f d** into **f f f f f f**. But having doubled that length of that light **f f f** into **f f f f f f**, that light shall be tripled <note>Leonardo's math here reflects an early attempt to calculate surface area and intensity; while doubling a linear dimension usually quadruples area, his geometric diagram leads him to a "tripled" conclusion here.</note> in the surface of that pyramid of rays, and by doubling the proximity **h h**, it shall be quadrupled. 

So there is a great difference between one doubling of power and the other, because if you double the proximity **h h**, it shall be of quadruple power <note>This is a remarkable early observation of the inverse-square law, suggesting that halving the distance (doubling proximity) increases intensity fourfold.</note>, and if you double the length, it shall be of double power.

The power <term>power</term> <note>original: "potentia"; referring to the intensity or concentrated force of light or heat.</note> of the solar rays is multiplied when the proximity of these rays is doubled through the reflection <term>reflection</term> <note>original: "rinflexione"; Leonardo uses this term to describe both the bouncing of light and the concentration of rays within a specific area.</note> of one ray upon another, in order to place them within the same surface, whether it be heat or light.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how the intensity of light and heat varies, concluding that doubling the proximity of a source to an object is far more effective—quadrupling its power—than simply doubling the size of the source itself.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light intensity, heat, inverse-square law, geometry of rays, pyramidal rays, reflection, proximity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s mechanical observations from the previous page. Whatever motion the counterweight makes that pulls the weight, that same motion, point by point, the weight will have; even though both descend along lines unequally distant from the center of the earth <note>Leonardo is considering the weights relative to the Earth's center to account for gravitational pull, though in practical terms he is discussing linear motion.</note> because what one loses in velocity in that same time, the other acquires. **a d** shall be the motion of the weight; **b e** shall be the motion of the counterweight; **o e** shall be of 1 <term>finger</term> <note>original: "ditta"; a Renaissance unit of measurement approximately equal to the width of a finger.</note>; **f e** shall be of 2 fingers; **h e** shall be of one finger.

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on pulley systems and the equilibrium of weights, Leonardo now transitions into the mathematical laws governing force and motion. He explores how "effect"—what we might today call kinetic energy or work—is not always linearly related to the force or velocity applied, utilizing geometric analogies like the "pyramid of force" to explain these proportions.</meta>

This is proven by the proportionality of the pyramid, which cuts the <unclear>semidiameter</unclear> <note>original: "semidiametro"; the radius of a circle, which Leonardo is relating to the cross-sections of a cone or pyramid.</note> proportionally to their distance from the apex of the said pyramid. Since these circles <insert>①</insert> are similar to that proportionality, it follows that the movement of the force setting such circles in motion will be proportional among themselves.

---

It follows below: if the motion is doubled, the effect is quadrupled; or if it is tripled, it will be 9 times greater. This is because if the motion is 1/2, the effect is 1/4; and if the motion is 1/3, the effect is 1/9; and if the motion is 1/4, the effect is 1/16; and so it continues through its degrees, etc.

And if the force is increased, the motion will be 1/2; and if the force is 1/2, the motion will be 1/4, etc. Because a force of 1/2 cannot put into effect half of the motion, but only 1/4, since the motion resulting from force follows the proportionality of its inverse doubling. <note>Leonardo is observing that doubling a force does not necessarily double the resulting speed in a simple linear fashion, prefiguring modern debates on the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration.</note> The same thing happens with weight; this weight shall be of as much value as its force.

If a man pushes a cart with all his strength through a space of 10 <term>braccia</term> <note>original: "braccia"; a common Italian Renaissance unit of length, literally "arms," measuring approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters depending on the city.</note>, and you give him another companion, it will not be true that they will push it for a space of 20 braccia, nor that it will move with doubled velocity over the said 10 braccia. <note>Leonardo is refuting a common Aristotelian misconception of his time, noting that adding more "movers" does not result in a simple linear increase in distance or speed.</note>

<summary>Leonardo examines the non-linear relationship between force, motion, and "effect," arguing that doubling a force or velocity results in a squared increase in the outcome. He uses the practical example of men pushing a cart to demonstrate that mechanical effects do not increase in simple linear proportions.</summary>
<keywords>proportionality, pyramid of force, dynamics, velocity, braccia, mechanical advantage, Leonardo da Vinci, physics of motion</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>Continuing from the discussion on the relationship between force, motion, and weight, Leonardo shifts his focus from the mechanics of pulleys and carts to the optical effects produced by objects in motion. He applies the same principles of geometric proportionality—previously used to calculate force—to explain how the human eye perceives a wheel spinning at "infinite" speed, moving from physics into the science of perspective and vision.</meta>

If the eye is placed at the center of the circle of a wheel that turns through the air, it will see the entire wheel composed of circles that touch one another, provided this rotation is of infinite velocity. <note>Leonardo is exploring the phenomenon of "persistence of vision," where an object moves so quickly that the eye perceives it as a continuous solid shape rather than a moving part.</note>

---

Every part of the wheel causes a circle, of which it is either the diameter or the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "corda"; a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc.</note>. This circle will maintain a consistent height throughout the portion of the wheel’s circumference visible to the eye. If the wheel turns through the air, it will be observed by the eye between the endpoints of its diameter; the space between one endpoint and the other will appear filled with circles that touch one another across the diameter of the wheel. The circle will appear thicker the closer it is to the eye and thinner the further away it is from the eye.

---

If the wheel is viewed edge-on <note>original: "per taglio"; literally "by the cut," meaning viewing the wheel from its side profile so it appears as a thin line.</note>, it will appear to the sight that the circles all align on a straight line. This line will appear thicker the closer it is to the eye and thinner the further away it is. It will possess varying thicknesses <note>original: "grozze"; referring here to the perceived breadth or thickness of the lines in perspective.</note> that converge toward the same point, depending on whether the edges of the wheel are nearer to or further from the eye.

<image-desc>Red institutional stamp: "B.M." (British Museum) below a crown.</image-desc>
</insert>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, where Leonardo examined the optical perception of rotating wheels and the persistence of vision, he now returns to his foundational studies of mechanics. He transitions from how we see motion to the physical laws governing why and how objects move, specifically focusing on the relationship between weight, balance, and the "center of the world"—the Earth's center of gravity.</meta>

Every weight desires to descend by the shortest path, and counterweights raised out of the water vary their positions somewhat.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a quadrant of a circle. From the center (top left), a line drops vertically to a weight marked with a cross. Another line extends horizontally to the right. An arc connects the two points. A diagonal radius line extends from the center to a pulley on the arc, with a cord and a weight 'n' hanging from it. Another weight 'm' hangs from the horizontal line's end point via a pulley.</image-desc>

Regarding counterweights raised out of the water, their positions vary somewhat because those that are further from the center of the world <note>original: "centro del mondo"; in the science of Leonardo's time, the center of the Earth was considered the universal center toward which all heavy things tend to fall.</note> possess more heaviness than those that are closer. Therefore, that counterweight which descends is always drawing closer to the center of the world and becomes lighter <note>original: "s'alegieriscie"; Leonardo suggests here that as an object nears the Earth's center, its effective "heaviness" changes relative to a counterweight.</note>, and that which rises is always moving further from that same center and becomes heavier. Thus, through this variation of weight, the motion is either accelerated or delayed.

<image-desc>A diagram showing a horizontal lever arm with a weight hanging from the end. To its right, a cord passes over a pulley to another hanging weight, illustrating a mechanical balance system.</image-desc>

---

One weight compared against another does not move except by the shortest path. That path is shortest which departs from the center of the world along the smallest line. Therefore, between two weights that counterbalance each other, the one that is further from the center has more <term>heaviness</term> <note>original: "grauezza"; the physical quality of being heavy or the force exerted by a weight.</note>.

<image-desc>A small diagram of a horizontal line with regular markings (a scale) and a weight hanging from a central point.</image-desc>

---

One weight against another does not move except by the shortest path. Among all the lines that depart from the center of the world, the shortest is that which is closest to the perpendicular; and the perpendicular is the shortest of all paths by which weights can descend.

<image-desc>A sector of a circle representing a swing or arc. Multiple radii are drawn from the center at the top left. The word "opposition" is written inside the arc. A weight hangs vertically from the center point.</image-desc>

---

If one of the counterweights moves only by a short path, it is because the counterweights act as a single weight in motion. The counterweight moves only as much as it descends. The descent of the weight is that portion of the motion which approaches the center of the world. Therefore, the more one weight is heavier than the other due to its distance from the center, the lighter it becomes through the short path of the descent.

If one of the weights descends by a line of less <term>obliquity</term> <note>original: "obbliquità"; refers to the slant or angle of the path of descent compared to a vertical line.</note> than the other, it is heavier than the one descending by a path of greater obliquity. The portion of the motion of the weight that approaches the center of the world is the true descent of that weight.

<image-desc>A narrow triangular diagram representing a vertical centerline and two slightly diverging lines, possibly indicating the swing of a pendulum or the resolution of forces. A weight hangs at the bottom vertex. Letters 'm' and 'n' are at the top endpoints.</image-desc>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mechanics of balance and gravity, proposing that an object's effective weight changes based on its distance from the Earth's center and the angle (obliquity) of its descent. He defines "true descent" as the motion specifically directed toward the center of gravity.</summary>
<keywords>gravity, mechanics, center of the world, counterweights, obliquity, heaviness, perpendicular motion, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, where Leonardo explored the relationship between an object's distance from the "center of the world" (the Earth's center of gravity) and its effective weight, he now applies these mechanical principles to the laws of motion, force, and air resistance. He investigates the dynamics of impact and why speed does not increase in a simple linear relationship with power.</meta>

Experience shows that upon impact <note>original: "percussione"; Leonardo refers to the force exerted when a falling object hits a surface.</note>, a descending weight exerts a force as much greater than its actual weight as its motion is greater in velocity.

---

It is impossible for the motion of an object to double simply by doubling the heaviness of its cause <note>The "cause" refers to the force or weight driving the movement.</note>. It is likewise impossible for the effective weight of an object to double simply by doubling the velocity of its motion.

---

If a slender object moves through the air among other objects of equal weight, it will move faster than the others in proportion to how much smaller its body is compared to its equals. This occurs because the weight of the air that the slender body must divide is less than that which a thick body must divide; therefore, it encounters less resistance. Furthermore, a slender object penetrating the air has to displace a smaller quantity of air than a thick one. For this reason, when moved by the same power <term>motore: the "mover" or source of force, such as a falling weight or a spring</term>, it will achieve a faster motion.

---

Every object weighs as much as it resists its mover, and the mover resists the moved object as much as that mover weighs—or we might say that the mover moves as much weight as its own power, and therefore by doubling the mover, you should double the motion.

---

If the mover were doubled, it would double the motion of the moved object, provided that the resistance of that object did not increase due to the doubled velocity. But because an object moved through the air encounters a fourfold <note>Leonardo correctly observes that air resistance increases disproportionately (quadratically) as speed increases.</note> resistance from the air when its velocity is doubled, it is impossible for a doubled mover to result in doubled motion.

---

### motion and weight

By doubling the power of the mover, the motion of the moved object is not doubled.
If the mover is doubled, it will not double the motion.

In what way can one double the motion of a moved object? 
The motion is doubled by doubling both the mover and its weight; that is, if the mover doubles its weight and its power, it will double the motion of the moved object.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's study of motion and weight return, Leonardo shifts focus here to the static principles of the balance. He explores how the placement of weight—specifically at the fulcrum or "pole"—affects the equilibrium and the total load on the support system.</meta>

If a weight is suspended from the pivot <note>original: "polo"; here referring to the fulcrum or central point of rotation</note> of the balance, such weight will not be felt by the balance, unless that weight is greater than the weight of the balance itself.

If at the end <note>original: "capo"</note> of a balance with two equal arms there is placed a weight of 2 pounds, and at the pivot <note>original: "polo"</note> there is placed a weight of 4 pounds, I say that such a balance will be at the limit of its equality <note>meaning it remains perfectly level</note>, and the addition of the weight placed at the pivot will not be felt by the balance.

If there is a balance with equal arms and a weight is suspended from any part of its length, its weight will always maintain the same gravity <note>effective weight or pressure</note>. Because of this, if weight **m** is suspended from the pivot **a** in the middle of the balance **n m**, and the weight is as much as the balance, I say that such weight will not be felt by the pivot of said balance **n m**, unless the balance itself already had weight. And if in the balance **a b**, the weight **p** is suspended from arm **a c**, and the weight **p** is suspended from arm **c b**, I say that the weight of the balance will not be increased by weight **m**, since that weight **m** is suspended from the center of gravity of said balance, which is the pivot **c**. 

And if weight **m** weighed 2 pounds and the balance weighed just as much, the pivot **c** would support 4 pounds. But if you were to weigh the balance **a b** with another balance above it, **r s**, you would not find that such weight varied by the movement of weight **m** from the pivot **c** toward one or the other end of that balance. This is proven by the sixth proposition of the present work, which says: the weight that hangs from the pivot of the balance does not weigh down <note>original: "aggrava"; meaning to disturb the equilibrium or add "effective" weight to one side</note> that balance. And here weight **m**, by the cords **m o**, hangs from the pivot **c** of the balance **a b**; therefore, such weight **m** does not weigh down the balance **a b**, but indeed hangs from the pivot **c**.

**Technical Vocabulary**
*   **Balance** <note>original: "bilancia"</note>: A weighing scale.
*   **Weight** <note>original: "peso"</note>: The mass or force exerted by an object.
*   **Pivot/Fulcrum** <note>original: "polo"</note>: The central point on which the balance rotates.
*   **Equal arms** <note>original: "bracci equali"</note>: A scale where both sides of the beam are of the same length.
*   **Center of gravity** <note>original: "centro di gravità"</note>: The point at which the weight of the object is balanced in all directions.
*   **Pulleys** <note>original: "pulee, carrucole"</note>: Grooved wheels used with a cord to change the direction of a force.
*   **Gravity** <note>original: "gravità"</note>: In this context, the downward pressure or "heaviness" of an object.
*   **Equality** <note>original: "equalità"</note>: The state of being balanced or in equilibrium.

He uses geometric diagrams to explore how moving a weight along the beam changes the strain on the structure but not the overall balance of the system.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's study of the "polo" (pivot) and how weights are perceived by the balance beam, Leonardo now expands into the fundamental definition of the center of gravity and how it shifts when part of a mass is removed or when weights are distributed along a lever arm.</meta>

### Naturally

The center of gravity of every solid is that point which, if it were suspended from it, would be indifferent <note>original: "indifferēte"; in mechanics, this refers to neutral equilibrium, where an object remains in any position it is placed without rotating.</note> to any orientation of that solid; and such a center is the middle of that solid.

---

If from a quantity <note>original: "quātità"; here meaning the mass or physical magnitude of a body.</note> another quantity is removed, the center of the remaining quantity will be in that part which remains.

---

For every solid, the center of its quantity shall be that point from which the other weights hang.

---

For every solid with equidistant surfaces <note>original: "superfītie equidistāte"; Leonardo is likely referring to regular, symmetrical geometric solids like cubes or spheres.</note>, its center will be in the middle of its length, width, and height.

---

Under equal intervals given on a line equidistant to the line of equal gravity, unequal weights are given in proportion <note>original: "pōderatōe"; referring to the weight's effective force or "ponderosity" relative to its position.</note> to their intervals.

---

<image-desc>A series of marginal diagrams illustrating mechanical principles: 1. A horizontal line intersected by a vertical one. 2. A vertical cord suspending a circular weight. 3. A complex pulley system with weights hanging from a horizontal support. 4. A semicircular arc with weights suspended at three points. 5. A larger arc with weights at the ends and center.</image-desc>

The further a part of a balance is from its center, the heavier the weight placed there will act; and the weights of the quantity on the arm of the balance do not change, because if the length from which it hangs is where one can make the weight hang from above or below in a straight line within which the pivot <note>original: "polo"</note> of such a balance resides, and the weight is in the direct line where the air is divided, where the motion will not be less heavy, where the long line of the suspended weight, where the arm of the balance is a long quantity, where the straightness is the long length of the weight hanging above such length. <note>Leonardo is exploring the "law of the lever," explaining how the effective weight (torque) increases with distance from the fulcrum, even if the physical mass remains constant.</note>

---

For any two weights suspended on a balance, the different intervals between such weights differ among themselves; if they are in their direct line, they are balanced and not varied between them, and one will be as much less than the other as the interval is less.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A diagram of a horizontal balance beam with three weights suspended at equal intervals, labeled with points or letters.</image-desc>

If three equal weights are placed at three equal intervals, the center of their quantity will be in the middle interval; one will be heavier than the others the further it is from its center.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s exploration of geometry and "quadrature"—the mathematical challenge of finding a square with an area equal to that of another shape. He is particularly focused on how a square can be subdivided into smaller, proportional triangles and rectangles.</meta>

# After the squaring of any contemplated part, send the product of the same with a rectangle *ab* and a rectangle *cd*

Let there be a square *abcd*; let its diagonals <note>original: "diametri"</note> be *ac* and *bd*. On the diagonal *ac*, let there be the center *k*. From angle *a* [comes] triangle *n*; from angle *b*, triangle *m*; from angle *c*, triangle *o*; from angle *d*, triangle *v* and triangle *h*. From the center *k* [come] the angles *v*, *o*, *r*, and *m*. Let these be similar because they are formed between equal angles with equal sides between equal parallels, and each shall be the fourth part of the whole, as shown by triangle *abc*, which is half of said square and is divided into two equal parts by the diagonal line *kb*, so each part shall be a fourth.

<image-desc>A square diagram with vertices labeled a, b, c, d. Diagonals ac and bd intersect at a central point k. The square is divided into four equal triangles by these diagonals.</image-desc>

After this operation, many other similar triangles in the same spaces will lead to the same conclusions; however, let the aforementioned operation be performed according to what is necessary for me.

Let the measured part be *abcd*, which is <term>squared</term> <note>Squaring (quadrature) is the geometric process of constructing a square with an area equal to a given shape, like a circle or triangle.</note> by *f*. On the opposite side of said figure, let there be a quadrilateral *fg-hl*, which is seen to be one of the parts of that figure, as well as the triangle *abc* and the other *adc*. And if this is true, angle *a* will be common through diagonal *ac* to triangle *abc*, and will be similar to such triangle *abm*, and similarly to *mbk*, and similarly to *kbh*. Regarding *hl*, the angle of that *abc* will turn out to be similar to *fg*. Furthermore, let the part *fg* be the twentieth part of triangle *abc*; whereby triangles *fg* and *kl* are the same terms, so that *f* is similar to *l*. In this way, *fg* with *hl* will truly be the fourth part of the half of that triangle *abc*. 

But for this to be true, one must give the measure of that part through which the operation of triangles *fg* and *hl* is performed; and *f* shall be 1/2 of *g*, and *h* shall be 1/2 of *l*. Then, *l* shall be double the part *fg*, from which *hl* has come to be 1/2 of the part *fg*. These will come to be, through similar lines, *fg* similar to triangle *k*, *h* similar to *m*, and *l* similar to *o*; and similar rectangles only through *ac* lead to the measurable parts. Let *ac* be divided into 12 parts; let one be *fg*, the other *hl*, and let one be for itself *m*. Let one be the sixth part of the diagonal *ac*. They shall be of the same proportion, and thus there will be 1/2 for one and 1/4 for the other. *k* shall be 1/2 of *n*, and *m* shall be 1/2 of *l*, and *o* shall be 1/4 of *r*.

<meta>This page transitions from Leonardo’s abstract geometric studies of triangles to the practical application of geometry in optics. If the light source is smaller than the illuminated object, the <term>pyramidal shadow</term> <note>Leonardo uses the term "piramidale" to describe a shadow that tapers to a point, like a cone or pyramid.</note> will have its tip pointing into the air. The shadow of the object is composed of infinite acute angles, but this shadow is not seen because the air is filled with light rays and composite shadows, through which the pyramidal shadow of the object is interrupted and destroyed; thus, of such a shadow, only that part remains which is seen upon the wall or another object. This part of the shadow is called the "shadow of the object." This pyramidal shadow will be as long as the lines of the light rays that cross between the light source and the illuminated object:

This pyramid *b d* comes to an end at *o*, which is the vertex of angle *d*. I say that the pyramid *a d c* is composed of light rays and the shadow of the object *a c*. Because this shadow is in the visible air, it is not seen; but only that part is seen which strikes the wall. It is shadow everywhere except where the light penetrates. ->It must first be understood that all the <term>apothem</term> lines <note>original: "cateti"; Leonardo uses "cateto" to describe the perpendicular line from the center of a polygon to the midpoint of its side.</note> that start from the center of the circumference<-
->of that circle and end at the midpoints of the sides of the figures<-

Regarding the <term>isoperimetric</term> <note>From the Greek "isos" (equal) and "perimetron" (measure around); shapes that have the same total perimeter length.</note>: for every isogonal figure <note>A figure with equal angles.</note> of equal angles and sides: if it is equilateral, its proportion to the circle that surrounds it is as the apothem that starts from the center of that circumference and ends in the midpoint of its sides is to the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "semidiametro"</note> of that circle. And if said figure were isogonal with equal angles but not equal sides, the proportion of that figure to the aforementioned circle is as the apothem that starts from the center of the circumference and ends in the midpoint of those sides is to the radius of that circle.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a regular pentagon inscribed within a circle. Lines are drawn from the central point (m) to each vertex (a, b, c, d, e) and to the midpoints of the sides. The diagram illustrates the relationship between the apothem (cateto) and the radius (semidiametro).</image-desc>

Suppose an isoperimetric pentagon is given alongside a given triangle **m o n**, and one wishes to know which of these is larger: to know such a thing, we shall make of that pentagon a triangle which shall be of equal height to that pentagon and with a base equal to the perimeter <note>original: "circuita"</note> of that pentagon; and so that such a thing can be done, we shall make the line **a b** equal to the perimeter of the pentagon and from it we shall make the base of a right-angled triangle, the height of which shall be the apothem that starts from the center of the pentagon and ends in the midpoint of one of its sides; this triangle thus made shall be equal in surface area to that pentagon. Then we shall make from the given triangle **m o n** another right-angled triangle that is equal to it in surface area; and whichever of these two rectangles <note>Leonardo often uses "rectangles" and "right-angled triangles" interchangeably when discussing the calculation of area through base and height.</note> has the greater height, being of equal base, shall be the larger figure.

Suppose an equilateral triangle **a b c** is given and it is isoperimetric with a pentagon: the question is which is the larger figure.

The pentagon is larger than the triangle; this is proven by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], which states that of all isoperimetric surfaces, that which is most similar to the circle is the largest; therefore, as the pentagon is more similar to the circle than the triangle, it remains that the pentagon is larger than the triangle.

<image-desc>A second geometric diagram positioned at the bottom right. It shows a pentagon base with a triangle extending from its vertices, labeled with points a, b, c, d, e, and o. It includes vertical altitude lines (cateti) used to calculate the area transformation described in the text.</image-desc>

And if we wished to know how much one was larger than the other, we would make from them two right-angled triangles of equal bases; and the one which has the greater height shall be the larger figure; and the difference of their heights shall be the difference of their <term>capacity</term> <note>Here, Leonardo uses "capacità" to mean surface area.</note>.

---

<summary>Leonardo explains how to compare the areas of different shapes with the same perimeter, concluding that as a shape becomes more like a circle (such as a pentagon vs. a triangle), its area increases.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo's exploration of the geometry of movement. The operation <note>original: "ovramento" — referring to the active function or working effect of a physical process.</note> they provide of themselves, which [occurs] in the air; and being moved by this motion, no parts remain of this motion, which travels through the air in a straight path and has a straight end. Nor does it lengthen through obliquity <note>original: "obbliquità" — a slant or diagonal direction relative to a straight surface.</note> of motion, but travels by a straight line. This line, by percussion <note>original: "percussione" — the point where a line of motion or light strikes a surface; an impact.</note>, bends into various motions, and such obliquities of motions are created with the straight line of the percussion. This line is divided into three equal parts, and the angles themselves are equal, which are generated between that percussion and the line of straight motion. This motion, of itself, from the side of the percussion of one another, which are generated within the angles; and the angles which emerge from the said percussion are equal to each other, along with the other obliquities of motion born from the aforementioned percussion of the equal line. This line is made by the first percussion through the said obliquity of the first line, with the straight percussion between the said [parts].

## Excellent method for going underwater

### Also for resupplying air to the breathing apparatuses if they were
### underwater, or for resupplying fresh air

<insert>B.M. <note>An abbreviation for the British Museum stamp, "B.M.", marking the collection.</note></insert>

To resupply air to the lungs of divers <term>divers: original "somozzatori", meaning those who submerge themselves</term>; also how by this means one can stay underwater for the space of an hour, staying clinging to the rocks with a container of air <note>original: "bozza d'aria"</note> and 3 glass vessels in which the air has been forced in and sealed. And when there is a need, open them a little at a time so that it is not all consumed at once, so that over time the air is refreshed for the man who breathes within the body of the sphere that he wears on his head. This sphere will have a glass eyepiece <term>eyepiece: original "spiracolo", used here to mean a viewing window</term> so that the man may see where he is going and perform the task for which he went.

---

But above all, do not attempt to go unless during times of calm weather, so that the waves do not carry him onto the rocks and break the glass of the viewing window; and also by this same method, the air could be refreshed many times without having to return to the surface of the water frequently.

---

But this is not of the art of war, but for allowing the rescue of those shipwrecked by storms.

---

Furthermore, I have thought it well to advise the shipwrecked that they should not carry vessels of air, but only fresh air; let the air he breathes be that which is in the helmet <term>helmet: original "palla della testa", or head-sphere</term> and let that be refreshed over time when necessary. But let them not go to the surface, but stay underwater as long as the air lasts; and this is useful only to save lives <note>original: "anime", literally "souls"</note> and not to harm enemies through treachery <note>Leonardo famously refused to reveal his full designs for diving suits and submarines because he feared they would be used for the "evil nature of man" to commit "assassinations at the bottom of the seas" by sinking ships in secret.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s observations of water, shifting from the practicalities of diving and breathing (as discussed on the previous page) to the optical and physical properties of water in motion. # — On the movement of water —

<image-desc>A perspective drawing of a rectangular box or cistern, situated to the right of the first text block. The interior of the box features a slanted rectangular plane and a central vertical partition with a window-like aperture. A thin line with an arrowhead extends from the right side of the device, indicating a directional flow of water or a light ray.</image-desc>

Because water is of one and the same substance <term>substance: original "sustãtia", referring here to its uniform physical nature</term>, it will be of one and the same clarity if it is moved by one and the same motion. But if it is moved by different motions, then it will appear to have different levels of clarity. This diversity is caused by the air positioned between the eye and the moving water, as was stated above. The cause of such darkness arises from the rocks on the bed, which, because of their depth <term>depth: original "bassezza", referring to their position at the bottom</term>, are less luminous than the air above; whereas the movement of the water's surface, by virtue of being in motion, is more
->luminous.<-

If the water of a river is of equal clarity across its entire surface, then it is a sign that throughout its entire course it is of equal velocity. But if it is clearer in one part than in another, then it is a sign that the clearer part is in greater motion than the rest.
->— This rule applies to clear waters —<-

<note>Leonardo is observing that turbulent or fast-moving water catches and reflects more light from the sky, making it appear "clearer" or brighter than still water, which allows the eye to see through to the dark riverbed below.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how the visual clarity and brightness of a river's surface indicate its underlying velocity and the presence of obstacles on the bed.</summary>
<keywords>hydrodynamics, optics, water clarity, river velocity, reflection, light, riverbed</keywords>

--- Page 58 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the physical properties of light and air passing through apertures (Page 24) to the celestial and optical mechanics of reflection. Leonardo applies his observations of light hitting water on Earth to explain the luminosity and physical composition of the moon.</meta>

->**Another proposition of the moon: when it joins with the impact <term>impact: "percussione," a term Leonardo used to describe the physical strike or impulse of light rays or waves against a surface</term> of the solar rays upon the sea waves, etc.**<-

The eye, however, [viewing] the reflection of the moon or of the sun upon the water, never sees more than a single part of that sun for each of the waves; because all the rays of the sun that can be **struck** <note>original: "p(er)cossi"; here meaning the reflection or "bouncing" of light rays</note> by the waves all reach the eye, provided it is focused as a single point.

The other part of the wave sees only a particle of that sun; and for this reason, the expanse of the wave that reflects that sun is entirely **clothed** <note>original: "uestimeto"; Leonardo often uses the metaphor of "clothing" or "vestment" to describe how light covers a surface</note> in small particles of that sun, in such a way that if the waves were small and all of the same proportion, they would all appear to be a single sun.

And this is what confirms that proposition by which it is proven that the moon is dense and spherical, and that its water is moved with a variation of waves, etc. <note>Leonardo theorized that the moon’s "shining" was caused by its surface being covered in water, which reflected sunlight back to Earth much like a choppy sea.</note>

We speak proverbially of every truth. The smaller circle is in a **fourfold proportion** <term>original: "quadruplicata proportione"; a ratio of 4:1, which Leonardo correctly identifies as the relationship between the areas of two circles when one's diameter is double that of the other</term> to the larger circle.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a square with internal divisions and points labeled with letters. A diagonal line runs from the bottom-left corner 'd' to the top-right corner. Points are labeled a, b, c, d, e, f, k, and m. A horizontal line passes through k and m.</image-desc>

Circle **b** is in a fourfold proportion to circle **a**, because the **diameter** <term>original: "diametrale"; the line passing through the center of a circle</term> **k b** is double the diameter **k a**. Therefore, circle **b** is four times the size of circle **a**.

If circle **a** is given, which is half of circle **b**, I say that circle **b** is **doubled** <term>original: "dupplicato"; meaning twice the area</term> in relation to circle **a**, because the side of square **b** is <unclear>equal</unclear> to the side of square **a**. <note>Leonardo is likely exploring the "duplication of the square" theorem, where a square built on the diagonal of another square has exactly twice the area.</note> Thus, just as the square is doubled compared to the other square, so the **inscribed** <term>original: "inscritto"; a shape drawn inside another so that it touches its boundaries but does not cross them</term> circle is doubled compared to the other inscribed circle.
