<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the "vocal organ" and hydraulic analogies of the throat into a technical investigation of mechanics. Having explored the "canals" of the body, Leonardo now applies similar principles of proportion and force to the physics of projectiles, weights, and the mechanical tension of crossbows. This folio represents his attempt to codify the laws of motion into universal "norms."</meta>

<margin>
The proportion of the powers <note>original: "uirtú"; in this context, Leonardo uses it to mean the inherent physical power or kinetic energy of an object.</note> and the motions shall be equal to the proportion of their causes.
</margin>

If a ball were moved by one of those weights which were born of the same force and diminished by the same power <term>potentia: the potential energy or capacity to perform work</term>, and if one of those weighed twice as much as the other, and if it moved through the air, it would not go as far as the lighter one, nor would the lighter one go as far as the medium one.

The motion with which the crossbowman <term>balestrieri: a soldier or operator of a crossbow</term> places the string into the nut <term>nuca: the rotating catch or trigger mechanism of a crossbow that holds the string under tension</term> of the crossbow is equal to the force that the string exerts upon the nut. But if the crossbowman places the string into the nut with less force than that which the string itself exerts upon the nut, it would be impossible for such a string to stay in that nut, unless the nut were so deep that it was the cause of the string not being cast out by its own power.

<margin>
If the motion is equal to the force, the motion of the weights shall be equal to the proportion of the weights.
</margin>

---

-> Sixth norm <-

| K | O | A |
|---|---|---|
| L | P | B |
| M | Q | C |
| N | R | D |

-> Seventh norm <-

| a | o | b |
|---|---|---|
| c | p | d |
| e | q | f |
| g | r | h |

---

If a force were joined with an equal force of weight throughout the arc of the force, it would move as slowly in the first moments as in the middle or the final moments. But because the force that moves the bow, when it is drawn, decreases in its final movements, for this reason the motions at their final ends are thinner <note>original: "rari"; here Leonardo suggests the motion becomes less dense or loses its "impetus" as the tension of the bow is released.</note> than at their beginnings.

If a force were distributed by equal parts of time in a motion, such motion would be equal; that is, it would traverse equal spaces in equal times. But if the force were to decrease by equal parts of time or of space, the motion would decrease in that same proportion that its force decreases.

<summary>Leonardo outlines the proportional laws of motion and force, specifically examining how weight affects projectile distance and how the decreasing tension of a crossbow string dictates the speed of a bolt.</summary>

Just as the weight that is attached to the diameter of the circumference of the wheel cannot move the wheel with more force than its own weight, so likewise it will not move the hub <term>eye of the wheel: the central opening or hub through which the axle passes</term> of the wheel along its central line with any more force than its own weight, [the weight] of its mass <note>original: "mōtagna" (mountain). <meta>This page continues the exploration of mechanical forces, specifically focusing on how the effective weight of a lever changes as it moves through an arc. While the previous page touched upon the motion of wheels and air resistance, this page returns to the fundamental statics of the lever, examining the "accidental" weight change caused by the shifting center of gravity relative to the vertical axis.</meta>

It is impossible that through any movement of the lever, the weight of that lever does not increase or decrease <note>original: "s’auenti o diminuisca." Leonardo is observing that the "effective" weight—the force it exerts around a pivot—changes based on its angle.</note>. This happens because any weight moved away from the **perpendicular** <term>perpendicular: a vertical line passing through the point of support or pivot</term> of its **support** <note>original: "sostentaculo"</note> becomes lighter, and it will be as much lighter as it is further removed from that perpendicular. Therefore, the lever moved **obliquely** comes to be further removed from the perpendicular of its support, whereby it becomes lighter. And the same is true of the weight moved by it, which increases or decreases according to whether it comes to be removed from or brought closer to the perpendicular of its support.

But let us see: if the lever **b s** is of equal thickness in all its length and its center is at point **b**, I say that if it is extended in the line of equality—or truly the horizontal—its weight will be 3 pounds. If you turn it downwards as far as the line **d b**, I say that its weight will be 2 and 2/3 pounds, because its center of gravity, which was at **m**, has come to **n**; this **n** is closer to the perpendicular **b o** by the 3rd part of **b m**.

If we wish to see how much the lever **b s** weighs at point **b**, and its length is 6 and its weight is 3, the half of it [the length] will be the center of its gravity, and this will be 3 <note>The center of gravity of a uniform 6-unit beam is at the 3-unit mark.</note>. Therefore, the space **b 3** will be 3 and the weight will be 3; if you turn this lever to **b d**, **b 3** will be moved 1 unit closer to the perpendicular; therefore, of the 3, 2 will remain, because 3 has become 2. If you turn it downwards by 2/3 of its [arc from] **b s**, then 3 will become 1. And if you turn it downwards through the whole [arc to] **b s** <note>meaning until it is vertical</note>, 0 will remain.

Wherefore you will see that the weight of the lever diminishes by the degrees of distance that its center of gravity makes closer to the perpendicular **b o**. ### On the powers of fixed and movable pulleys

On the powers of fixed and movable pulleys and how the one
must be considered with the weight and the other not, and how that weight

you shall do it in this way: you must see into how many parts the rope

will be sustained by 100 branches of rope, each of which branches shall be
pulled by one pound of force.

He who lowers himself by means of the motion of his base exerts as much force with his weight as the length of the rope that sustains him; and he descends in that same time that the base of the weight moves.

A weight that descends by a certain amount shall be pulled by a pulley <term>taglia</term> <note>A "taglia" refers to a block and tackle or a system of pulleys.</note> as much as the descent of the mover of said pulley .d. .e.

### [f. 44r]

<margin>
It is done with ease <note>original: "fassi con facilita"</note>
</margin>

That motion is performed with ease whose center <note>original: "mezo"; here referring to the axis or center of rotation.</note> does not change in any of its parts; and this shall be through circular motions that revolve upon the poles <note>original: "poli"; Leonardo uses this term to mean the pivots or stationary points of an axis.</note> of such motion. These poles are immovable and in the center of such circular motion, as appears in the instruments for grinding grain, and millstones, and similar motions. Such motions are by nature durable for a long time because they have a great amount of matter <note>original: "gran materia di moto"; likely referring to the momentum or mass of the rotating object.</note> moving around their poles.

The movement of the object shall be equal in every part when the circumference of its circle shall be equal in every part to the movement of its center. If, therefore, the object moves above point **.a.** so that the circumference is equal to the center **.a.**, the motion will be equal. ### [Folio 59 Recto]

<note>Text block at the top regarding the movement of weights.</note>

If you wish for the weight to be moved equally in every part of the motion, it is necessary that its center be moved equally in every part of the motion; and the flight <note>original: "uolare"; used here to describe the path or trajectory</note> of the weight shall be compared to the flight of its center; that is, the circumference of every circle shall be as great as the circumference of the circle of the motion of the center.

<note>Text block in the middle right discussing the proportion of weights relative to the perpendicular line.</note>

The weight removed from its perpendicular line <note>the vertical line of gravity</note> has the same proportion to that weight as the proportion that the center of the removed weight has from its perpendicular to the center of said weight. <note>This is a fundamental principle of the lever and statics: the "potential arm" or horizontal distance from the pivot determines the weight's influence.</note>

<term>weights (pesi)</term>: In Leonardo's mechanics, this refers both to physical objects and the force of gravity acting upon them.
<term>circumference (circuferentia)</term>: The outer boundary or path of a circular motion.
<term>center (cientro)</term>: The axis of rotation or the center of gravity.
<term>proportion (proportione)</term>: The mathematical relationship between two quantities, central to Leonardo's "science of weights."

<summary>Leonardo defines the laws of uniform motion, asserting that the speed of a rotating object depends on the distance between its circumference and its center. He also establishes a proportional relationship between a weight's position relative to its vertical axis and its mechanical effect.</summary>

<keywords>mechanics, circular motion, center of gravity, geometry, proportions, statics, physics, weights</keywords>

### [Folio 44 verso]

In every movement, the line of the descent of the weight is seen to maintain the center of the support of the base where such weight rests. <note>Leonardo is describing the center of gravity; for a body to remain balanced, its vertical weight line must fall within its base of support.</note>

The knot of the neck <note>The Adam's apple or the laryngeal prominence.</note> creates a swelling in front when the man looks up, and creates a swelling behind when the man looks down, and creates a swelling to the right and left when the man turns his head to those sides.

The pit of the chest <note>The suprasternal notch at the base of the throat.</note> lowers when the man raises his arms, and rises when the man lowers them.

<margin>
This shall be divided into 3 parts.
</margin>

Raise the arm from the side and the chest muscle <note>The pectoralis major.</note> creates a swelling, and when the man drops it, it lowers.

The shoulder rises when the man raises his arm, and lowers when the man drops it.

The swelling of the shoulder muscle <note>The deltoid.</note> rises when the man raises his arm, and lowers when the man drops it.

The chest rises when the man breathes in and lowers when the man <unclear>breathes out</unclear>.

The knot of the arm <note>The elbow or perhaps the joint of the humerus.</note> rises when the man bends his arm, and lowers when the man extends it.

The muscle of the arm <note>The biceps.</note> rises when the man bends his arm, and lowers when the man extends it.

The knot of the hand <note>The wrist joint.</note> rises when the man bends the hand, and lowers when the man extends it.

The muscle of the hand <note>Likely the muscles of the forearm or the thenar eminence of the palm.</note> rises when the man bends the hand, and lowers when the man extends it.

-> The Proportion of the Head <- <note>original: "laraione dilla testa"; 'ragione' here refers to the mathematical ratio or 'ratio' of proportions.</note>

From the nape to the hairline, its diameter shall be 1/12 times. <note>Leonardo is using a fractional system where parts of the body are measured against the total height or other units.</note>

# Folio 39 verso

(○) The straight motion of a weight will be greater the further it is from the **center of the earth** <note>Leonardo is exploring the concept of gravitational acceleration and the path of falling objects</note>; the heavier it is; the more it overcomes the **dense air**; and the more it is of a straight and dense body, the faster it will be in its straight motion.

Because the earth will not always be of one and the same size <note>original: "grādeza"</note>; for it would not be necessary, when water consumes its surface with its currents, that the storm-water <note>original: "tēpestiua"</note> within should fill the voids below. For if the earth were not covered and dense inside, it would not fill the voids with air; it could not draw the water into its internal fillings. Because if the descending water did not displace the air, it would not fill [the void]. Because if the air were not of a **liquid nature** <note>Leonardo identifies air as a fluid, similar to water, which must flow to fill a vacuum</note> to fill the voids of the dense water, it could not come beneath the water inside its fillings.

Because dense water, which fills the vacuums of the dense air, will not fill those of the void while it descends through its courses, except by means of the air that will be driven out of the dense void. Therefore, the water could not descend if the air did not yield to it. And as the air yields, it will be rising through the courses not filled by the water, and will be the filler of the voids that the water, in leaving, will have left behind. Or if the air were not of a liquid nature, the water could not descend, for it could not fill the voids left by the water. Therefore, **air is of a liquid nature**.

(○) Why water of the same quantity will be faster in greater sloping courses than in its lesser sloping ones.

Greater will be the greater slope than the lesser over straight, drawn courses; because water comes from high to low, and it will be as fast as the slope is [steep], which velocity is lacking in the [lesser] courses.

(○) Or what would become of a **ball of lead** <note>original: "palla di piōbo"</note> which should fall toward the center of the earth, if it traveled through a void; where would the air be greater than its velocity?

Greater will be the greater velocity of the ball from high to low than in the middle of the void of the earth.

Greater will be its velocity when it is further from the center of the earth, and lesser when it is nearer. <note>Leonardo's theory here contrasts with modern Newtonian physics; he is grappling with how "weight" behaves as it approaches the center of gravity</note>

Greater will be its velocity when there is greater velocity in the middle courses.

<margin>so much</margin>

# 57

As has been said in the chapter above, every opaque body <note>original: "chorpo onbroso," literally "shadowy body," referring to an object that blocks light</note> appears larger than its true size for the reason already stated, and the proof is this:

<note>Small circular diagram with tangent lines on the left</note> Let the opaque body be *a.b.* and let the eye be *m.* I say that *f.g.h.i.k.l.m.n.o.* <note>Small circular diagram with tangent lines on the right</note> are the various positions of the eye. Now I say that when the eye is at *m.*, the part *f.* of the eye will see the part of the opaque body *b.*, and the part *g.* will see the part *a.* of the same body; therefore the eye at *m.* will see the entire face of the opaque body *a.b.* under the angle *f.m.g.* And if the eye is at *p.*, it will see the face *a.b.* under the angle *h.p.i.*, which is more acute <note><term>acute angle</term>: an angle less than 90 degrees; here Leonardo uses it to show how the visual perspective narrows as the observer moves further away</note> than the angle *f.m.g.*, as the sixth [proposition] of this book proves; and thus the eye will go on diminishing until the eye is at point *d.*, where nothing is seen except point *c.*

<note>Small circular diagram with rays crossing behind it</note>

I say, as has been said above, that shadow is divided into two types: one shall be the **original shadow** <note><term>original shadow</term>: known today as "attached shadow," the darkness on the object itself</note> and the other shall be the **derivative shadow** <note><term>derivative shadow</term>: known today as "cast shadow," the darkness projected onto another surface</note>.
The original shadow shall be that which is attached to the opaque body.
The derivative shadow shall be that which separates itself from the opaque body.
And they shall be of different shapes from one another and of various proportions.
Let the luminous body <note>the light source</note> be *d.* and the opaque body be *a.b.o.c.* I say that the original shadow shall be *a.b.c.* and the derivative shadow shall be *e.f.g.h.*
And that the original shadow *a.b.c.* shall be of a pyramidal shape, and its base shall be the face of the opaque body *a.b.*, and its point shall be *c.*, which is the center <note>original: "cienitro," likely referring to the focal point or center of radiation</note> of the luminous body. And the derivative shadow shall be of an inverted pyramidal shape, and its base shall be *f.g.h.*, and it shall be infinite, and its point shall be in the same center *c.*
Because just as the luminous rays are a pyramid with the luminous body as the base and a point as the tip, the shadow shall be a pyramid with half the shape of the opaque body as the base, and for its tip, the shadow shall be infinite.

<margin>
The original shadow shall be of a pyramidal shape and its base shall be half the circumference of the opaque body.
</margin>

# Folio 53

That which is further from the eye, *m*, shall be the darkest. <note>original: "quella fia più schura . che fia più lontana dal ochio . m ." Leonardo is observing that as a shadow recedes from the observer's eye toward a specific point, its perceived intensity or geometric concentration changes.</note>

<note>Geometric diagram showing a circular body with projected lines of light and shadow. This is a study of the <term>derivative shadow</term> (the cone of shadow extending from an object) and perspective.</note>

In the conjunction of two shadows
which depart from the <term>derivative shadow</term> <note>The "derivative shadow" is the portion of the shadow that exists in the air between the object and the surface it falls upon.</note> one from the other,

as would be *a*, *n*, *m*, *o*, *p*, and the shadows shall be *n*, *p*,

Just as the point is the beginning of the line, and the line is the beginning of the surface, and the surface is the beginning of the body, so the instant is the beginning of time, and time is the beginning of motion.

And the proportion that the point has with the line, such is that of the instant with time; and such is that of time with motion; and such is that of motion with the space which must be measured by its motion.

If I say that motion is the proportionality of moved bodies with the space of their courses and with the times of the motion.

Furthermore, motion is that thing which destroys the body; and space shall be made by the moved line, and the surface by the line, and the body by the surface, and time by motion, and motion by the motive force.

The proportion that the force has with its mover, such is that of the motion with its force.

If I say that motion is the proportionality of moved bodies with the space of their courses and with the times.

Motion shall be the proportionality of the force with its mover, and such shall be the space with the instant of motion, and such the time with the continuity of the motive force.

The instant of motion shall be the proportionality of space with time, and such shall be the time with the force, and such the force with the continuity of its mover.

That proportion shall be of the force with the space as is that of the time with its mover, and such shall be the instant of motion with the continuity of its force.

If the mover <note>term: mover (motore) - the force or source of energy initiating the movement.</note> moves a weight through a certain space in a certain time, that same mover will move half of said weight in that same time through double the space; and the same mover will move double said weight in that same time through half of said space. And that same mover will move the whole weight in half of said time through half of said space. And without doubt this shall be the truth, because this mover has the same proportion <note>term: proportion (proportione) - the mathematical ratio between physical quantities.</note> with the weight it moves as half the mover has with half the weight; and just as the whole mover has the same proportion with half the weight as the double mover has with the whole weight, for this reason, it moves through double the space in the same time. 

But because a weight gathers force in its motion through any space, and its velocity increases, for this reason, the motion of the weight is worth as much as its weight multiplied by its velocity; and such shall be the percussion <note>term: percussion (percussione) - the force of impact or the "strike" of a moving body against another.</note> of the weight in whatever place it strikes. And you will produce that same percussion if you move the weight by the velocity; yet it would not be a similar percussion if you moved the velocity without the weight, because velocity always wishes to be in a subject <note>term: subject (suggetto) - the physical matter or body that possesses the quality of motion.</note> that moves, and without that subject, it has no existence at all. 

Wherefore we can conclude that the weight in motion shall be equal to the percussion that said weight will make in whatever place it strikes. Thus, if the space **m n** is double the space **o n**, the percussion of a weight at **m** will be as much as that of double the weight at **n**, if the velocity be equal; and if it be not equal, then it is necessary to multiply the weight by the velocity, and the sum that results from it shall be the true power <note>original: "uirtù" - meaning the physical potency or energy.</note> of the percussion. If **n b** be the space that consumes the weight **n a n c** in velocity in the compass, it shall be as...

### f. 65v (Left Page)

->percussion<-
<note>original: "perchussione". In Leonardo's physics, this refers to the force of impact or the momentum of a moving body.</note>

If the water which is divided into equal parts through opposite channels is then collected
into a single channel, that channel shall be of double the capacity of either of the
first ones, and its velocity shall be equal to that of the first channels.

The reason for this is that the quantity of motion is composed
of two things: namely, the velocity and the quantity of the motion,
or rather the body moved. And if the velocity is equal in both
channels, it is necessary that the body of the united motion be equal
to the body of the divided motions. And because the velocity is the same in each
and in the united motion, its quantity will be collected in one and the same
space, which will be as much more capacious as is the union of
its bodies of divided motions. The proof of this will be manifest
by making the specific figure which is below: if channel *a b* and channel
*c d* are of equal force and velocity in each of their parts, and if
these are joined into a single channel *e f* which is of double the
capacity of *a b* or *c d*, I say that the velocity of the flow
of channel *e f* will be equal to the velocity of the flow of channel *a b*;
and similarly, the velocity of channel *e f* will be equal to that of channels *a b* and *c d*.

<margin>
The water that
moves through the
channels must
be moved
by equal weights if it
is to have equal
velocity.
</margin>

<note>Diagram of a balance lever with a circular track and weights, labeled with letters a, b, c, d, e, f, m.</note>

by so much will its percussion be of lesser force...

### f. 66r (Right Page)

Furthermore, it will be proved that whatever arc is passed by the
pendulum *b m*, it will be measured by a time equal to the motion of
its chords *m d* and similarly *m f* and *f m*.
<note>Leonardo is observing the <term>isochronism</term> of the pendulum—the idea that the time it takes to swing remains constant regardless of the width of the arc.</note>

The counterweight *m* weighs as much in position *m* as in *f*, because
in every place the arc of the outward journey will be equal to the arc of the return
until such time as the motion ceases. And if *m* were heavier in *f* than in *m*,
it would not return to *m*, but rather would reach higher than *m*,
which is impossible. But it will be proved in *m d* or *d f*
that *f* is heavier than *m*, and *d* heavier than *f* in the chords;
but the arcs are all of one and the same gravity.

There will not be *x d*, hence there will not be *d o*, but there will be *r d m d*,
and *r d* will be half of the weight *m d*, because if *m d* weighs 1,
then *r d* will be half, because the space *d o* is half
of the space *m o*. Wherefore the *m o* of *m o* will be force, and therefore
half of the weight *m d* will be half of the force. This *m o* will be
followed by *r d*, and *d o* will be followed by *m o*, wherefore *m o*
will be force and *o d* will be *m d*, and therefore *r d* will be to *o d*. Wherefore the
resistance of the axis will be in *f d o d*; of this *r d* will be
followed by half of the weight *m d* in *o d*, wherefore the arc *f d* will be
of weight *f d* and will be followed by *r d*, wherefore *o d* will be of weight
*m d* of that half, and *o d* will be followed by *r d* of that half of the weight.
<note>This dense passage uses geometric points to calculate the "effective weight" or lateral force of a pendulum at different points of its swing.</note>

->because<-
If the percussion is made
along an oblique line,
the line of the weights of the percussion
will also be oblique.

Regarding the balance with equal arms, it is asked why,
being loaded with equal weights, one of them does not
descend before the other, since they are of an equal nature;
but if one of them is heavier than the other, the cause
is manifest as to why the prevailing weight should sink.

Regarding the balance with unequal arms, if one part
of it is longer than the other, why, when loaded with
equal weights, is the longer part more powerful?
The answer is this: that the longer part,
in descending, travels through a longer motion than
the shorter part; wherefore, by the ninth [proposition] of this [treatise],
it is made manifest that the motion which is faster
is of more force; and that motion will be faster which
covers a greater distance in the same time; wherefore the
longer part of the balance will be faster because
in one and the same time it describes a longer circle.
<note>Leonardo correctly identifies that the "power" of a lever is related to the velocity/distance traveled by the ends, a precursor to the principle of virtual work.</note>

<note>Diagram of a T-shaped balance with horizontal beam 'm-n'.</note>

Why does the weight on an arm of equal arms
depart from the position of its equality?
Because in descending it acquires force
according to the tenth [proposition] of this [treatise].

<note>Diagram of a T-shaped balance with two weights hanging from the ends of the beam.</note>

If the weight is equal to the weight on one side
of equal arms, why does such a weight move toward
the side where it is inclined? Because every weight
tends toward its union with the earth by the
shortest way; and such a way will be that by which it
is moved least by the other weight with which it is
weighed.
<note>Leonardo uses the Aristotelian concept of "union with the earth" to explain gravity's pull toward the center of the world.</note>

<note>Diagram of a horizontal balance beam with two weights 'p' and 'q' at the ends.</note>

Why should the weight that is above the center of equal arms,
being of equal weight, be of more force in the direction of
its declination than the other which does not
move? Because one is faster than the other.

## [Folio 75v]

Therefore, once the shaft <note>original: "albero," literally "tree," used here for a central axle or pump rod</note> is pushed, a vacuum of water will follow.
If, then, the shaft of the pump <note>original: "timone," literally "rudder," but here referring to the handle or steering mechanism of a pump</note> is filled with water, and this pump handle is higher than the water in the channel so that the water comes to enter the void of said handle, then the water of the channel will fill that handle just as water fills a pump <note>original: "bomba," a suction pump</note>. And the effect of the weight of the water will be as great as the depth of the channel combined with its width. And if the channel is smaller, the force of the shaft of that pump will be less, so that if the shaft is as long as the depth [of the water], there will be as much force as the weight <note>original: "scotto," literally a "tax" or "bill," used here to mean the burden or weight</note> of the void of that shaft. If it is empty of water and air, there will be as much [force] from the water at the bottom as there is from the air in the void, so that the water comes to fill that void <unclear>filled</unclear> with air.

<margin>
[Series of diagrams showing forces on vertical lines, balances, and pulleys]
</margin>

By the logic of linear motions, as various motions are made in the filling of water channels, so that the water comes to fill that void...

By the logic that water is heavier than air, and as the water descends through one channel, the air descends through the other channel, and both fill the void of that shaft...

<note>The following diagrams illustrate the fundamental principles of Renaissance engineering: the transmission of force and the conversion of motion.</note>

### Studies of Mechanical Advantage

<note>Top Diagrams: Balanced Levers</note>
These sketches demonstrate the equilibrium of horizontal levers. Leonardo is calculating how weights of different sizes can balance one another by varying their distance from the central pivot point.

<note>Middle Diagrams: Concentric Pulleys</note>
These systems show concentric wheels of different diameters. By wrapping cords around wheels of different sizes, a smaller force can lift a much heavier weight, albeit over a shorter distance—a concept known today as mechanical advantage.

<note>Lower Middle: Rack-and-Pinion Systems</note>
These diagrams show a central circular gear <term>pinion<gloss>a small cogwheel</gloss></term> positioned between two vertical toothed tracks <term>racks<gloss>a linear bar with teeth</gloss></term>. This mechanism is used to convert the circular rotation of a handle or wheel into the straight-line vertical movement of a load.

<note>Bottom: Weight-Drop Configurations</note>
Simple studies showing how a falling weight can be used as a "prime mover" to trigger or power a mechanical sequence.

<summary>This page features a collection of mechanical diagrams where Leonardo analyzes the efficiency of levers, pulleys, and rack-and-pinion gears for the transmission of force. It includes a philosophical note on the value of understanding such principles.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, levers, pulleys, rack-and-pinion, gears, engineering, Codex Arundel, mechanical advantage</keywords>

# Folio 81r

<margin>
<unclear>of water</unclear> which does not move by itself if it is not moved
<insert>for the same reason</insert>

I say that whatever force moves a weight of one pound <note>original: "libra," a standard unit of weight</note> through the distance of one arm's length <note>original: "braccio," a common Florentine measure of length, roughly 23 inches</note> will move a weight of half a pound through the distance of two arm's lengths; and it would be the same if you move half a pound through the distance of two arm's lengths, it will move the pound through one arm's length. I say likewise that whatever force moves half a pound through the distance of one arm's length will move the pound through half an arm's length. For which reason, that force which moves half a pound in a motion of half an arm's length shall be equal to the force that moves one pound in a motion of a quarter of an arm's length. And thus you shall go on multiplying or diminishing the powers <note>original: "potenzie," referring to the mechanical advantage or potential force</note> with the motions; by which proportions it shall be concluded that the force which moves the pound through one arm's length moves ten pounds through a tenth of an arm's length.

Because as the percussion <note>The impact or striking force</note> will depart from a sudden motion, so the reasoning <note>original: "raggion," referring here to the mathematical principle or logic governing the movement</note> shall be the same, and it shall be through the angles that arise from said departure.

If the smoke <note>original: "fumo," referring to the expanding gases of gunpowder</note> were applied to the underside of the artillery ball, and if said ball departed with the greatest fury from every side, and the percussion were always of equal force, then said ball would be carried along a straight line. It follows that if there is air between the water and the vessel where such water turns, it is necessary that such water stays still. How the motion of a thrown thing shall be.

<note>Geometric diagram showing a horizontal axis labeled 'm' and 'd', with a vertical axis and a trajectory line.</note>

The ball thrown through the air shall have equal angles at the point of equality of the powers <note>original: "potenze," referring to the forces of impulse and gravity</note> that move it.

If the ball be thrown through the air so that it moves along a line which recovers its equality of angle with the line equidistant to the horizon: let .a. be the ball moved by accidental motion <term>accidental motion: the temporary force or impulse given to an object by a thrower, as opposed to its "natural" downward motion</term> and let .n. be the horizon and let .m. .d. be the line of equidistance. This ball shall be at .s. in the middle of its motion, at which point the accidental motion shall be terminated; and at this point, the angle .a. .s. .n. shall be equal to the angle .s. .n. .d. And because the ball .a., having reached .s., is at the end of its accidental power, it shall be ruled by no other force than its weight <note>original: "ponderosità"</note> which throws it along a perpendicular line toward the center of the world. And because this ball still has within itself a part of the accidental motion, the ball does not fall along the line .s. .n., but falls along the oblique line .s. .d. and falls at .d.; and the angle .a. .s. .n. shall be equal to the angle .n. .s. .d. And of this, proof is made by the reasoning of a ball bounced on the surface of water, which in striking makes equal angles.

<note>Large circular diagram exploring angles of "local motion" with multiple radiating lines and chords.</note>

Of local motion
and how the ball shall have equal angles.

If the ball be moved along a straight line and it strikes obliquely upon a plane, the angle of its percussion shall be equal to the angle of its bounce <note>original: "balzazione"</note>; and if this ball strikes the plane obliquely along a curved line, its bounce shall be along a curved line, and the angle of the curvature shall be equal to the angle of the curvature of the bounce. And this arises because the curved line of the ball is composed of two motions, that is, of accidental motion and of natural motion <term>natural motion: the inherent tendency of heavy objects to fall toward the center of the Earth</term>; and at the point of the bounce, the accidental motion is in the middle of its declination and the natural motion is in the beginning of its increase, whence it is that the curved line of the bounce is similar to the curved line of the accidental motion.

# [Folio 190 recto]

Of the motion of a ball thrown through the air.

Let .a. be the ball which shall be thrown through the air and let .c. .b. be the horizon. I say that such a thrown ball will describe a line which shall have equal angles at the middle point of that line; and let .s. be the middle of that line: the angle .a. .s. .n. shall be equal to the angle .n. .s. .d. And this arises because the ball .a., having reached .s., has finished its accidental power, and not being aided by natural motion it would fall along the line .s. .n.; but because there remains in this ball a part of the accidental motion, it moves along the line .s. .d. and falls at .d., and the angle .a. .s. .n. shall be equal to the angle .n. .s. .d.

<note>Column of semicircular diagrams on the right, showing 90-degree and 45-degree angles.</note>

Every thing that is thrown through the air will never move in a straight line, because its weight pulls it toward the center of the world and its accidental power throws it in a straight line; and from these two powers there arises a mixed line, which shall be straighter the more the accidental power is greater than the weight, and shall be more curved the more the weight is greater than the accidental power.

Let .a. .b. be the line of the ball moved by accidental motion and let .b. .c. be the line of the ball moved by natural motion. I say that the ball .a. will not move along the line .a. .b. nor along the line .b. .c., but will move along the line .a. .c., which shall be curved; and it shall be more curved the more the accidental power is less than the weight.

Let the accidental power be directed by the motion of the ball thrown through the air and let it be .a. .b. I say that such power shall always be decreasing and the weight shall always be increasing, whence it is that the curved line .a. .c. shall always be more curved toward the end of its motion than at the beginning.

-> <-

If .a. .b. be the line of accidental motion and .b. .c. be the line of natural motion, the ball .a. will move along the curved line .a. .c., and it shall be more curved the more .b. .c. is greater than .a. .b.

He also briefly notes the optical phenomenon of sunlight forming a circular image after passing through a rectangular aperture.</summary>

And because the ball .a., having reached .s., is at the end of its accidental power, it shall be ruled by no other force than its weight <note>original: "ponderosità"</note> which pulls it along a perpendicular line toward the center of the world. ### Notes on the drawings and annotations

<note>Top right: An optical diagram illustrating the convergence of rays toward a focal point. Leonardo labels the point of convergence as "eye" (ochio) on the left. The vertical plane through which the rays pass is labeled as "glass" (vetro). The space above is labeled as "air" (aria).</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues against the 'extramission' theory of vision, asserting that eyes do not emit rays but rather receive light like a mirror. He reasons that if the eye emitted rays, they would have to travel impossibly fast to cover great distances in an instant.</summary>

# On the ball

-> regarding the ball <-

If the air were of uniform density ahead of the ball, the ratio of the movement would be of such a sum that the parts <term>members; original: "mēbri"</term> of that air, maintained by the local motions of said air, would always be equal in ratio to the distance from the ball. But because the air moved by the ball goes on condensing in front of that ball and rarefying behind that ball, the ratio of the motion of that air does not remain equal <unclear>in such</unclear> density, but goes on varying, as is seen in this <note>pointing to the first diagram</note> of the ball . a . which, by the preceding arguments, sends its air ahead of itself as in d . e . f . and moving its own parts so much more slowly as they are more rare and as they are further from the mover; and as the said parts are thinner, they offer so much less resistance to the motion that pushes them, and they maintain the motion so much more insofar as <unclear>one</unclear> of these parts leans upon the other because of its density.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the movement of a ball through air, Leonardo now transitions from the physics of projectiles to the optics of light and atmosphere, specifically how distance and the medium of air affect the perception of flames and colors.</meta>

# Figure

The air that is near a flame will be so much less luminous the closer it is to the eye of the viewer.
The truth of this is proved by the 4th [proposition] of this [treatise], which says: that part of a luminous object will be less seen which is seen under a smaller angle; because the air that is interposed between the eye and the light is dark.

Of two flames of equal brightness, that one will appear darker which is interposed between the eye and the light of the sun. To see the truth of this, place a lit candle near the eye so that you see the light of the sun through that flame, and you will see that flame to be as dark as smoke; and this arises because between the eye and the candle there is not a single atom of light, while between the candle and the sun all the air is luminous and full of solar rays; and this causes the flame to appear dark. Between two lights of varying power, the weak light will be more seen under a smaller angle, and that one will be of lesser splendor which is seen under a larger angle. This happens because the more powerful light is closer to the weak one, and that weak one will be more seen under a smaller angle because the air which is between the eye and the weak light is closer to the powerful one than is the air which is between the eye and the powerful light, which is seen under a larger angle.

Among things of equal whiteness placed at varying distances from the eye, that which is more remote will be closer to the color of the air that surrounds them. The reason is because, being seen through the medium of the air which is of an azure <note>sky blue; original: "azureo"</note> color, this air interposes itself between the eye and the white object; and being of an azure color, it tints the whiteness of the seen object with such a color; and the more remote such an object is, the more air is interposed between the eye and that object, and consequently it will be more bluish <term>azurreggiante; the effect of atmospheric perspective where distant objects appear blue</term>.

<margin>
Why the air that surrounds the light appears more luminous near the light than far away: it is proved by the 4th [proposition] which says that the part of the luminous body that is seen under a larger angle will be brighter; and the air that surrounds the light is luminous, and that part of said air which is closer to the luminous body will be seen under a larger angle than that which is remote from it; therefore it will be brighter.
</margin>

<margin>
Why the light that moves away from the eye appears to diminish: it is seen by the seventh [proposition] of this [treatise] which says that the luminous body appears so much smaller the more distant it is.
</margin>

<margin>
It is proved how things that move away from the eye lose their shape and make of every light a spherical body, and of every long light a round part.
</margin>

<note>Two diagrams at the bottom illustrate the optics of viewing a light source through an aperture</note>

If the eye is placed at .d. and sees the light .a.b. through the aperture <term>spirachulo; a small hole or vent</term> .c., it will see as much of that light as is comprised by the lines of its vision, which, if they pass through the aperture .c., will end at .a.b.; and you will see the part .a.b. of the light, which will be so much smaller as the aperture is closer to the eye.

The air that is between the light and the eye .d. is so much more luminous the closer it is to the luminous body .a.b.; from which it follows that the closer the air is to the flame, the more luminous it will be, and consequently that part of the flame which is seen through much luminous air will be less visible.

<summary>Leonardo explores the optical effects of the atmosphere on light and color, explaining why distant white objects appear blue and how the brightness of a flame's surrounding air changes based on the viewer's perspective.</summary>

<note>Technical Vocabulary:
- Eye (ochio): The organ of sight, often treated by Leonardo as a geometric point or a sphere.
- Concave mirror (spechio concavo): A curved reflective surface that converges light.
- Visual [ray] (uisuale): The imaginary line along which sight travels.
- Angle (angulo): The angle of incidence or reflection, essential for Leonardo's geometric optics.
- Sphere (spera): The geometric form upon which the mirror's curvature is based.
- Visual ray (raggio uisuale): The beam of light or "species" entering the eye.
- Extremities (ostremis): The outer edges or limits of a surface or ray.</note>

### [Left Folio]

<note>The diagram at the top depicts a large circle on the right (labeled 'sun') projecting light rays toward a smaller sphere on the left. The rays converge and outline the shaded regions.</note>

-> Parallel rays of the sun <-

Even though the density of the sphere is bounded by its circumference, nonetheless, when it is illuminated by the sun, it produces a shadow from a great distance in a pyramidal shape. This pyramid of shadow is larger the smaller the light source is compared to the sphere, and it is smaller the larger the light source is compared to said sphere. And when they are equal, of one and the same magnitude, the shadow will be of one and the same thickness; this shadow will extend to infinity with the same thickness as the diameter of that sphere.

The further the eye is from the illuminated body, the smaller the part of it it will see; and the closer it is, the larger the part it will see, as is demonstrated here below.

If the light source is equal to the sphere, its shadow will be of the same thickness for an infinite length; but the shadow will be pyramidal <note>Leonardo uses "pyramidal" to describe a cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point.</note> if the light source is larger than the object, and the pyramid of the shadow will end in a short space.

The closer the illuminated eye <note>Leonardo often uses "eye" and "observer" interchangeably with the point of perspective.</note> is to the sphere, the smaller the part of it it will see. The further the eye is from the illuminated body, the less it will see of the illuminated part of that body.

---

### [Right Folio]

Let it be proved how the shadow of the sphere illuminated by the sun is of the same thickness for whatever length it extends. And this would not be possible if the eye did not see more than half of that sphere.

<margin>
<note>Small diagram on the right margin illustrating a light source and a ray angle.</note>
sun
</margin>

But concerning the same sphere, how is it that the shadow of the spherical body—being of the same magnitude as the light source—extends for its length with the same thickness unto infinity, given that one cannot see more than half of the other?

From the same body illuminated by the sun, a shadow is produced which throughout its entire length is of the same thickness; and this happens because the sun is so distant from the earth that its rays are almost, at their ends, parallel to one another.

That part of the shadow will be darkest which is closest to the body that produces it; and this happens because the light of the surrounding air penetrates less into the shadow near the body than into the shadow far from it.

The shadows of bodies will be more distant from their bodies the lower the light source is, and they will be shorter the higher the light source is.

Of local motion <term>local motion: the movement of a body from one place to another</term> that results in impact, and if impact

### [Left Folio - f. 120v]

<note>Leonardo discusses the relationship between force, movement, and pulleys/scales.</note>

Whatever the proportion of the motion of the force that moves the weight is to the motion
of said weight, such will be the proportion of the weight to said force.
This shall be proven with balances <term>bilichi: scales or balances</term> and with the circumference of pulleys.

Every line that, starting from the center of a ball, is straight and passes through the
base of a weight placed upon that ball, shall be that line which
supports said weight, which shall be the center of the base of that weight
and shall be perpendicular to the center of the earth; and if that weight is
placed in such a position that said line does not pass through the middle
of its base, that weight will move until it is
placed in a position where said line passes through the middle of that base.
**A** is the mark.

The proportion of the motion of the rope to the motion of the weight that is
pulled by it, shall be the same as that of the weight to the force that pulls said weight.

The perpendicular upon which the center of the base of the weight rests, when placed upon
a curved surface, shall be that which supports the said weight; and it shall be straight to the center of the world <note>original: "centro del mondo" — Leonardo uses this to mean the center of gravity of the Earth.</note>.

The closer the perpendicular—which rests in the center of the base of the weight placed upon the
curve—is to the middle of that weight, the more it will weigh; and the center of that weight will be
with the center of the world.

### [Right Folio - f. 121r]

The ball that is moved upon the surface of the plane.

<margin>
The middle of every weight must join with the center of the earth.
</margin>

<note>This passage discusses the nature of rectilinear (straight-line) and circular motion, and the impossibility of perpetual motion in a purely rectilinear system without the inclusion of circularity (like a rolling sphere).</note>

That ball which is moved upon the plane of motion shall be of
perpetual motion, if said line does not pull in a direct straight line to the center of the world;
but because such motion is imperfect—since circular motion is the only one
that can be of perpetual motion, and not rectilinear motion—the reason is
because rectilinear motion cannot be of perpetual motion unless it is composed
of circular motion, as is the ball that is moved by itself,
which ball has within itself rectilinear motion and circular motion. The rectilinear motion
comes from that weight which gives motion to said ball, and the circular motion is
in the ball itself, which is moved upon the surface of a plane;
therefore, if you move the ball upon the plane of motion, it will be moved with
perpetual motion; and if the ball is moved upon the plane of motion which is upon
a circle, it will be moved with circular and rectilinear motion; and if said ball is
moved upon the plane of a triangle, it will be moved with rectilinear motion and with
circular motion. But if said ball is moved upon the plane of perpendicular
motion, it will be moved with rectilinear motion; and if said ball is moved
upon the plane of motion which is upon a circle, it will be moved with
circular motion.

<note>Technical vocabulary used on this page:</note>
<term>balances</term>, <term>pulleys</term>, <term>perpetual motion</term>, <term>center of the world</term>, <term>perpendicular</term>, <term>base</term>.

<summary>Leonardo defines the law of work (the inverse relationship between force and distance) and explores how a body's center of gravity must align with the Earth's center. He also analyzes how a rolling sphere combines rectilinear and circular motion, touching on the theoretical requirements for perpetual motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s observations on physics, moving from the optics of the previous page to the mechanics of flight and the density of air. He uses the pigeon as a primary model for understanding how a bird's tail and wings manipulate air pressure to ascend, descend, or remain stationary.</meta>

### [Verso - Left Column]

If a pigeon <note>original: "colunba"</note> catches the air beneath itself with its tail spread, and the air beneath the wings strikes them, then that pigeon will rise upward and remain still.

---

That part of the air will be denser which is struck by a swifter motion. This is proven by the 7th [proposition] of this [treatise].

---

Will the pulses of the air struck by the wings be equally distant from the center of gravity of the bird <note>original: "uciello"</note> or not? No, because the air struck by the tips of the wings is denser than that which strikes the parts closer to the body.

---

Dense air cannot penetrate through thin <term>rara: low density or "rare"</term> air that is in motion, except along the straight line of its movement.

---

When the bird wishes to rise without flapping its wings, it then turns the tail to the percussion <note>the forceful impact or strike</note> of the air; it catches the air under the tail and thus it rises, both by the hidden motion of the wind and of the tail.

---

Why, if the bird wants to rise without flapping its wings, it extends the tail; and without bending it, the air strikes it from below and lifts it high. And the more it extends it, the more it lifts it; and the wider it spreads it, the more it stays still in the air.

---

When the bird descends, then the tail is narrowed and it bends the tip downward; and the more it bends it, the faster it falls. When the bird turns its head, it then turns the tail in the opposite direction.

### [Recto - Right Column]

Every body that strikes against dense air is of longer stay <note>remains suspended longer</note> than if it were in less dense air.

---

The air is dense where the air struck by the wings catches the air beneath itself, and that [air] strikes the air above it through hidden motion.

---

That part of the air will be denser which is more compressed. This is proven by the 9th [proposition] on the density and rarity of the air.

---

The air will be denser where it is struck by the swifter motion. This is proven by the 7th [proposition] on motion and percussion.

---

If the tail of the bird is struck by the air on the upper part, then the tail will bend and the tip will turn downward, and the bird falls because the air pushes it down.

---

If the tip of the tail is turned upward, the air strikes it from below and lifts it high.

---

The tail of the bird is the cause of its staying still; the air strikes beneath the tail as was said above.

<note>Below the text are two geometric diagrams and a library stamp.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the aerodynamics of bird flight, specifically how the tail acts as a rudder and elevator by manipulating air density and pressure. He also includes geometric studies of cubes in perspective to explore spatial volume.</summary>
<keywords>aerodynamics, bird flight, air density, tail movement, mechanics, geometry, perspective, pigeon</keywords>

### Mechanical Diagrams

<note>The sketches at the top of the page (oriented landscape) depict mechanical transmission systems.</note>

- **Crank Mechanism**: A detailed study of a vertical shaft with integrated pins or teeth, likely part of an escapement or a mechanism to convert rotary motion from the crank into vertical or flapping motion.

<summary>Leonardo defines the principle of relative motion, explaining that a bird's lift increases with its speed against the wind because the air becomes "denser" (more compressed) beneath the wing. He also describes a state of equilibrium where a bird can remain stationary in the air if its forward speed matches the wind's opposing speed.</summary>

### [Mechanics of the Crossbow]

On the pulling of the crossbow string

<note>Drawing of a lever system for a crossbow string</note>

Whoever wishes to pull a great weight of string with the help of a small force, I say that it should be done in this way: let a pulley be made which, by moving a little away from the point of the pull <note>original: "tiron"</note>, will have little resistance. And this is that which has such great force in its beginning and little in the end, which is contrary to the nature of a crossbow, which in its beginning has little force and at the end of the string has very great resistance. Therefore, we want to remedy this by saying that the pulley has to be made in such a way, moving away from the straight line as much as the resistance of that string. And behold, the crossbow will be tensioned with the help of the <term>lever-arm<note>Leonardo uses "balestra era," likely referring to a spanning tool or lever mechanism</note></term> which, with the help of a small force, puts into action one of great weight, as would be the pulling of the string of a crossbow for infinite time and for infinite force with little effort. Let there be made, therefore, a pulley which has its pulls in such a way that it is proportional to the resistance of the string, and thus there will be equal force in every place of the movements of that string. I say that if the resistance of the string is <unclear>5 less</unclear> of a pound at its beginning and at the end is 1000 pounds, you should make it so that the pulley has its lever as much longer than that of the pull of its beginning than that of the pull of its end, as is the difference from the small resistance to the great.

---

### [Hydraulics]

How water should be divided into infinite branches so that all are of the same equality.

<note>Detailed drawing of a horizontal water distribution channel with multiple outlets</note>

This is the way to divide the water into as many parts as you please and of equal measure for the use of the inhabitants of various parts of a land <note>Leonardo is likely referring to an urban water distribution system for a city</note>.

### [Mechanical Joints]

<note>Drawings of mechanical hinges or joints labeled 'm' and 'n'</note>

This <term>hinge-joint<note>original: "anichilio," a term Leonardo used for a type of knuckle-joint or pivot</note></term> shall be that which keeps the movement smooth; it should have nothing to do with the force of the man.

> If the hinge-joint is of brass and the axle of steel, it will wear down less and will be of excellent durability; and to make it light, it should be hollow.

If it is turned by the force of a man, and if it is lubricated <note>original: "mēto," likely "unguento" or "memento"</note> so that there is little friction, it will be light and of minimum weight so that it may be moved with ease by the man.

<summary>Leonardo explores mechanical advantage in crossbows, a hydraulic system for equal water distribution in cities, the geometry of vision within the eye, and the use of dissimilar metals (brass and steel) to reduce friction in mechanical joints.</summary>

### On the motion of heavy bodies moving upon flat surfaces

Every body that moves along a straight line between two points takes the shortest motion between them.

A heavy body <note>original: "grauezza"</note> that moves by its natural motion, if it finds an opposing resistance, does not stop nor slow down until its center of gravity is pushed by its weight.

A heavy body that moves from high to low, or rather moves along a transverse line, if it is forced to move from said low to high, that weight hangs upon the resistance.

<note>Study of a cylinder on a plane, possibly analyzing friction or the center of gravity during rolling motion.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the mathematical relationship between a circle's radius and its area (the square-cube law) and defines the role of the center of gravity in determining the path of a moving body.</summary>
<keywords>geometry, center of gravity, proportions, circles, physics of motion, mechanics, area calculation</keywords>

### Proportional Solids and Perspective

<note>Center right: Three distinct geometric studies exploring how shapes occupy space.</note>

1. **The Perspective Cube**: A rectangular prism or cube drawn in perspective. Leonardo has included internal diagonal lines to show its structure and used horizontal **hatching** <term>hatching: a technique of drawing closely spaced parallel lines to create effects of shade or texture</term> at the base to ground the object on a flat plane.

2. **The Bisected Square**: A simple vertical rectangle or square divided exactly in half by a vertical line, likely a study in symmetry.

3. **The Proportional Square**: A square containing internal diagonal lines and a central horizontal line. This is a classic exercise in **geometry** <note>original: "geometria"</note> used to determine proportions and find the exact center of a two-dimensional plane.

<margin>
<note>Red library stamp: Crown over B.M.</note>
</margin>

### [Bottom Right Quadrant]

# Folio 137r

<note>Optical and mathematical note on the top right, discussing diffraction or vision through eyelashes. Leonardo is exploring how looking through the narrow gaps of squinted eyes or eyelashes multiplies the perceived images of a light source, like a star.</note>

The spirit <note>original: "spito" (spirito). In Renaissance optics, the 'visual spirit' was thought to emanate from the eye to meet the light.</note> that issues from the hole
in the middle of the hairs <note>eyelashes</note> and goes in a straight
line to the star, one [line] shall be
above the other hairs; and just as
the row of hairs is, so shall be the row of
stars. + If there are 4 hairs, there will be
16 stars. + If there are 16 hairs, there
will be 256 stars, and so it will be;
by multiplying it will be 16 times 16,
which is 256. + Follow such a rule:
if there are 4 hairs, there are 16 stars;
if there are 16 hairs, there are 256 stars;
if there are 256 hairs, there are
65,536 stars. And so it shall be.
And know that every single hair
looks at all the stars
at one time.

<note>Physiological note regarding the distribution of force in muscles. Leonardo uses a hydraulic metaphor, comparing the nervous or "force" impulses to water flowing through pipes.</note>

The force will travel through the branches of
its origin and will depart through various
branches, just as the water of a spring does,
which divides itself into many conduits
through which no fluid <note>original: "umore" (humor)</note> departs
except the specific water from which that
force was born. And if any of said conduits
were blocked, then the motion of that
force would go through the other conduits

one of the muscles is impeded, the others
double their force, and
especially those muscles that
have the same office <note>function or purpose</note>.

### [Folio 137 verso]

Because that part of the rope which is closer to the pivot <term>pernesso: the axis or central pin of a balance</term> of the scales will be heavier, just as that which is further away will be lighter; wherefore, as the weight **m** follows its course toward **n**, it will be driven by the weight **n** between **m** and **n**, and such motion will be slow...

<note>Study of mechanics involving pulleys, ropes, and weights on inclined planes.</note>

If you wish to know what weight will be required to support the ball **p** placed on the plane **ob** which is oblique to **r**, know that the weight **p** will have the same proportion to weight **m** as the line **o r** has to the line **o b**. That is, if the line **o r** is one-third of **o b**, the weight **m** will be one-third of the weight **p**; and if **m** is to support **p**, this **m** must be a weight of one-third of **p**. And this assumes that **o b r** is of uniform substance... <note>Leonardo is describing the law of the inclined plane: the force required to hold a weight in equilibrium is proportional to the ratio of the height to the length of the slope.</note>

### [Folio 138 recto]

The force of the powder in the mortar <note>original: "mortaro," a short-barreled cannon</note> is divided into two parts, one of which escapes through the touchhole <term>fochile: the vent or hole where the fuse ignites the gunpowder</term> and the other through the mouth of the mortar; therefore, the wider the touchhole is, the less will be the force of the powder remaining in the mortar, and the smaller will be the motion of the ball.

<note>Observations on the ballistics of a mortar and the escape of gases through the touchhole.</note>

Like these two furnaces, where one is taller than the other—that is, the one at **n** is taller than the one at **m**—wherefore **n** will be hotter than **m**. And the reason is this: that **n** has beneath it more ignited air than **m**... <note>Leonardo correctly identifies that a taller chimney or furnace creates a stronger draft, increasing the intensity of the fire.</note>

<note>Drawing of two conical furnaces or kilns illustrating the effect of height on heat/draft.</note>

If you want to make a line that goes straight without the eye having to watch it as you turn toward it, take a string and dye it with charcoal or another color, stretch it against the wall, and then quickly strike <insert>snap</insert> it, and thus the line will be made... <note>A description of a "chalk line," a tool still used by builders today to mark long, straight lines.</note>

Because smoke willingly enters into arches where it is not struck by the wind...
These arches ought to be turned toward the wind so that the air striking into them cannot be scattered...

<note>Architectural sketches of niches and vaults, possibly related to acoustics or the movement of air/smoke within structures.</note>

### Description of Sketches

The page is filled with various diagrams focused on structural engineering and mechanical advantage, specifically for the transport of heavy weaponry.

**Left-hand page:**
- **Top left:** A study of a timber scaffold or support frame, possibly for a crane or a protective housing.
- **Top center:** Vertical beams with pulley wheels at the top, illustrating how ropes can be directed to lift weights.
- **Middle:** A horizontal beam mechanism containing multiple pulley wheels. This device is intended to multiply force, allowing heavy artillery pieces to be lifted "without effort," as mentioned in the text.

**Right-hand page:**
- **Top:** A large hoisting apparatus consisting of two vertical posts and a crossbeam with curved supports and internal pulleys.
- **Middle:** A refined study of the horizontal lifting beam, showing a complex arrangement of four central pulleys and peripheral wheels.
- **Bottom:** Various structural details, including an X-shaped cross-brace and sketches of ropes passing through pulley blocks at different angles.

</margin>

<term>Unloading (scaricare)</term>: The process of removing heavy cargo from a transport vehicle.

Because the shadow does not manifest itself except through the diminution of light,
that diminution will be more or less powerful according to whether the light
is more or less powerful between which the shadow is interposed.

If the shadow is maintained where the light of luminous air is interposed,
that shadow will be denser and more luminous the closer the eye is
to the most luminous part of the air.

If the shadow is mixed with the light, the shadow will be less manifest
the more the air is luminous; the air will be denser and more
luminous the closer the eye is to the most luminous part of it.

The more the shadow is luminous between the eye and the light, the less
manifest it will be, because the air is maintained by shadow or light, or dense or rare <note>Leonardo uses "rare" to mean thin or low-density air.</note>,

# f. 144

## [Left Folio]

Wishing to remedy the pendulum of the clock which lengthens with heat and shortens with cold by creating a certain counterweight for it.

While the rod **. a . b .** lengthens due to the heat, this rod inclines toward **. c .** and the point **. b .**, which is the center <note>The "center" here refers to the center of oscillation or the position of the pendulum bob.</note> of said pendulum, will be as much lower as the said pendulum has grown. And to remedy such growth, make it so that the foundation <note>The suspension or mounting point.</note> of this pendulum is **. d .**, and let this point **. d .** be as much higher as the said pendulum has grown; and this remedy shall be made by a balance <term>bilancia</term> <note>A pivoting lever or scale beam.</note> **. f . g .** which, by means of the length of the rod **. h . f .**, moves the point **. d .** upward.

<note>Drawing of a thermal compensation mechanism for a clock pendulum. It features a vessel (possibly containing a substance with high thermal expansion) connected to a lever system (balance) intended to raise the suspension point as the rod lengthens.</note>

The pendulum **. a . b .** lengthens with heat and makes its center **. b .** lower by as much as its growth. Now, make it so that the point **. a .** from which it hangs rises as much higher as that growth, and the remedy will be perfect.

Again, you could make it so that the foundation from which the pendulum hangs rises as much higher as the pendulum lengthens. Make it so that the rod **. a . b .** lengthens with heat as much as the pendulum **. c . d .** lengthens.

Let the rod **. a . b .** lengthen with heat and shorten with cold. Now I want that, through such growth, the point **. a .** rises as much as the point **. b .** drops.

If the rod **. a . b .** lengthens due to heat, the point **. b .** will drop by half of that growth. Make it so that the point **. a .** rises by half of that growth, and you will keep the center of the pendulum always at one and the same height.

## [Right Folio]

To know by how much space the pendulum of the clock lengthens due to the heating of said pendulum—and likewise how it lowers with the foundation of the <unclear>sound</unclear> <note>Possibly "suolo" (base/ground) or referring to the clock's striking mechanism support.</note> that sustains it—and by how much it retracts due to the cold. To know the motion made by the point of the clock which moves through the height of a pendulum that lengthens and shortens due to heat and cold. <note>Geometric diagram of a right triangle.</note>

Again, you could do it in this way: Let the rod **. d . a .** be the pendulum and the rod **. a . b .** be how much it lengthens due to heat, and make the line **. d . b .** the hypotenuse. By as much as the line **. d . b .** exceeds **. d . a .**, by that much the pendulum will have dropped. **. b . d .** will be the length of the pendulum after growing, and **. d . a .** will be the length of the pendulum before its growth. And let **. b . e .** be a line parallel to the rod **. d . a .**, and let the rod **. a . e .** be perpendicular to the rod **. d . a .**, and it will be as much as the difference between the line **. d . a .** and the line **. d . b .**; or you could say **. a . e .** is as much as **. b . d .** exceeds **. a . d .**.

<note>Geometric diagram showing nested triangles to calculate the difference in length.</note>

If the pendulum **. a . d .** <unclear>reaches</unclear> **. a .** by as much as its growth **. b . d .**, make the length **. b . d .** as if it were the chord of some circle like **. d . c . b .**, and let **. d .** be the center of that pendulum. Draw the line **. d . e .** perpendicularly to the line **. d . a .**, and the space **. a . e .** will be the amount of the drop of that pendulum.

<note>Geometric diagram involving a circular arc and chords.</note>

If you know the length of a pendulum whose height varies due to heat and cold, and having learned how much that growth is due to heat, you will know how much it has dropped; and consequently, you will know how much the time of its motion has varied. And conversely, you will know how to remedy such an error: to make the pendulum as much shorter as it drops. Make the rod **. a . b .** the length of the pendulum and let the rod **. b . c .** be the growth acquired through heat, and let it be the chord of the circle **. b . d . c .** whose center is **. a .**, the point where the pendulum hangs. Let the rod **. a . d .** be perpendicular to the rod **. a . b .**, and the space **. b . d .** will be the length of the rod that serves as the remedy for such an error.

# In this way it is proved that the moon has no light of its own

<note>The following text is situated around diagrams showing the geometric relationship between the Sun (b), the Moon (e), and the Earth (a).</note>

The sun **b** illuminates the moon **e**, and this moon cannot be seen from the hemisphere of the earth **a** because the air is illuminated by the sun between the earth and the moon **e**.

By this it is proved that the moon has no light of its own; and if it did indeed have its own, it would not be obscured within the shadow of the earth, which obscuration is called an eclipse.

The light that appears to us <note>on the dark part of the moon</note> is that which is reflected back to it from the water of the earth, which earth is struck by the solar rays; and if the earth were dry, it would not give off any <unclear>reflected</unclear> light; and if the moon were dry, it would appear as nothing other than a dark and shadowy <unclear>body</unclear>.

---

<note>The right-hand side of the spread is mostly blank, containing only faint circular geometric sketches and bleed-through from the other side of the folio.</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues that the Moon does not generate its own light but reflects sunlight and "earthshine"—light reflected from Earth's oceans—while explaining that eclipses prove the Moon's lack of inherent luminosity.</summary>

### Description of Drawings

The page is filled with dynamic sketches executed in red chalk <note>also known as sanguine</note>. On the right side, a large, vigorous swirling form dominates, which appears to be a study of turbulent water flow—a recurring theme in Leonardo's scientific and artistic investigations where he compares the movement of water to the braiding of hair.

To the left and across the lower portion of the page are more structured, linear sketches. These resemble topographical maps or plans for hydraulic engineering, perhaps showing the course of a river or the layout of a canal system <note>Leonardo was famously involved in a project to divert the Arno River during this period</note>. The lines are marked with cross-hatches and specific numbers, suggesting a technical survey or a proposal for terrain modification. The contrast between the rigid, measured lines of the survey and the organic, chaotic swirls of the water study highlights Leonardo's dual approach of mathematical precision and empirical observation of natural forces.

<summary>This page features red chalk technical drawings and notes by Leonardo da Vinci concerning hydraulic engineering and the physics of water flow. It combines precise topographical measurements with a fluid study of turbulent water patterns.</summary>

<keywords>hydraulics, fluid dynamics, surveying, red chalk, Arno River project, Renaissance engineering, topography</keywords>

# Folio 157

<note>Leonardo frequently uses dots between words in this section, a habit that may have helped him pace his thoughts or manage the ink flow while writing in reverse.</note>

Because the air, like the water, moves
within itself more quickly than
water does, for no other reason than for
its rarity <note>meaning its low density or thinness</note>, it does not resist as well
the force of the bird's oars <note>original: "remi," Leonardo's term for wings</note> as
the water does for the boat; therefore it is necessary
that the bird moves its oars more rapidly.

---

In the leap that the bird makes against the air,
it helps itself more with its velocity than with the
resistance of the air; therefore it is necessary that... <note>The sentence ends abruptly in the manuscript.</note>

---

Because the air condenses beneath the bird,
and the air above the bird becomes rarefied,
because the air beneath the bird descends more
quickly than the air is able to escape;
in such a way that the air resists the air by way of the oars.

---

The bird descends more quickly than the oar
does not descend, because the air resists the air;
because the air that descends beneath the bird
cannot escape.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of flight, comparing the density of air to water and explaining how a bird's wings (which he calls "oars") create lift by condensing the air beneath them. He concludes that the speed of the wingbeat must compensate for the air's low resistance compared to water.</summary>

## [Column 2]

If a weight be moved by one and the same force
toward one and the same velocity, the motion shall be of so much
longer duration as its motion shall be more tempered
by the resistance of the air, which shall be so much less as
the said weight shall be smaller and of heavier material.

---

If a weight be moved through the air by the said force
and its velocity, the heavier the material is, the
longer its duration will be, continually displacing the air.

---

->Heavy<-

If a weight be moved, as above, by a given
force and velocity, placing that weight closer to the
center of the said circumference, its duration will be
so much longer as its weight shall be closer to the said
center, and as its circle shall be smaller.

---

->Velocity<-

If a weight be moved, as above, the
smaller its circle is, the swifter its
motion will be; and the swifter it is, the longer its
duration will be, just as its weight is heavier.

---

->Duration<-

The swifter its motion is, the longer its
duration will be, just as its weight is heavier; because
it will create a longer duration, continually displacing the air
swiftly, when it is moved by the said velocity;
and so much less returning the air when it is smaller,
because the smaller it is, the less air will be moved;
when less air is moved, less air will be returned; and
when less air is returned, the longer its duration will be.

---

->Air<-

If a weight be moved, as above, the
smaller its circle is, the less the air returns;
because the air that is within the smaller circle is less,
the smaller the said circle shall be.

---

->Percussion<-

The percussion is so much swifter as the motion
is more tempered by the resistance of its path.

---

->Motion<-

The motion shall be of so much less duration as the
motion is swifter in its circumference; because
air that is sent more swiftly will be returned
swiftly; and it will be moved so much more as the velocity
is less; and as the velocity is less, so much
less will the air be returned.

---

And the air swiftly returned will be so much swifter in lessening the duration.

<summary>Leonardo investigates the relationship between a projectile's mass, its velocity, and the resistance of the air, noting that denser objects (like iron) maintain momentum longer. He also explores the mechanics of circular motion and pendulums, observing how the radius of a swing affects the duration and speed of the weight.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the weight of air and the center of the world, Leonardo now transitions into a series of numbered geometric propositions.
