1 By the ratio <note>original: "ragiõ" (ragione); in this context, it refers to a mathematical proportion or relationship</note> of a circle whose circumference passes through the center of circles of which one is the center and the other <note>The sentence appears to break off or imply a second center</note>.

3 How much a part of a circle decreases by the removal of its circumference from its center, and the same for other ratios.

--- Page 235 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with geometric propositions regarding circles and ratios. Here, Leonardo shifts abruptly from geometry to a series of allegorical or philosophical reflections on Truth, Falsehood, and the permanence of nature, using the metaphor of a woman and the "bones" of mountains.</meta>

The excessive size of the person is made to reduce it to the
form of a child or indeed of a woman, because through the excessive
size of such a form, the lie comes to be recognized.

It is done to give effort, even if the man is held to be of the
same weight in gold; if he is made defective or
false through his movements, it comes to be seen that he is a counterfeit.

It is done so that everyone who is held for their learning may be held
as a devourer of the truth and of the confusion of such a woman;
if such a woman is shown from one movement to the other, she shall not be
the victor over the other surpassing truth.

---

The surpassing truth is made in the form of a woman who
is not of excessive size, because truth shall not be surpassed,

If the force that moves is equal to the resistance, the motion will never take place.

# On the crack

A crack being nothing other than a break in the continuity of a body that was once a single whole, this break is caused by the inequality of the ground where such a body rests. This inequality causes one of the parts that was divided by the crack to hang lower than the other, and thus it comes to crack. And this is the primary reason for the crack, which is proven as follows:

### [Folio 158 recto - Right Page]

# On the cracking of arches

The arch will not break if the outer <term>chord</term><note>original: "corda"; here referring to the outer boundary or line of tension</note> of the arches is not touched by the inner arches. This is the 7th [proposition] of the <term>sectors</term><note>original: "sesti"; likely referring to a specific geometric treatise or section on compass-work</note>, and it is proven by the sector of weights which says: "That part of the chord will be more burdened which is more remote from the center of its <term>pole</term><note>original: "polo"; the pivot point or fulcrum</note>." Therefore, the pole of the arch will be the angle of its crack from below, and the weight will be the entire mass of the arch that moves upon that pole. Thus, the arch acts like a <term>lever</term><note>original: "lieva"</note>, which, the longer it is, the more easily it lifts its weight. Hence, the arch being long from the outer angle of its rupture to the inner chord, that chord moves with ease, a small force pushing such a part of the arch outward.

<note>Drawing of a pointed arch with geometrical lines illustrating the centers of gravity and forces (labeled with letters a, b, c, d, etc.).</note>

On the cracking of buildings made of bricks and <term>mortar</term><note>original: "calcina"; lime-based mortar</note>, and how the center of gravity of the cracked part changes because of the crack.

<note>Diagram of an arch segment showing the vector of weight and a pivot point.</note>

Such is the cracking of stones in arches and in walls, as is the motion of the cracked parts; and this is manifest through experience.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the velocity and density of air, Leonardo now shifts his focus to the internal mechanics of fluid motion—specifically how layers of water or light rays "penetrate" and "intertwine" with one another due to differences in speed and angle.</meta>

### Left Page

->propa<- <note>Likely an abbreviation for "proposition" or "proportionality."</note>

Because of the **reflected rays**, that which comes from the lower part penetrates within the ray that comes from the upper part, with that same **obliquity** <note>The angle of slant or inclination.</note> with which it enters within the upper ray; which likewise penetrates within the lower ray. And if one should wish to say that the reflected ray goes above the other and does not penetrate it, reason will not allow it, because that which enters within the other is forced to move with its own obliquity. And if it were constrained to go along one of the two surfaces of said ray, it would have to bend its straight path, which would be impossible, as a motion that finds no obstacle cannot change its obliquity. And so, that ray which is lower will be slower in its start, and that which is higher will be faster in its start; and thus, step by step, it will be slower or faster. For this reason, the lower ray, being slower, is forced to remain behind the upper ray; and thus, that ray which was below comes to turn backward, and that which was above comes to be below, and that which was below comes to be above. And so they **revolve one within the other**. And this is the motion that water makes when it falls from a height to a depth; because the motion from above being faster than that from below, the one from above comes to turn backward, and the one from below comes to turn backward, and so they revolve one within the other.

<margin>
<note>Geometric diagram of two intertwined waves or rays, with numerical annotations 1, 2, 3, 4 at the nodes.</note>
</margin>

Because the motion from above is faster than that from below, the one from above comes to turn backward, and the one from below comes to turn backward, and so they revolve one within the other. And this is the motion that water makes when it falls from a height to a depth; because the motion from above being faster than that from below, the one from above comes to turn backward, and the one from below comes to turn backward, and so they revolve one within the other.

And not penetrating into the water because of its weight <note>The density/gravity of the water resisting the air.</note>, it is forced to turn back in a radiated form over the surface of the water. And its motion will be as much faster as it is closer to the **center of the blow**, and as much slower as it is further away. And thus the water will be moved more near the center of the blow, and moved less near the circumference of the circle.

## Proof of the calculation of value <note>Leonardo uses "value" here to refer to the magnitude or force of a weight.</note>

The weight that is placed and supported upon the middle circle of the body will never overturn such a body if it does not rotate through the circle of its foundation. But if such a weight moves toward any part of the circumference of the middle circle, failing to rest above the center of such a body, then the movement of its overturning is born in that body.

<note>The drawings on the left page illustrate a gimbal mechanism (suspension in cardanic rings), often used for ship compasses or lamps to maintain a level orientation regardless of the movement of the support.</note>

(Right Page - Recto)

## Concerning the overturning of that lower part

In every body that is supported beneath itself in whatever part it may be, its weight will be diminished toward the part opposite to the site of its support by as much value as the proportion of the distance interposed between the circle of such a support and the center of the weight of such a body is to the semi-diameter <term>semi-diameter: the radius of a circle</term> of such a support. And this arises because in whatever direction such a body wishes to overturn, it must necessarily rise upward above the circle of its support; this it cannot do if such motion does not turn in a circle surrounding the circle of such a support. And because such circles are of various diameters, as the sites of their circles are various, the accidental weight <term>accidental weight: the effective weight or force exerted by an object when it is out of its natural equilibrium</term> arises from the middle circle, which circle never moves except in a straight line toward the center of the world <note>original: "ciercho del mondo" — Leonardo refers to the center of the Earth, the point toward which all gravity pulls.</note>.

<margin>
<note>In the right margin, there is a sketch of an architectural element, possibly the springing of an arch or a decorative cornice detail.</note>
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of stability and overturning, using a gimbal mechanism (concentric rings) to demonstrate how a central weight remains balanced. He concludes that stability is governed by the relationship between the center of gravity and the points of support relative to the Earth's center.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, gimbals, equilibrium, center of gravity, cardanic suspension, accidental weight, geometry</keywords>

When the bird, through the percussion <note>original: "percussione" - the impact or striking force of the air against the wing</note> of the air, wishes to maintain itself aloft without beating its wings, it is necessary that it pull its wings toward the tail in a manner that extends them and causes itself to incline through the air.

<margin>
It is manifested by experience that the air passes between the feathers.
</margin>

<note>Two sketches of birds in flight, showing wing positions relative to the body.</note>

But if the bird wishes to rise upward without beating its wings, then it spreads the wings in such a way that they form a sort of concavity on the underside, and it pulls the wings toward the tail and helps itself to do the same with its tail. The path of the wind through the percussion of the wings is manifested in the upper part, where the air strikes the wings, and by its exit, it traverses the wings in such a way that it appears as if the air strikes the underside of the wings...

### On the movement of birds

The bird, for its descent, throws the wings toward the tail, and for its ascent, it throws them toward the head. The bird, for its descent, pulls the wings toward the tail, and for its ascent, it throws them toward the head; and for its level path, it pulls them toward the back; and for its stability, the bird pulls the wings toward the breast. And if the bird wishes to leap upward, it pulls the wings toward the tail.

It is proved by line A, which is the one through which the air passes between the feathers of the bird's wings. I say that if the bird wishes to descend, it must pull the wings toward the tail, because the air that passes between the feathers of the wings strikes the upper part of the wings; and by its exit, it traverses the wings in such a way that it appears as if the air strikes the underside of the wings. And if the bird wishes to rise, it must throw the wings toward the head, because the air that passes between the feathers of the wings strikes the underside of the wings; and by its exit, it traverses the wings in such a way that it appears as if the air strikes the upper part of the wings.

By reason of the exit of the air: the air that traverses the wings passes along line A, which line traverses the wings between one feather and another and strikes the underside, or rather the upper part, according to whether the wings are thrown toward the head or toward the tail. Because if the wings are thrown toward the tail, the air strikes the upper part, and by its exit, it traverses the wings in such a way that it appears as if the air strikes the underside; and this is what assists the bird in its descent.

---

On the movement of the wings of birds that move without beating their wings. Because that bird which moves without beating its wings undoubtedly moves above the wind A in a line.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the aerodynamics of soaring flight, explaining how a bird maneuvers by shifting its wings toward its head or tail to control ascent and descent. He notes that air passing between feathers creates pressure changes that simulate striking the wing from the opposite side.</summary>

# [Folio 168v]

If the column that supports the weight is made of different types of wood, and one is thicker than the other, the one that is thicker will have more strength; and this happens because the thickness maintains the straight line of the weight, and it will be more stable. The opposite will be true for the one that is thinner, and the reason is because thickness maintains the straight line and thinness does not.

Because falling weights maintain the line of their fall in the air, and likewise a body moving through the air maintains the line of its motion—as seen with a bow: the greater the force, the more the line of the motion of the arrow <note>original: "saetta"</note> will be maintained—so it is for a body maintained in the air. Thus, a falling body maintains the line of its fall, and for this reason, if a ball is held in the air, it will maintain the line of its fall; and likewise, a body moving through the air will maintain the line of its motion in proportion to its force and weight.

---

# [Folio 169r]

The line of the straight fall of a heavy object will be maintained for a longer time in proportion to its weight and heaviness; and likewise, the opposite will be the weakness of the line of fall of a light object, which is moved out of its line by every small wind.

If the cord that holds the weight is of such greater thickness than the weight, that cord will move the weight out of its line, because the cord maintains its thickness against the weight which is thinner; it will be pulled by the line of the thickness of the cord, which maintains its straight line and will not be bent by the weight that is thinner. And likewise the opposite: if the weight is thicker than the cord, that weight will maintain its straight line and will bend the cord.

<margin>

This is because the thickness of the cord will maintain its straight line and will have more strength, and thus it will maintain its straight line and will not be bent by the weight of the bow. And likewise the opposite is true of the bow that is thicker than the cord.

<note>Left Side of the Spread</note>

Which water will move more quickly: that which falls along its natural bed, or that which falls outside of said natural bed through the open air? And what is the weight of the fall of one and the other upon their respective bottoms?

->the fall<-

The water that falls through the open air will undoubtedly be faster than that which falls along its natural bed; and the weight, or rather the impact <term>percussione</term> <note>Leonardo uses this term to describe the force or "blow" delivered by a moving body</note>, will be greater for that which strikes the bottom through the open air than for that which falls along the bed of said water.

->the proof<-

Suppose there is a large bucket <term>secchione</term> of water with a hole <term>buso</term> in the bottom through which the water exits, and let the water exiting be of such a quantity that the bucket is always kept full. I say that the water exiting through the hole will be faster than the water moving across the surface of the bucket toward that same hole.

### On the impact of water.
Water that falls from a height and strikes other water will penetrate so much deeper into its encounter as the height of its fall is greater.

### On the impact of water.
That part of the water which falls perpendicularly will have a greater impact than that which falls along an oblique line.

If the water falling through the open air is of such a height that it converts into smoke or mist, such a fall will be without any impact upon the bottom.

<note>Right Side of the Spread (f. 173r)</note>

If water moves in its bed by the motion of the wind striking its surface, the water will undoubtedly move at its bottom due to the motion of the air striking its surface.

<note>Small sketch depicting wind (represented by lines and a face-like profile) striking the surface of water, creating waves.</note>

->the proof<-

If the air moves the water on the surface, and the moved water sets in motion the water it touches, undoubtedly the very bottom will be moved by such motion, even if it is at a great depth.

That part of the "skin" of the water <note>Leonardo's term for the surface tension or top layer</note> moves most quickly which is struck by the wind at more right angles; and it will be slower when struck at more acute angles, and it will be moved between the motion of the wind and the impact of said wind.

### On the wave
The wave is moved by the air or by the impact of some weight thrown into said water; and the motion of the wave will be so much faster as the impact is more powerful or moved by a greater weight. And the wave will be so much higher as the impact is more sudden.

If water that is on a slope and is struck by the wind—without any obstruction from the shore—is struck by wind hitting its surface, that water will be doubled in its velocity.

### On water
Water that falls suddenly from a certain height will never be of equal thickness in itself, because it divides through the air-vents <term>spiracoli</term> <note>literally "breathing holes," here referring to the gaps or pores in the air</note> and resolves into spray and the smoke of mist. And if the water falls for a long distance, it will be so much thinner toward the end as it is further from its source.

And if water is moved by the same weight of air, it will be of so much faster motion as it is on the same slope.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of falling water and wave formation, concluding that water falling through free air gains more velocity and force than water flowing along a bed. He also explores how wind transfers energy through the surface of water down to the very bottom of a channel.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, fluid dynamics, velocity, impact, waves, wind resistance, surface tension, gravity</keywords>

<margin>
The further a weight is from the center of the world <note>original: "cietro del mōdo" — Leonardo refers to the center of the Earth, which in the Aristotelian physics of his time was considered the center of the universe and the point toward which all heavy things naturally fall.</note>, the less it weighs; and the closer it approaches, the more it weighs. <note>Mechanical studies of levers and weights. Leonardo investigates how the angle of suspension and the distance from the pivot affect the effective gravity or force of a weight.</note>

If the weight is movable between point **m** and point **o**, and it is pulled by the cord **p** along the line **m-p**, I say that the closer the weight is to point **o**, the heavier it will be. The reason is proven because the straight line **m-p** will have a <unclear>deficiency</unclear> <note>original: "mancamēto" — possibly referring to a loss of mechanical advantage or a change in the angle of tension.</note>, and it will be straighter the closer it approaches point **o**.

If the weight is fixed at **m** and the force is at **p** along the line **p-m**, the weight will be less heavy the straighter the line **p-m** is.

<note>Geometric diagrams showing segments of circular arcs and their corresponding chords (linea della corda). The text explores the relationship between the length of the arc and the distance of the chord from the center.</note>

Because the line of the chord **f-g** is further from the center than the line **e-d**; and likewise the line **h-i** is further away than the line **f-g**; and so, step by step, the further they move away from point **a**, the longer the lines of the chords become, and consequently, the further they are from the center **m**.

But the arc **s-t** is of no account <note>original: "de nullo" — perhaps meaning it does not follow the same rule or is a null case.</note> because the centers are **v**, **m**, and **r**. For you see that the straight line **v-r** will be further from the center **m** the larger the arc is; and if the arc is small, the chord will be closer to the center **m**.

The larger the arc is, the further its center is from the center of the sphere; and the smaller it is, the closer it is.

See for what reason the air interposed between the eye and the object—even if it is of the same uniform density—will always show the part of the <term>pyramid of species<note>The "pyramid of species" (piramide delle spetie) is Leonardo's term for the cone of light rays carrying the "image" or "essence" of an object to the eye.</note></term> that is further from the eye to be thicker. Consequently, the edge of the object that is more remote from the eye will be more obscured.

<note>Drawing of a geometric diagram illustrating visual rays (pyramid of vision) passing through layers of air from an eye at point 'p'.</note>

I say that if the eye is at *p* and the object is *v r*, I say that the air is divided at *m n, s o, p*. And the air at *p n m* will be as much thicker than the air at *p s o* as the pyramid *p m n* is wider than the pyramid *p o s*. The reason is that, by the ratio of the circumference to the circumference of this pyramid, there is a greater thickness of air <note>original: "mē grossezza d’aria"; Leonardo likely means "more" (maggiore) here, as the wider part of the cone encompasses a larger volume of atmosphere.</note>. And because of this, you will see the boundaries more darkly as they move further from the eye, and fewer of their subtle details will be shown, because the air that is interposed is thicker and will render them more turbid.

<note>Technical Vocabulary:
- **Pyramid**: The cone of vision.
- **Eye**: The point of perspective.
- **Object**: The thing being viewed.
- **Thickness**: The density or volume of air.
- **Species**: The visual information or image.
- **Perspective**: The science of representing distance.
- **Interposed air**: The atmosphere between the viewer and the subject.</note>

<summary>Leonardo uses geometric diagrams to prove that as the "pyramid of vision" widens with distance, it encompasses a larger volume of air, which obscures the clarity and color of distant objects. ### Description of Drawings

The page features several drawings concentrated on the left half, illustrating concepts of both structural engineering and optical geometry.

1.  **Top Left Structural Study:** A schematic drawing of a vertical support or mast-like structure. It features horizontal platforms and measurements. Annotations include characters such as <term>p 3</term> <note>likely "piccoli" or "punti," units of measure</note> and <term>p 1</term>.
2.  **Top Center Architectural Perspective:** A detailed perspective view of an architectural structure, appearing to be a system of timber floor joists or ceiling beams viewed from below. It shows complex interlocking and cross-bracing. Some beams are labeled with small numerals, like <term>p 4</term>.
3.  **Bottom Left Geometric Diagram:** A scientific diagram illustrating the "pyramid of vision" (or "visual pyramid"). Lines converge from a vertical representation of a viewing plane towards a single vanishing point on the right. This diagram serves as a visual aid to the adjacent text regarding the geometry of sight and its perpendicular relationship to the plane of vision.

### Geometric Studies of the Circle

The primary focus of this page is a large, sophisticated geometric diagram. It consists of several concentric circles intersected by a central vertical axis. Within the upper-right quadrant, Leonardo has constructed a dense network of intersecting lines and arcs, creating a series of subdivided triangles and smaller curved segments.

<note>These types of drawings are frequently found in Leonardo’s later notebooks, such as the Codex Atlanticus. They often relate to his attempts at "squaring the circle" or calculating the area of <term>lunulae</term> (crescent-shaped figures), a classic problem in Greek geometry.</note>

In the right-hand margin, there is a smaller, secondary sketch:
*   **Proportional Study:** A small diagram showing a circle perfectly inscribed within a square. This is a fundamental exercise in exploring the relationship between linear and curved dimensions.

# [Folio 204r - Right]

On seeing

If the eye is placed at **f** and the light is at **b**, and that light passes through an opening **d e**, and the space **f b** is full of air illuminated by the light **b**: I say that the eye **f** will not see well the object **c** which is bounded within that luminous air—which object **c** is illuminated by that light **b**—because the air interposed between the light **b** and the eye **f** will be illuminated by the same light. Whereby that air is made luminous, and because the air made luminous is of greater <term>splendor<note>original: splendore — brightness or intensity</note></term> than the object **c** which is placed in that luminous air, the eye will be offended by the light of the air and will not see the object **c**, which has less splendor than the air surrounding it.

<note>Below this paragraph is a diagram showing the eye (ochio) looking through an aperture at a light source (lume), illustrating the text above.</note>

If there are two lights which <unclear>strike</unclear> one another in the eye, a shadow will be created between one light and the other, because the air will be illuminated by both one light and the other; and because one light will be more powerful than the other, the shadow will be created toward the weaker light; and because one light will have the value of two lights, the other light will be overcome and the shadow will be created toward the weaker light.

<note>Several diagrams follow showing eyes and light rays interacting. One shows two circles (lights) and an eye in the center.</note>

# [Leonardo da Vinci Manuscript Page - Folio 213]

<note>This page contains observations on acoustics and the perception of sound, written in Leonardo's characteristic right-to-left mirror script. Leonardo often applied the same laws of physics to sound as he did to light and water.</note>

->The rule of the voice<-
<note>Leonardo uses "voice" (original: "uoce") here to refer generally to sound or an acoustic signal.</note>

Every sound shall be so much older the further it is from its origin,
and it shall be so much younger the closer it is to its origin.
<note>Leonardo conceptualizes the "age" of a sound as the time and distance elapsed since its creation, implying a loss of energy or clarity over time.</note>

->On the hearing of the voice<-

Every voice shall be heard in part if you listen with one of the ears as much as with the other.

->On the sensing of the voice<-

If you wish to hear a voice from very far away which, being weak, would not reach you,
it is necessary to stop one of the ears with one of the fingers of the hand, and with the other ear
one captures what sensing one can, which shall be much more <unclear>perfect</unclear> than if both were opened.
<note>Leonardo suggests that by blocking one ear, the brain can focus more intently on the auditory input from the other, a practical observation of sensory concentration.</note>

<margin>
<note>Red stamp in the lower left and middle right: "B.M.", indicating the British Museum collection.</note>
</margin>

# Left Page (Folio 215v)

<margin>
Of things that move equally
</margin>

Let .a.b. be the moving object, .a.c. the line of motion, and .b.d. the other line of motion parallel to .a.c. And let the eye be at .n. from which the base .a.b. is seen. Let the lines .a.c. and .b.d. be equal, and let the motion be from point .a. to point .c. and from point .b. to point .d. And let the base .c.d. be seen from the same eye .n. I say that such a base .c.d. will appear smaller than the base .a.b. because the angle .c.n.d. is smaller than the angle .a.n.b.

<note>Diagram: A rectangle a.b.d.c. with diagonals and lines of sight from point n. This illustrates that even if an object stays the same physical size, it occupies a smaller portion of our field of vision as it moves further away.</note>

---

Let the line .a.b. move toward .c. through the space .a.c. and let .b. move toward .d. through the space .b.d. equal to .a.c. and let the eye be immobile at point .n. I say that such a line .a.b. in its motion will appear to diminish; that is, the angle of its being seen will always be smaller. Because if such motion were circular around the eye .n., it would remain of equal size, but moving along a straight line, it moves further from the eye; therefore, it appears to diminish.

<note>Diagram: Illustrating angular diminution of a moving line relative to a fixed eye at n. Leonardo distinguishes between "natural" circular perspective and "linear" perspective on a flat plane.</note>

# Right Page (Folio 216r)

Let .a. move toward .c. through the space .a.c. equal to the space .b.d. and I say that .a.b. will appear to diminish. The eye .m. being at .n. sees the base .a.b. through the <term>pyramid</term> <note>Leonardo uses "pyramid" to describe the cone of light rays traveling from an object to the eye.</note> .m.a.b. and let the base .c.d. be moved through the space .a.c. equal to .b.d. and let it be seen by the eye .m. through the pyramid .m.c.d. Therefore the angle .m.c.d. is smaller than the angle .m.a.b. and by this it is proved.

---
->By experience<-

By experience, the eye never moves to see one and the other extremity of a line if that line does not form a semi-diameter of the circle of which the eye is the center. As is seen, .n. in the middle of the line .a.b. sees that line through the angle .a.n.b. and then if it turns to see the extremity .a. and then .b. the angle will be smaller; but the angle .a.n.b. will be that which encompasses the whole line .a.b. because the eye does not see except through a single point which is the center of its motion and of the circle of which its visual line is the semi-diameter.

---

If the eye be immobile and the thing seen moves along the <term>ordinate</term> <note>A line perpendicular to the axis of vision.</note> of that eye, it will appear to diminish in size at every stage of its motion, even though it moves between the boundaries of two parallel lines. And let the base be .a.b. which moves between the two parallel lines .a.c. and .b.d. I say that moving .a. toward .c. and .b. toward .d. that base .a.b. will appear to diminish because the angle .m.c.d. is smaller than the angle .m.a.b.

---

<margin>
Of the line seen in foreshortening
</margin>
Line .a.b. seen from point .m. is seen through the angle .a.m.b. and if such a line is turned to .c.d. it will appear smaller as the angle .c.m.d. to which it subtends is smaller.

<note>Diagrams at bottom right: Two geometric studies showing how the angle of vision (the pyramid of vision) changes as a line segment is rotated or moved further away, demonstrating the principle of foreshortening (scorcio).</note>

<summary>This page details Leonardo's optical theories regarding how objects appear to shrink as they move away or rotate (foreshortening). He uses geometric proofs to show that the "visual angle" or "pyramid of vision" decreases as the distance from the eye increases.</summary>

# Folio 217 Recto (Right) and Facing Page (Left)

### [Left Page]

<note>Drawing of a serpentine or zig-zag structure, possibly representing a defensive wall or a water channel design.</note>

If one object is heavier than another, that one will be of lesser weight which is moved by a lesser force. For example, if we had two pieces of wood of the same weight, and one was long and the other <unclear>thick</unclear>, and they were <unclear>placed</unclear> in water so that they lay along the path of their length, and were pulled through the water by means of a weight—the weights being equal—we would see that the long one will be faster than the <unclear>short</unclear> one. This happens because the long one cleaves a smaller quantity of water than the short one. <note>Leonardo is observing early principles of aerodynamics and hydrodynamics: a streamlined shape encounters less resistance.</note>

In whatever way the nature of things is disposed, in a body of that figure which is most fit to penetrate the air or the water, it will be moved by that air or water with so much less effort as it has a thinner beginning and a wider end. <note>This describes a "teardrop" or "wedge" shape, which Leonardo correctly identified as efficient for movement.</note>

<note>Red stamp at the bottom left reads "B.N." (Bibliothèque Nationale de France).</note>

---

### [Right Page - Folio 217r]

<note>At the top right, a diagram of a triangular stack of circles (spheres or weights) and a horizontal line with marked intervals.</note>

Movement will be easier through the space of a same equality of time when the thing is moved by a same force; and this will be because the movement will be more united and will be more powerful in resisting the air or the water than if it were more scattered.

That thing which is moved by <term>percussion</term> <note>original: "percussione"; refers to a sudden impact or blow</note> will have so much less velocity as it is of greater quantity than the thing that moves it. This is proved by the sixth [proposition] of this [treatise] which says that if a force moves a thing through a certain space in a certain time, it will move half of that thing through the same space in half the time.

<note>Large diagram on the right illustrating optics and shadow formation. A point source of light projects rays past an object onto a surface.</note>

<margin>
luminous ray
</margin>
<margin>
point of the shadow
</margin>
<margin>
opaque body
</margin>
<margin>
light
</margin>

That thing will be heavier which, by an equal force, is moved with more slowness. That thing will be lighter which, by an equal force, is moved with more velocity.

That thing will be of lesser weight which is moved by a lesser force.

<note>Vocabulary list: percussion, luminous ray, opaque body, light, weight, velocity, force</note>

<summary>Leonardo investigates the relationship between an object's shape and its resistance in water or air, alongside fundamental laws of motion and the geometry of shadows. He concludes that streamlined shapes move faster and that the speed of an object under impact is inversely proportional to its mass.</summary>

### [Folio 220r]

If the air is tinted with green-blue between the eye and a dark object, it will make that object appear to be of the same color; and the more remote that object is from the eye, the more it will be tinted by such a color.

---

No body will be seen in its true color if the space between the eye and that body is tinted with any color, just as the blue air makes the distant mountains appear blue, and tinted glass makes every object seen through it appear to be of its own tint.

No object will be seen in its true form if the space between the eye and that object is of non-uniform density, such as air dense with smoke or vapors, or air that is heated by the sun, or <term>wavy glass</term><note>original: "uetro ondiato"; likely referring to crown glass or glass with imperfections that distort light.</note>, or water that is moving and of varying densities. That body will be of its true form which is seen through a uniform medium, such as clear air or <term>still water</term><note>original: "acqua quieta".</note>.

<note>Optical diagrams at the top right show light rays passing through apertures into an eye or chamber.</note>

<note>The bottom right section contains geometric studies, including circles with inscribed triangles, squares, and pentagons, as well as sketches of complex polyhedra (icosahedron and dodecahedron).</note>

<summary>Leonardo explores how the medium—such as fog, tinted air, or moving water—distorts the perceived color and shape of objects, a foundational principle of his 'atmospheric perspective.' The page also includes complex geometric studies of regular polyhedra and light projection.</summary>

<keywords>atmospheric perspective, optics, color theory, density, geometry, polyhedra, icosahedron, dodecahedron, visual perception</keywords>

# Manuscript Folio 223

The ratio of weights that hang perpendicularly in the center of other weights,
and what their power shall be in respect to one another, and how one
of the weights can be moved without the other; and how, if one wishes to
move two weights perpendicularly, one in the middle of the other, which is
of double or triple weight, what force will be
necessary to pull such a weight; and how the ratio of weights
in <term>equilibrium</term><note>original: "ponderanti"; referring to weights in a state of balance or being weighed.</note> shall be, and how the weight shall be greater if it is moved from one side
or the other; and if one happens to pull perpendicularly in the middle,
what force will be <unclear>required</unclear>.

If you double the weight, you will double the force that it will have
in the middle of the weight of another weight; and if it is of doubled
weights, it will be of a weight of sixths, and how many sixths it will be doubled;
and if it is of a weight of nine, and how much the weight will be moved;
and if you double the weight, the upper weight will have 8 in the pulleys;
and if you have 12, how much it will be moved in the middle of the weights
perpendicularly, the force being doubled; and if you double
the weight, you will have doubled the force, and thus the force goes on
re-multiplying as you double the weight in the
middle <unclear>of the</unclear> perpendicular.

<margin>
<note>Small diagrams of divided prisms/blocks inserted into the text flow on the left.</note>
</margin>

All the weights that hang perpendicularly upon the lever
on one side and the other of the weights that are in the middle
shall be of equal force in respect to the weights that remain above
which one wishes to move; and if you double the weight, you will have 12
of force in the pulleys; and if you double the weight again, you will have
24 of force in the pulleys; and thus the force goes on doubling
as you double the weight in the middle of the weights that you have
above which one wishes to move; and if you have 12 weights in the middle of the
6 weights above, you will have 48 of force in the pulleys.

---

From 3 of the weights on this side <unclear>they come</unclear> to 8 on the part over there;
and if you double the weight, you will have <unclear>double</unclear> force in the middle,
in the center of weight A which one wishes to move.

<note>Drawing of a pulley system with weights and a central balance beam.</note>

<note>Large geometric diagram showing a rectangular container or frame with organic shapes inside, possibly representing weights or centers of gravity.</note>

<note>Bottom right: Study of a heavy leather weight or bellows-like object.</note>

<note>Technical vocabulary used in this folio:</note>
*   **Weights** (pesi): The masses being moved or balanced.
*   **Perpendicularly** (perpendichularmente): Acting vertically, at a right angle to the horizon.
*   **Lever** (lieva): The mechanical advantage gained by a rigid bar.
*   **Pulleys** (poleggi): Blocks used to redirect force and gain mechanical advantage.
*   **Double/Quadruple** (raddoppierai/quadrupla): The proportional increase of force.
*   **Power** (potentia): The mechanical potential or force exerted.
*   **Sixths** (seste): Fractional divisions of weight or measure.

<note>The following sections contain drafts of letters or legal statements prepared by Leonardo during the inheritance dispute with his brothers following the death of their father, Ser Piero, and later, their uncle Francesco.</note>

If it is true that my brother must share in the property that my father has left us, [then] if my father has never left any vineyard, for this reason my brother is my debtor for the portion of the fruits of the vineyard that my uncle, Master Francesco, has given me; and this is because such a vineyard was bought by my uncle with his own money <note>original: "pecunia"</note> and not with that of my father.

Because the vineyard that my uncle gave me, he gave during my lifetime and gave me possession of it; and if it is true that my brother is to want a share of it, [then] if he is to give me [a share] of the property that my father left us—to this I respond that my father left no property—and if it is true that my brother is to have a share of the property that my uncle gave me, [he gave it] having given me possession during my lifetime.

# Folio 229
## British Museum <note>Indicated by the 'B.M.' stamp</note>

<margin>
The further it is from the **striker** <note>the source of the impact or force</note>, the slower the motion of that **wind** <term>c . d .</term> will be. And because **air** is a body that **compresses** much and **rarefies** much, it will be necessary to rarefy the calculation of its motion, which should be done according to these same rules; because air, when struck with velocity, **condenses**, and it flees from that condensation with a velocity equal to its percussion.
</margin>

This wind, because it passes between the two winds <term>c . d .</term>, will be a **collateral wind**. It is called "collateral" because it is a wind between two winds, which winds will be of equal power. Therefore, the course of this new wind will be through the middle of the base of the **triangle** <term>c . a . d .</term>. And because the triangle <term>a . b . c</term> has equal sides, the angle <term>b</term> will be of the same quantity as the angle <term>d</term> or <term>a . d . c</term>. Or rather, the motion of wind <term>d</term> will be like wind <term>c</term>. But if one of the winds is more powerful than the other, then wind <term>b</term> will be more bent toward the weaker wind, just as <term>d . a . b</term> would be.

<margin>
All the motions of winds that depart from the same cause will be of the same velocity at equal distances.
</margin>

---

-> This triangle of air will become sharper every day <-

<note>Study of the acceleration of falling bodies and the law of odd numbers.</note>

<margin>
If the motion of the falling object <term>cosa cadente</term> is of perpetual acquisition of velocity, and there is as much velocity in the final degree of its percussion as there is length in its motion, then the percussion of the motion <term>b . c . d .</term> will be as great as its length.

---

The space that is passed in the **second time** will be **triple** the space of the **first time**; and in the **third time** it will be **fivefold**; and in the **fourth time** it will be **sevenfold**. And thus follow the **odd numbers** <term>numeri impari</term>. And by this way, one finds the quantity of time and of the space that remains.
</margin>

<note>Central diagram showing a vertical line representing time/distance of a falling body, with arcs and horizontal divisions labeled with letters a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h. It illustrates the geometric progression of speed and distance.</note>

<margin>
If the motion is as 1 to 2, the space will be as 1 to 3. And if the motion is as 1 to 3, the space will be as 1 to 4.

---

This is proven by the triangle <term>a . b . c .</term>
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the behavior of converging winds and the physics of gravity, correctly identifying the 'law of odd numbers'—that a falling body covers distances in a ratio of 1, 3, 5, 7 over successive intervals of time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigations into fluid dynamics and mechanics. While the previous page focused on optics and atmospheric density, this page shifts to the physical movement of bodies through the air, specifically examining the relationship between a moving object, the resistance of the air in front of it, and the vacuum-filling force behind it.</meta>

### [Left Page]

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
If the matter of the <term>vapor</term> <note>original: "uapore" - here referring to a fluid or gaseous substance like air</note> shall be unequally moved by force, it will be of perfect sphericity.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
The air moved by the <term>impetus</term> <note>original: "i(n)peto" - the force or momentum imparted to a moving body</note> of the motion of the heavy mover strikes the posterior part of the motion.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
The air, being struck and giving way because it cannot divide itself with swift velocity, heaps itself up and creates density in front of the motion, and this is that which is the cause <insert>of resistance</insert>.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
The density of the air struck by the movement of the swift heavy body that moves within it is the cause of resistance to its course; and the motion of the air that moves within it to fill the <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "uachuo" - Leonardo often explored the Aristotelian idea that "nature abhors a vacuum," using it to explain propulsion</note> which that body leaves behind itself shall be that which drives the said body.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
If the air moves faster than the heavy body that moves within it, the heavy body will be driven by the air moved from behind; and if the air shall be less swift, it will be a resistance to the course of the said heavy body.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
The parts of the air shall be more or less thick according to whether they are more or less struck by the heavy body that moves within them; and those parts of the air shall be denser which are closer to the point of the motion of the bodies.

### The motions of bodies moved through the air
The motion of the heavy body through the air ought to be divided into 3 parts: of which the first shall be of the resistance of the air in front of itself; the second shall be of the driving of the air behind itself; the third shall be of the <term>rarity</term> <note>original: "rarita" - the thinning or lessening of density</note> of the vacuum created behind itself.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of aerodynamics, identifying three forces acting on a projectile: frontal air resistance, the compression of air, and the "push" provided by air rushing to fill the vacuum behind the object. <meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigation into mechanical motion, shifting from the specific gear mechanisms of the previous page to the fundamental physics of kinematics—specifically how multiple forces combine to create a single resulting path of movement.</meta>

## [Left Page]

If the same object is moved by two different powers <note>original: "potetie" - forces or powers</note>, one moving in a straight line and the other moving in an oblique line, the object moved will travel along a transverse line. This motion will be part of the motion of the first and part of the motion of the second; it will be closer to the line of motion of whichever power is the stronger <note>original: "gagliarda" - vigorous or strong</note>. The stronger that power is, the more its path of motion will be a straight line, as is shown by the motion of a ball fired from a <term>bombard</term> <note>original: "bombarda" - an early type of cannon or mortar</note>.

But if one of these powers is equal to the other, and the motion is mixed, as is seen in the motion of the pole of a ball or a circle <note>likely a wheel or disk</note> that turns upon a smooth plane, and this ball moves away from said pole in a straight line, I say that the motion of such a thing will move along a line which will always be curving. This is because circular motion is nothing other than a curved line and rectilinear motion is a straight line; therefore, since the object is moved partly by one and partly by the other line, it is necessary that it creates a line mixed of straight and curved, which will be a perpetual curvature. This is shown by the motion of a ball moved through the barrel of a <term>rotola</term> <note>original: "rotola" - likely a rotating device or a type of round shield used in a mechanical context</note> above its pole, and similarly by the tiller of a mill that is moved by water.

<margin>
But if one of these powers is double the other, and one is along a straight line and the other along a curved line, the motion of the object will be triple the movement of the single power and will be more similar to the line of the <unclear>greater</unclear> motion.
</margin>

---

## [Right Page]

If two powers, one of which is double the other, move along straight lines, I say that the motion of the object moved will be along a straight line which will be double in length to that of the lesser power, and it will be <unclear>longitudinally</unclear> <unclear>equidistant</unclear> between the two lines of motion of the two powers.

<note>Leonardo illustrates these principles with several diagrams showing intersecting vectors. The labels (a, b, c, d, p, o, etc.) denote points of origin and destination for the forces described.</note>

<margin>
.a. .b. .c. .d.
.p. .o. .n. .m.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the "composition of motions," explaining how an object moves when acted upon by two different forces simultaneously, such as combined linear and circular paths. He correctly identifies that the resulting path (the resultant vector) depends on the relative strength and direction of the contributing forces.</summary>
<keywords>kinematics, composition of forces, ballistics, circular motion, rectilinear motion, physics of water mills, geometry of motion</keywords>

### [Left Page - Folio 244v]

The air moves as much by the percussion <note>impact or strike</note> made in it by the instrument that strikes it, as the motion of that instrument itself. The air is moved by this percussion, and this happens because the air cannot be compressed without giving way to the instrument that strikes it; wherefore the air, fleeing the site occupied by the instrument, <unclear>bends</unclear> and occupies the site that the instrument <unclear>leaves</unclear>. And this which I say is proven by the reasoning of a <term>vessel</term> <note>original: "vasi" - a container or jar</note> full of water, in which, while the water does not exit, no other body can enter; and if it should exit through a crack, as much of a body enters as much of that water will exit. And as much air is driven out by the instrument as the instrument moves through the air; and as much as it spreads out, so much less will its force be. Wherefore, by this it appears that the greater the distance from the member <note>the part of the machine or body</note> that strikes, the less will be the force of the percussion of that air.

### [Right Page - Folio 245r]

#### On percussion in liquid bodies

If a blow should be given in the middle of a body of liquid matter, it will be felt in every part of it at the same time and with equal force at the boundaries of that liquid body. Because, giving the blow in the middle of a liquid body, that liquid cannot be compressed in the part struck without pushing the neighboring parts on every side; for which reason the pressure of those parts penetrates from part to part, so that the blow is felt throughout the whole body. And this same thing will happen with the air, the more it is compacted within itself; the more it is compacted, the more it will become similar to the <term>nature</term> <note>original: "natura" - the inherent physical properties</note> of water.

<note>Horizontal bar diagram divided into four sections labeled n, m, p, q</note>

The longer the percussion made by the air against an instrument of equal width, the more laborious will be the motion of that instrument through the air; because the air will be so much less flexible <note>original: "piegabile"</note> the further it is from the sides of that instrument; and the further it moves away from the sides, the less it bends; and the less it bends, the more resistance it creates.

<margin>
<note>A column of four right-angled triangles of varying heights, illustrating geometric proportions related to the text on percussion.</note>

n p d
n p d o
n p d q
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo explains that air and water are incompressible in certain contexts, meaning they must displace or "bend" around a striking object. He concludes that air resistance increases the further the air is from the edges of the object, as it has less room to move out of the way.</summary>

## f. 245v

<margin>A</margin>
On the right and oblique <term>antiparallel</term> <note>A geometric term Leonardo uses to describe lines or figures that are inversely proportional or positioned in opposition to parallel lines.</note>.
If a right antiparallel is made to the oblique triangle, and it is right to the right triangle, it will be of as much <term>power</term> <note>original: "potētia" - in this context, it refers to the area or geometric value of the shape.</note> as the oblique triangle and its right [counterpart], when they are of the same height above the same base. This thing could not be done without making a right antiparallel to the oblique triangle, because by making the right [triangle] upon the same base, it would result in less power than the oblique one; which difference would be as much as the oblique antiparallel made to the right triangle.

And concerning the right antiparallel to the right [triangle], let it be of the same height and the same base. One shall be of the same <term>ratio</term> <note>original: "ragiōe"</note> to the other as one is to the other right [line] of the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "ipotenusa" - the longest side of a right-angled triangle.</note>. Because one right [shape] results in a ratio to the other according to its base and height, when one is of the same base and same height as the other; while they are made of the same ratio to one another, while one results as right and the other as oblique. So that the difference will be right to the hypotenuse; [the] worst <note>Leonardo likely means the most extreme or least efficient case.</note> shall be of the same base and height, and of the same ratio to one another as results while it is of the same base.

The water that strikes a blade of a water wheel never moves it with as much force as it would if that same water—

<note>Main text at the bottom right, expanding on hydraulic theory.</note>

By this, it is demonstrated how water striking the blades of a water wheel never moves it with as much force as if that same water were applied with the thrust of weight <term>thrust of weight: the pressure exerted by the volume/mass of water (gravity) rather than just its speed</term> upon that wheel. This is because the impact <note>original: "urto"</note> by itself has no weight, and therefore it cannot give force to something that does not have it.

# [Folio 258]

<note>Sketch of a stone fortification wall with battlements and a circular gun port.</note>

<note>Sketch of a large bombard (a heavy medieval cannon) on a wooden sled carriage, shown at the moment of firing with smoke and flame erupting from the muzzle and the touch-hole.</note>

To make coarse gunpowder of good quality: take for every pound 8 parts of <term>saltpeter: a key ingredient in gunpowder, also known as potassium nitrate</term>, 2 parts of charcoal, and two ounces of sulfur. Mix everything together and grind it until it is sufficiently fine. When you load the <term>bombard: a large-caliber cannon used for hurling heavy stone balls</term>, to make a hundred-pound charge, put in 25 pounds of powder. The carriage must be positioned at the mark, being 400 paces from the target; or soon you will have the measurement, and it will be necessary for you to keep the aim a little low because of the way the shot rises <note>Leonardo is noting the "loft" or trajectory of the projectile, advising the gunner to compensate for the natural upward arc of the ball</note>.

<margin>
B.M. <note>British Museum ownership stamp</note>
</margin>

---

<note>Sketch of a thorny, knotted branch or root.</note>

To make a dried <term>ox sinew: the tough fibrous tissue (tendon) of a bull, used in mechanical devices for its elasticity</term> burn: take the sinew and boil it in <term>petroleum oil: "olio petronio," likely a crude mineral oil or naphtha</term> and in common oil <gloss>with wormwood</gloss>. And when you have boiled it for two hours or more, put it in running water and let it stay for 10 to 12 hours. Then place it in the air and bend it with your strength, and it will become like a living spring or <unclear>spropicie</unclear> the sinew in this way. Afterward, put it in a nearby willow casing and first let it boil in <term>aqua vitae: "water of life," a concentrated alcoholic spirit</term> <gloss>with wormwood</gloss> in a bowl. Then put it in the water, and it will suffice to burn for a long time; and this is a proven thing.

To dye bone white into green: put the bone in a copper vessel and boil it with <term>verdigris: the green pigment that forms on weathered copper</term> and as much milk as is needed to keep the bone submerged. Seal the vessel and place it in warm manure <note>Manure was used in early chemistry as a source of steady, low-level heat for fermentation or slow reactions</note>. At the end of 6 days, you will find the bone turned green throughout.

To make bone yellow: take <term>verjuice: "agresto," the tart juice of unripe grapes</term>, the juice of sweet oranges, and <term>turmeric: "curcumina," a yellow spice used as a dye</term>. Mix them together and then put the bone inside. Afterward, wash it with cold water and wipe it well. Then place it in <gloss>wine</gloss> <insert>in wine</insert> of a type that is not too strong, and let it stay for 12 days, and it will be done.

To make <insert>glue</insert> that is very strong and fears neither water nor fire: take white earth <note>original: "terra biacha," likely pipe clay or kaolin</note> and pulverize it, and mix it with egg white, and coat whatever you wish; it is most excellent.

To make another very strong glue for joining glass and crystal: take liquid varnish <note>original: "vernice ligha," likely a resinous spirit varnish</note>, <unclear>pucha</unclear> and <unclear>tupira</unclear>, and temper it with egg white; apply it and coat what you wish, and it will be sealed.

To make glue for sticking stones together: take mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, good minium <note>red lead pigment</note>, dragon's blood <note>a bright red plant resin</note>, pitch, and white lead—take an equal amount of each. Add a third part of the aforementioned things and boil them all together in a pot over the fire with the blood of a goat boiled with vinegar and <term>apella: likely a reference to a specific plant juice or a corrupted chemical term</term>; put it inside and cook it.

To make <term>pasta: a thick adhesive or cement</term> for sticking marble: take liquid varnish and white lead, and grind it 3 times with clear water; each time you have passed it through, mix it together and coat what you wish to join.

To break iron: take the scale of the iron <note>original: "ferrughine," the flaky oxidation produced when iron is forged</note> when it is beaten and pound it very well; make it into a powder and then take "man's water" <note>a common Renaissance euphemism for urine, used for its ammonia content in tempering</note> and fresh goat's blood and a little <unclear>panatara</unclear> and mix them together. When you have finished, temper the iron 3 times in the aforementioned things, and the fourth time in water, and you will cut with confidence.

To make paper cannons <note>original: "schioppi di charta," small pyrotechnic devices or firecrackers</note>: first, make the spindle according to their shape, and you must put some layers of parchment <note>original: "charta pecora"</note> and then others of fine powder. Close it up and <unclear>it will be hardened</unclear> on top, going layer by layer. To make the wicks: take a pot, put [the materials] inside, and add copper scale and powder to make a black soot; make small skeins of already spun wool the thickness of a man's thumb <note>original: "grossi come l'uomo," likely referring to the thickness of a finger or thumb</note> for the large wicks. Put them in the pot and let them boil until they are almost dry; then they are taken out and will be joined with <unclear>prepared bread</unclear> of that powder until it is equal to the others. Then they are placed on certain hot, dry stone slabs for <unclear>one hour</unclear>, or as long as is required.

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's focus on industrial adhesives and pyrotechnic mixtures, Leonardo now shifts his attention to the chemical extraction of saltpeter—a vital ingredient for gunpowder—and the construction of a specialized explosive device or firework.</meta>

To want to make saltpeter <note>original: "anitro," a variant of salnitro</note>, I want the crust or the earth from a pen in which there have been pigs or sheep or similar animals. And put this ground earth to soak in water from the Arno <note>the river flowing through Florence</note>. Make a <unclear>mixture</unclear> and let there be one and a half times more water than earth, and provide such a <unclear>stirring</unclear>. And let them incorporate one into the other, and let it stand for two days; and then stir it together again and strain the aforementioned material. Take the strained water and make it boil in a cauldron, and let it boil for 4 or 5 hours, or as much as you deem necessary, and skim it often. And then put the aforementioned water into refined vessels made of earth or wood, in small casks or flasks; and every day change the cloth <note>likely used as a filter or to cover the vessel</note> and let it stand for two hours in the open air. And then you will find the <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate, the primary oxidizing agent in gunpowder</term> attached to the bottoms of the flasks; and throw away the water and keep the saltpeter, and place it in the sun to dry until it is thoroughly dried.

# Equilibrium

<note>Mechanical diagram at top left: A horizontal beam system with multiple vertical supports and labeled points (a, b, d, s, m, p), illustrating a series of compound levers.</note>

The weight **a**, which is placed upon the arm of the lever **a b**,
which has 1/8 of the lever arm **c b**. The proportion
that **a b** has with the power <term>potenzia: the force or effort applied to a machine</term> **d f**, which is seen at the
point **f** between **s r** of the balance <note>original: "bancia," a variant of "bilancia" or balance beam</note> **s o**. For which
reason I say that the weight **a** shall be 8, and the weight **b** shall be 4,
and the weight **d** shall be 2, and the weight **s** shall be 1, and the weight **p** shall be 1/2,
and the weight **o** shall be 1/4, and the weight **m** shall be 1/8. And so, by
proceeding to infinity, one would go on multiplying the said weights.

---

<note>Mechanical diagram at top right: A horizontal graduated scale with numerical values in circles (100, 25, 200) and labeled points (r, a, s, b, d, f) representing a study of leverage ratios.</note>

It is the same to move 8 lbs <term>lb: abbreviation for libbra, the Italian pound</term> with a force of 4 as it is to move
100 lbs with a force of 50, and the same as moving **a** with **b**,
where the force is at **b** and the weight is at **a**; or rather at **s**, which
moves with the force **p**, [where the weight] is 100 and the force <insert>at</insert> **p** is 50.

Furthermore, if the force is at **d** and is 10, it will move 100 at **r**.
And if the force is 100 and is at **a**, and the weight is at **f**, which is
8—how much would the force be at **f** to move 800 at **a**? It
would be 100. And if the force is at **r**, and is 10, it will move 100 at **a**,
because the weight at **a** is 10 times slower than the motion at **r**. <note>Leonardo identifies the "Golden Rule" of mechanics: what is gained in force is lost in speed or distance.</note>

Having recognized that a weight of 1 lb at **r** overcomes a weight of 100 at **f**,
and a weight of 18 lbs at **b** overcomes a weight of 36 at **f**.
And if a weight of 100 lbs were at **a**, and the force at **b** were 12, and at **s** it were
6, and at **d** it were 3, and the weight at **n** were 1 1/2, and at **r** it were 3/4;
because 100 lbs at **a** is sustained by 12 at **b**, and by 6 at **s**, and by 3 at **d**,
and by 1 1/2 at **n**, and by 3/4 at **r**. And if the weight at **a** is 100, its force at **r** will be
a hundredth part, that is, 1 lb.

Concerning balances born from the multiplication of levers, which allow great weights
to be supported with little force, as you see above.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the mathematical ratios of compound levers, demonstrating how a small amount of force can balance a much larger weight through successive mechanical advantages. He concludes that the force required is inversely proportional to the distance from the fulcrum and the speed of the motion.</summary>

The reason that is made here is that one must imagine the eye <note>Leonardo is setting up a geometric proof for his theory of the "visual pyramid."</note>

### [f. 272v]

If the air were so dense that water could form hills upon it, as it does on the earth, the light of the sun, striking those hills, would create a ray of light in each of them, just as it does on the hills of the earth struck by the sun; and likewise, it would create shadows in its valleys.

We shall say, then, that the air below the moon is similar to the air above the moon, but the air between us and the moon is of another substance, which <unclear>facing</unclear> the sun is illuminated by the light of that same sun, just as the pupil of the eye does; from which light the moon is the shadow of the dense substance, and it is similar to the light that we see in the air above the moon, which light is taken from us and hidden by the air that is between us and it, because such air is more luminous than the light which is beyond that air. And such light would not be darkened by the shadow of the earth, because the air that is between us and the moon is illuminated by being in view of the sun, and hides such light; but when the moon is eclipsed <note>original: "ecclisata"</note>, then the air, which is interposed between us and the shadow of the earth, does not receive light from the sun and consequently hides that shadow of the earth, which is beyond such air.

If you wished to prove in what way the rays of the sun pass through the hairs of golden hair <note>original: "peli de’ capelli del’oro"</note>, stain a glass in the smoke of a candle—nothing more than a <unclear>faint</unclear> smoke—and then place it in the sun and see if you see those same rays of light that I say are seen in the hairs of golden hair. And if this is true, you will be able to say that the golden hairs are permeated by the sun and are not the hairs of an opaque metal.

---

The mist which is interposed between the eye and the object seen has no proper quality of its own, nor a specific color, but it accompanies the air in front of it and that behind it, in such a way that by itself it has no <unclear>part</unclear> of mixed color, nor of brightness, nor of darkness. Therefore, the perspective practitioners <note>original: "prospetici" — referring to artists or theorists of optics</note> say that things which <unclear>stand</unclear> at a distance are seen through the thickness of the air and appear whiter; and this is false for two reasons. The first is that the interposed air is not of a denser medium <note>Leonardo is arguing that the air's consistency remains uniform rather than thickening like a physical lens</note>, and the other is that the radiant lines <note>visual rays</note> do not bend in passing through this air; therefore, objects do not enlarge or diminish because of such interposed air.

<note>Leonardo argues against contemporary perspective theories that claim air thickness magnifies distant objects, asserting instead that air density is uniform in these conditions and does not refract visual rays in a way that alters size.</note>

<meta>This page shifts from the optical theories of the previous page to Leonardo's hydraulic studies. ### On Motion

If a river <note>original: "fiumana" — a large or torrential river</note> flows for a short distance through a steep valley into a plain, it doubles its velocity over that distance; and through the space it flows in said valley, it increases in speed, so that as it enters the plain, it doubles its velocity.

When the bed of the river is of an unequal surface, the surface of the water will also be unequal, because it strikes against the heights of the bed and rises, and in the hollows of that same bed a descent is perceived; and such rising and falling causes the surface of the water to result in an uneven state.

<margin>
<note>Small diagrams of river junctions labeled with letters a, b, c, d, f.</note>
</margin>

There is much to investigate regarding the motion of water in rivers, which is varied for many reasons: namely, because of the winding course of the river, which strikes against one bank and then the other, becoming a reunited and rapid current. Such a river will have an oblique <note>slanted</note> surface, since the water that strikes the bank will be higher than that in the middle of the river; and the same happens on the other side of the bank, because it bounces back to the other bank, creating a continuous crossing of the water from one bank to the other throughout its entire course.

Of rivers of equal depth and width, the one that is straighter will be the more rapid, since a straight line is the shortest line between two points; and water along the shortest line will be more rapid than along a winding one, because in the winding one it strikes the banks and retards its motion, while in the straight one it does not strike any bank, but passes through the middle way of the river with all its velocity without any impediment.

---

### How one must give order to anatomy

In what way one should give order to anatomy: in your book, you shall first make the bare bones, and then you shall make the manner of joining them together; and then you shall make the nerves <note>tendons/ligaments</note> that join them together; then you shall make the muscles that move them; then you shall make the blood vessels and the veins; then the nerves <note>sensory nerves</note> that give sensation; and then the muscles that give motion to the arm and the shoulders; and then you shall make the skin that covers the man and his muscles and his bones and his vessels and his nerves.

Then you shall do the same for women, etc., and for children and for the elderly, because the anatomy of the man and the woman is different, and old age is different in the muscles and in the nerves and bones and in everything; because the old man is drier and more rigid, and has less blood and less heat, and less nerve <note>vital force/sinew</note> and less muscle, and is more bony <note>original: "ossido"</note> and thinner and more fragile and rougher and darker, and of weaker sense, and of weaker motion, and of weaker intellect.

### [Folio 278v]

<margin>
**The logic of weight**
</margin>

If a weight of 200 is placed upon 8 lengths of a support <note>original: "polo", referring here to a supporting point or pillar</note> and that support is the eighth part of the total length of the beam, I say that such a support will sustain 175 of the weight and the other support will sustain 25. The logic is this: you say that the support is the eighth part of the beam, therefore 7 eighths remain in the making; therefore, the eighth part of the weight will be sustained by the other support, and 7 eighths will be sustained by the one that is near the weight.

<note>Drawing of a vertical pillar or beam with horizontal markers and measurements (2, 8, 120)</note>

The weight that is between 2 supports will be sustained so much more by one than the other as it is closer to one than the other.
The logic is this: if the weight is placed on support **a**, that support **a** will sustain all the weight and support **b** will sustain none of it. And if the weight is in the middle of the beam between **a** and **b**, each support will sustain half of it.

### [Folio 279r]

<margin>
**The logic of weight**
</margin>

To know how much weight each support will sustain that holds up the beam loaded with weight in those places which are not equidistant to the supports.

If you wish to know how much weight each support will sustain when the weight is placed in any part of the length of a beam, do this: know how many times the weight is closer to the support that you wish to search for first than it is to the other support. As it would be if the beam were 8 <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement, roughly the length of an arm</note> and the weight were one braccio away from support **a** and 7 braccia from support **b**. I say that support **a** will sustain 7 times more weight than support **b**; and to know how much each will sustain, divide the whole weight into 8 parts and give 7 to support **a** and one to support **b**.

<note>Geometric diagram of a horizontal beam with weight distribution points</note>

---

960 / 64 = 15

<note>Drawing of a vertical column with a graduated scale on the right</note>

The weight that is placed upon the beam sustained by 2 supports will be sustained so much more by one support than the other as it is closer to one than to the other. The logic is this: look at how many times the length that is between the weight and support **b** goes into the length that is between the weight and support **a**, and that many times support **b** will be heavier than support **a**.

# Folio 250

If a lead ball weighing 2 pounds <note>original: "lb" or "libra"</note> were at the end of its fall through the air with a velocity of 100 <term>braccia</term> <note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note> per minute of time, and the motion were in rarefied air; and if a similar ball of the same weight moved through dense air—half as dense as the first air—and that ball in that dense air had at the end of its motion that same velocity of 100 braccia per minute; I say that if the ball falling through rarefied air strikes another similar ball that is immobile and suspended by a thread in free air (which is identical to the first ball in material and shape), I say that the impact <note>original: "percussione"</note> of the ball falling in rarefied air will be of double the power than the impact of the ball falling in dense air.

I also say that if the motion of a ball were at a speed of 100 braccia per minute, and the same motion of a similar ball were at a speed of 50 braccia per minute, I say that the faster ball will strike with quadruple the force into the other similar ball that is immobile and suspended as above; and this arises because the blow of double velocity quadruples the force <note>Leonardo is intuiting the relationship between velocity and kinetic energy, though his proportions here are specifically focused on the "doubling" effect of speed on impact</note>.

Furthermore, if you shoot a lead ball of one pound in rarefied air with a bow of a given power, I say that said ball will go further than if it were shot in dense air, and the motion will be faster in rarefied air than in dense air until the end of its travel; and these cases arise because dense air resists more than rarefied air and blunts the motion of the ball more than the rarefied. And this is proven in water, which is 800 times denser than air, and for this reason a ball shot into water immediately loses its motion; but it would not do so if it were shot in a vacuum, but because a vacuum does not exist in nature... <note>Leonardo touches on the Aristotelian "horror vacui," the belief that nature does not allow for empty space.</note>

<note>Small diagram on the bottom right: A triangular stack of spheres representing a pyramid.</note>

If you wish to know how many balls are in one of these triangular forms—to know how many balls are in small and large triangles—you must do as follows: multiply the number of balls that are along one side by itself, then add to that sum half the number of the balls of said side, and you will have the sum of the balls of that flat triangle. And if you wish to know how many balls are in the pyramidal triangle, multiply the sum of the balls of the flat triangle by one-third of the number of the levels <note>original: "gradi"</note> of the balls on the sides of that triangle, having added the number of levels of the same side.

<summary>Leonardo investigates how air density and velocity affect the force of impact and projectile distance, concluding with a geometric formula for calculating the number of spheres in a triangular stack.</summary>
<keywords>ballistics, air resistance, impact force, vacuum, geometry, pyramidal numbers, arithmetic, fluid dynamics</keywords>
