# Folio 263

<note>This page contains Leonardo’s characteristic mirror script, written from right to left. The text is accompanied by several geometric diagrams exploring the mechanics of the lever and balance.</note>

<note>Two diagrams at the top showing simple horizontal balances with weights marked a, b, c, and d.</note>

If a balance is given which moves upon the pivot <term>a</term> <note>original: "polo .a.", referring to the fulcrum or axis of rotation</note> and the weight **b** is removed from the perpendicular line of such a pivot, I say that the weight **b** desires to return itself under that pivot **a**.
And its force will be so much greater as it is further removed from the perpendicular of the said pivot; and the same will be true of the balance **c d**.

That part of the balance will be of greater weight which is more remote from the center of its revolution, and that which is closer to said pivot will be of lesser weight. The proof is shown by the first balance, upon which it has been proven how the weight **b** desires to fall under the pivot **a** along the perpendicular line **a n**; and the same will be true of the balance **c d**, through which one sees the weight **d** desiring to descend under the pivot **c** along the perpendicular line **c o**.

---

<note>Diagram in the middle showing a balance arm at an angle with multiple vertical lines indicating weights or forces.</note>

<margin>
On the force of weights that hang below the arm of the balance.
</margin>

Because that part of the arm which extends furthest from the center of motion will be of greater force, and the body of said weight will be in natural motion if it is <unclear>greater</unclear>.

---

<note>Two complex diagrams at the bottom showing balances with pulleys and multiple weights attached by strings.</note>

By what means it may be brought about that the arm of the balance weighs <unclear>equally</unclear> in the same proportion in which its power <note>original: "potenzia", referring to the mechanical advantage or potential force</note> of the weights is between the <unclear>center</unclear> and the power.

Concerning the balance in which the arms are equal and the motion of these arms is varied from equidistance; as much as one of the arms of this balance extends from the center of motion of said balance, so much the other is shortened, in such a way that neither the power nor the weight of this balance ever increases or decreases.

Every weight that is outside of its center of its support <note>original: "sustētatione"</note> desires to return itself to such a center.

<note>Technical vocabulary used: balance, pivot/pole, perpendicular, force, weight, revolution, power/potential, center of motion, support.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of the balance, explaining how a weight's "force" increases with its distance from the pivot and its tendency to seek equilibrium directly beneath the fulcrum. # [Folio 62v]

<note>Anatomical and geometric study of the eye and the transmission of light rays through pyramidal intersections. Leonardo conceptualizes light as traveling in "pyramids" where the base is the object and the apex is the eye.</note>

Because the boundaries of the pyramidal rays <note>original: "razzi piramidali"</note> stop in the center of the eye, within said eye they cannot occur one after the other, but all together in a single point filled with infinite boundaries of pyramidal rays. This is because the air fills itself with infinite luminous rays among which one gives way to the other without occupying <note>obstructing</note> one another. And thus the air fills with infinite boundaries among which the eye finds itself wherever it may be, and it moves through the air filled with such boundaries. And so the said boundaries fill the surface of the eye wherever it moves through the air. And because the air cannot be filled with infinite boundaries filled with the eye—because it is not possible for the air to be filled with boundaries of eyes, as the part would be lacking in what the whole lacks—because the eye is a very small part of the air and does not fill more of that air than its own size. For which reason the eye sees only through the boundaries of the pyramidal rays which are everywhere, because the air is full of these pyramids which stop everywhere upon opaque bodies. And thus they fill the air with themselves, just as they occur for the eye filled with such boundaries; for they fill the surface of the eye wherever it moves through the air. And because the air cannot be filled with infinite boundaries filled with the eye <margin>the reason is this</margin>

The reason is because the air that is in between is filled with infinite luminous boundaries, and the eye moves through that air; it does not move through boundaries filled with the eye, because it is not possible to fill the air with infinite boundaries of the eye. But the eye is only one, and only one has been given, filled with as much air as its size; and it moves through the air filled with boundaries of luminous rays, which fill its surface everywhere.

# [Left Page - Folio 157v]

<note>Diagram at top: A horizontal beam with pulleys and weights labeled 's', 'm', and 'b'.</note>

Whether it is possible for weight **m** to pull weight **s**, and let it be the weak force.
If the weak force **s** pulls weight **m**, let **s** be the weak force and **m** the weight; let **s** be 2 and **m** be 4, then the movement of **m** will be 2 <term>braccia</term> <note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally a "arm's length," roughly 23 inches</note> and that of **s** will be 4 braccia.
And if **m** is 4 and is pulled by **s** which is 2, the movement of **s** will be 4 braccia and that of **m** will be 2 braccia.
As **m** goes 2 braccia, **s** goes 4; therefore, half the weight of **m** will be found equal to the force of **s**.
And this occurs when the weight of **m** is in the middle of the rope **a b**, and the ends of such a rope are level on the same plane.

<note>Middle diagram: A central weight suspended by a rope passing through two lateral pulleys, forming a triangle.</note>

Let a natural experiment be made, and it will be found that the part of the weight that hangs perpendicularly is the entire cause of the motion, and that which hangs obliquely is not the cause except for as much as its obliquity approaches the perpendicular.
And this is proven by the reasoning of scales <note>the principle of the lever</note>, because from every weight that hangs obliquely, as much force is removed as there is obliquity; and it happens in this manner.
The angle **a b c** is the angle of the natural motion of weight **n**.

<note>Bottom text block</note>

In what way one must weigh the force of the oblique rope that pulls the weight, and how one must find the true natural weight that is pulled by it; and this is proven by the scale.
Let the scale be **a b c**, its center be **b**, its force be **a**, and its weight be **c**.
I say that the force **a** will be as much as the weight **c**, because they are at an equal distance from the center **b**.
But if you wished to weigh the force of the rope **a d**, which pulls the weight **c**, you must find the line <note>original: "corda," here meaning a geometric line or chord</note> **b e**, which is perpendicular to the rope **a d**, and that will be the true distance of the force **a d** from the center **b**.

The weight that descends through a perpendicular line does not lose any of its natural heaviness, but that which descends through an oblique line loses as much of its natural weight as its line deviates from the perpendicular line; because as much as the path of the heavy body is <unclear>longer</unclear> than the perpendicular, so much is the heavy body lighter.

# [Right Page]

Where one arrives at the science of things through their proper reasons, no doubt occurs. <note>Leonardo argues that certain knowledge is only possible when based on logical, geometric "reasons" or principles.</note> Straight <unclear>circulation</unclear> <unclear>filling</unclear> <unclear>arrangements</unclear> and the matter of the <unclear>pole</unclear>, circumfusion, hollow paths with circulation and the matter of <unclear>reasons</unclear>.

Each face of a solid body is **composed** in such a way that its reason <note>its mathematical proportion or logic</note> is terminated and **limited** within other **faces** of another body. And this is always fulfilled by the reason of **points**, which, being in the middle of two bodies, each of them has its part of the whole, always **undivided**, so that this point is between one and the other and participates in each. And if it is so that it belongs to both, even if it were divisible, it would still have one part of the one and the other part of the other, so that it would always have the reason of a body, being terminated between two **faces**, as has been demonstrated previously by the reason of the point of the gaze filled **with air**. <note>Leonardo is exploring the nature of boundaries: a point or a surface is the shared limit where one body ends and another begins.</note>

<note>Geometric diagram: A circle circumscribing a pentagon with internal lines connecting vertices, possibly exploring symmetry or division.</note>

If you find triangles, the triangle being <unclear>equal</unclear>, it is contained by the reason of **matter**; therefore the body is terminated between two faces, which faces are born between themselves and other bodies within which it is included, so that it is a body by the reason of a body and not of a point. Because if it is a body, it is a member of the whole sum of the body from which it is extracted; therefore it will fill with air just as the whole body filled. But if it were by the reason of a point, then it would fill by the reason of a point and not of air.

This is so clear in the nature of the cause of its simplicity that there is no need for any **demonstration** or proof; it simply suffices to open the eye of reason and look at the said proportion, which is always of equal **measure** at every point of its motion.

This pentagon will be filled by the reason of triangles within itself and other pentagons that **can** be made by the simple motion of one and the other **pole**, so that by the reason of triangles one will go on filling and terminating between them, filling the points through the spaces of the matter which is included within the said triangles. And if one increases through the other, one will always go on filling the points and the triangles between them in infinite ways until such time as the said matter is fulfilled by the reason of these triangles.

<note>Geometric diagram: A rhombus or diamond shape divided by its diagonals and further internal lines, likely related to the text on filling spaces with triangles.</note>

---

In this reason, one will go on filling the points through the spaces of the matter; by the reason of these triangles, one will go on filling in infinite ways.

The same force of a simple motion can be changed into an infinite quantity of motions of other diverse forms by the reason of circulation, changing the said force into triangles which are equal or unequal to each other by the reason of base and height, so that the force of each of the triangles will always be a member of the same simple motion; thus, by the reason of triangles, one will go on changing said force.

<note>Diagrams: Two small triangles with lines extending from the vertices through the opposite centers, illustrating geometric projections or centers.</note>

And this filling of one of the triangles can be done in infinite ways, whereby every triangle would always have the reason of a body, so that by the reason of triangles one will go on filling the force of each simple motion; whereby, filling the points through the spaces of matter, one will always go on changing the force of a simple motion by the reason of these triangles.

One force of a simple motion is always membered <note>divided into parts</note> into diverse parts of other forces by the reason of circulation, so that one force is always a member of the other and they will always go on changing between themselves, so that the said force is always membered by the reason of these triangles within which it is included.

The force of a simple motion can always be changed in infinite ways by the reason of circulation and of other motions within which said force is included, always changing the said force by the reason of triangles within which said force is membered by the reason of these triangles within which it is included.

This same thing is understood in triangles of equal sides; between them, one will go on filling the points through the spaces of the matter which is included within the said triangles, so that the said matter will always be filled by the reason of these triangles until such time as the said matter is fulfilled by the reason of these triangles.

<summary>Leonardo explores the geometric foundations of physical matter and force, arguing that complex bodies and motions can be subdivided into triangles in infinite ways. # On Rivers

If the flowing water of the same river<insert>e</insert> <note>original: "fiume"</note> should be, in any part of it,
thicker and less swift than in its common width, it will by
necessity be more level in such a part than in other parts;
and if the water of the same river in any of its parts should be narrower
and swifter, it will by necessity be more level in such a part than in the others.

Because the water that moves in the same river<insert>e</insert> in every part
of said river, there passes in the same time a same quan-
tity of water, even though it may be of varying width or narrowness
and of varying height or depth.
If in the middle of its course it should be of as much depth as
its width, and that such depth and width be
entirely reciprocal to the reciprocal width and depth that the water
has in that same river<insert>e</insert> in another of its parts; in such reciprocal
exchange of water, it will be equal, and such velocity will be in its course—the water
that arrives at these widths and depths—because the equality with the length
of the reciprocal proportion makes equal velocity of the rivers; or
if it were not enough... <unclear>the reciprocal current</unclear>...

</margin>

without an equal quantity of water passing through every degree of the length of the river<insert>e</insert>,

<summary>Leonardo defines the law of continuity in river flow, arguing that the volume of water passing any point in a river remains constant over time by adjusting its velocity relative to the channel's width and depth. He uses the concept of "reciprocal proportion" to explain how water speeds up in narrow sections and slows down in wider ones.</summary>

### [Folio 28 verso]

The force of the weight shall be compared to the force of the movement just as the force of the movement shall be compared to the force of the weight. And if the weight is 100 and is moved by a motion that has 1 degree of velocity, and if you wished that such a weight were moved by 10 degrees of velocity, it would be necessary for the force of the <term>motor</term> <note>original: "motore"; the source of power or the person/thing applying force</note> to be 10 degrees; and it shall be as 1 is to 10, so 100 is to 1000. And if you wished that the weight were 1000 and the motor were 1, it would be necessary for the motor to be moved by 1000 degrees of velocity so that the weight might move by one degree of velocity.

<note>This text describes the inverse relationship between force and velocity in a mechanical system, effectively stating the fundamental principle of simple machines: what is gained in power is lost in speed/distance.</note>

<note>Below the text on the left are two small sketches of balances or vertical levers with weights.</note>

---

### [Folio 29 recto]

<note>The right page is dominated by diagrams of overbalanced wheels, a common study in Leonardo's exploration of perpetual motion and his ultimate proof of its physical impossibility.</note>

<margin>
Proof in the hammer
of a saw: if it
strikes with
force, it shall be moved
by a lighter
force than the hammer
itself is.
</margin>

<note>Upper right diagrams show wheels with weighted arms. One arm is labeled 'm'.</note>

<margin>
b h o water and likewise a —
the end of its [path] so that a m r
becomes all one mass or rather a single weight.
</margin>

a, b, e, f are the centers of the weights which, in every circular motion, will always be in an inverse motion; and it will be that one is opposite the other with equal distance from the center of the wheel. But if one were to compose this wheel in such a way that the weight at **f** departs from the center **m**, and that the one at **e** approaches the center **m**, it would result in the weight at **f** being more powerful than the weight at **e**. In that case, there would be <term>infinite motion</term> <note>original: "moto infinito"; Leonardo's term for perpetual motion</note>, which cannot be done in nature—that **f** be more powerful than weight **e** in respect to a single center.

<note>Leonardo argues here that while one might design a wheel where weights shift their distance from the center to create an imbalance, such a system cannot create perpetual motion because the equilibrium of the system as a whole remains constant relative to the single pivot point.</note>

<summary>Leonardo defines the mathematical relationship between force, weight, and velocity (mechanical advantage) and uses these principles to argue against the possibility of perpetual motion wheels.</summary>

The percussion made by a cord upon the object it strikes will be equal to its force. The reason is this: if you pull a cord between two points so that it is very taut, and then strike it in the middle, it will pull those two points toward itself with as much force as that of its percussion.

Let the luminous body be *m. n.* and the shaded body be *o. p.* and let the eye be *f.* I say that if the shadow *f.* <note>Leonardo here uses 'f' to denote the perceived shadow area relative to the eye's position</note> is seen by the eye *f.*, it will appear to be as much larger than its true size as it is closer to the eye than to the object that produces it.

</margin>

And by the sixth and seventh, the shadow *f.* will appear so much longer as the eye is closer to the shaded object.

### [Right Page - f. 24r]

<note>The right page consists of dense blocks of Leonardo's characteristic mirror writing, organized into distinct thematic paragraphs. The text below is translated from his Italian, which he wrote from right to left.</note>

Every body that is placed under the air, in whatever position it may be, will be seen by the eye through straight lines which, even if they are infinite, all converge in one and the same point, which is the point of the eye. <note>Leonardo is describing the "pyramid of sight," where all visual data from an object narrows down to a single point within the pupil.</note>

If, with equal weight, a ball of gold, one of lead, one of stone, and one of wood were placed in the air at the same height and were let fall at the same time, one would see the ball of gold be the first to strike the earth, then that of lead, then that of stone, and last that of wood. And this happens for no other reason than that the air resists the light substance more than the heavy, because this air will be more easily penetrated by the massive and heavy matter than by the light. <note>Leonardo is observing air resistance, though he predates the vacuum experiments of the 17th century which proved all objects fall at the same rate without air.</note>

The reason for such movement cannot be well shown if one does not first consider the quality of the movements of weights made through the air; these movements are always gaining <term>velocity</term> <note>speed in a specific direction</note> at every degree of space. This occurs because as the weight moves, it displaces the air, which, closing behind the weight, strikes it and drives it forward; and thus, the displaced air strikes it again and again. Therefore, the gain in movement proceeds from nothing other than the pressure of the air which, closing behind the weight, drives it. <note>This is Leonardo's theory of "impetus," where he incorrectly believes the air rushing in behind a falling object helps push it faster.</note>

If the <term>percussion</term> <note>the impact or strike</note> is made in a straight line, it will be of much greater power the more the weight is of greater heaviness, or the more the movement is of greater velocity.

<note>In the right margin, there are small geometric sketches, including a triangle and a small circular diagram, likely illustrating the text on impact and linear motion.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explores the physics of vision, arguing that all sight lines converge in the eye, and investigates the laws of falling bodies, noting how air resistance affects different materials like gold and wood. He attempts to explain acceleration through the "closing" of air behind a moving object.</summary>

<keywords>optics, perspective, gravity, air resistance, velocity, percussion, impetus, mechanics, gold, lead, wood</keywords>

### [Right Page - Folio 65r]

If a cord is pulled by two such <term>opposite directions</term><note>original: "uer-so oppositi"</note> that it places a weight in the middle along a straight line between two movers, that weight will never remain in the power of said movers between them in a straight line, unless the cord breaks; and this is proved on the other side of this leaf, that a weight *n*, if it is pulled by *m* and *f* in a straight line <unclear>not</unclear> to *p*, this weight *n* will never stay between *m* and *f* in a straight line, even if the cord were 100,000 <term>braccia</term><note>A Florentine unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> long and the weight *n* were only a single grain; because a weight will be so much heavier as it is more removed from its <term>perpendicular</term><note>The vertical line of gravity.</note>, and the mover will be so much less powerful as its cord becomes more <term>oblique</term><note>Slanted or angled.</note>.

<note>The text above explains that no matter how much force is applied by two "movers" (motori), a weighted rope can never be perfectly straight because gravity always acts upon the weight, effectively increasing its resistance as the angle of the rope becomes more oblique.</note>

## [Left Page - Verso]

<note>Large diagram at the top illustrating rays of light reflecting off a concave (parabolic or spherical) mirror surface. The lines converge towards a central axis, demonstrating the focal properties of the 'burning mirror' (specchio ustorio).</note>

These lines are those which carry the <term>images</term> <note>original: "spetie" — species, the visual forms or "simulacra" of objects traveling through the air</note> of bodies to the surface of concave mirrors; and because the air does not possess a reflective quality in itself, <unclear>therefore</unclear> they will not be seen unless there were <unclear>dust</unclear> or mist.

<margin>
The closer the angle of reflection is to the center of the mirror, the more the ratio of its reflection will be similar to the ratio of its <term>incidence</term> <note>The angle at which the light first hits the surface</note>.
</margin>

<note>Geometric diagram in the lower half showing a curved segment (representing the moon or a mirror) with lines of incidence and reflection marked by letters, analyzed for their angular relationships.</note>

Whether it is possible that the moon, being spherical and polished, does not return the <term>image</term> <note>original: "idolo" — literally 'idol', used here to mean the reflected likeness or 'ghost' of the sun</note> of the sun in any part of itself to us who look at it.

It is proved <unclear>by</unclear> the logic of reflected rays that, the closer the angle of reflection is to the center of the mirror, the more the ratio of its reflection will be similar to that of its incidence.

Let the moon be at **m**, the eye at **n**, and the sun at **o**. I say that if the moon were polished like a mirror, the sun would be seen in it at that point where the angle of incidence is similar to that of the reflection.

The moon has no light of its own, but receives as much from the sun as it sees of the sun's surface; and the earth sees as much of it as the moon sees of its own <term>brightness</term> <note>original: "alburno". # On the Nature of the Moon and its Light

<margin>
moon
earth
->sun<-
</margin>

<note>Diagram showing the Sun casting light onto a smaller sphere (Earth/Moon) with rays forming a conical shadow.</note>

In this part, it is proved how the moon has no light of its own, but only receives from the sun that light which it then reflects to us; and of that light, it returns to us as much as it receives from the sun. And if the moon were a mirror <note>original: "spechio"</note>, it would return only a single point of the sun's light; and if the moon were of a polished surface like a mirror and were not spherical, it would return all the sun's light to a single place; but being spherical and of a surface that is not lustrous, it spreads the sun's light through the entire hemisphere that is illuminated.

And if the moon were a mirror and spherical, it would not return light to us except in a single point of its roundness, but not from its entire sphericity as it does now, where we see it all brightened, except for that part which does not see the sun.

Because the moon is a spherical and solid body, if it were transparent, it would not receive the sun's light, but it would pass through it; and if it were a mirror, it would not produce light except in a single point.

I say, therefore, that the moon has no light of its own, but returns to us as much as it receives from the sun; and of that light, it returns to us as much as it receives from the sun.

---

### To the Reader and the Nature of Shadows

O you who speculate on the nature of things, do not believe yourself to know the things that nature, by herself, ordinarily conducts; but rejoice in knowing the purpose of those things that are designed by your mind.

Every <term>opaque body</term> <note>A body that does not allow light to pass through it.</note> that finds itself between the sun and the eye will appear of a dark obscurity, unless its surface is illuminated by some other reflected light.

And if this light be wider than the opaque body, then its shadow will terminate in a point, and will be of a pyramidal shape.

But if the light be of equal width to the opaque body, then its shadow will be of equal width to the opaque body, and will be of a columnar shape.

But if the light be narrower than the opaque body, then its shadow will be in the shape of an inverted pyramid, and will grow into <unclear>infinity</unclear>.

<note>Leonardo is defining the three types of shadows (convergent, parallel, and divergent) based on the relative size of the light source to the object.</note>

<summary>Leonardo demonstrates that the Moon reflects sunlight rather than emitting its own, using its spherical, non-lustrous surface to explain why it appears fully illuminated. He also provides geometric definitions for the shapes of shadows—pyramidal, columnar, and inverted—based on the size of the light source.</summary>
<keywords>Moon, Sun, reflection, optics, shadow geometry, opaque body, astronomy, light theory</keywords>

If the weight **n** be 2 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "oncie"; a unit of weight</note> and the weight **m** be 4, the force must be 6, and such will be the stress on the attachment **g** above **n** and **m** as is the sum of the said 2 weights; and the weight **o** will be the resistance of the said 6 ounces. And if one pulls by **f** with 6 ounces, it will not move because the 6 ounces of weight **o** pull from below just as **n** and **m** do from above. And if the weight **o** be 3 ounces, it will move with such <term>speed</term> <note>original: "sveltezza"; literally "quickness" or "velocity"</note> as the motion of the force that moves it—that is, the speed will be doubled because the force of 6 is double the weight of 3 that it moves; whereby **f** pulling 1 <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; a Florentine measure of length, roughly 23 inches</note>, the weight **o** will move 1 braccio, and because **f** pulls 1 braccio, the 2 weights **n** and **m** will descend half a braccio each.

In this case, if **n** be 1 and **m** be 1 and the weight **o** be 2, the cord **f** pulling 2 ounces will move nothing; and if the weight **o** be 1, then **f** pulling 2 ounces will double the speed of the motion of the weight **o** that it moves, because **f** moves 1 braccio and the weight **o** moves 1 braccio, and the weight **n** and **m** move half a braccio each—that is, that **n** and **m** approach one another by 1 braccio.

Every movement of weights created by means of a cord is easier the longer the cord is, because that part of the cord which rests upon the <term>pulley</term> <note>original: "carrucola"</note> is shorter in the long cord than in the short one, and one cord offers less resistance than the other to bending around the said pulley.

That pulley which moves with less effort is the one that is wider, because the cord that wraps around it is less constrained to bend than that which wraps around a narrow pulley.

<margin>
Furthermore, the wide pulley
labors less because it turns
less, doubling the revolutions of
its <term>axle</term> <note>original: "asse"</note> compared to the narrow one.
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the relationship between force, weight, and velocity in pulley systems, calculating how the distribution of weight affects the speed of motion. He also observes that larger pulleys and longer cords reduce mechanical resistance and friction.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, pulleys, weight distribution, velocity, friction, physics of cords, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<note>Technical Vocabulary:
- **Balance** (original: *bilancia*): A weighing scale or the state of equilibrium.
- **Gravity/Heaviness** (original: *gravezza*): The natural tendency of weights to move downward.
- **Perpendicular** (original: *perpendiculare*): A line at a right angle to the horizon, pointing to the Earth's center.
- **Oblique** (original: *obliqua*): Slanted; any line of motion not perfectly vertical.
- **Force** (original: *forza*): The power applied to move or sustain a weight.
- **Center of the world** (original: *centro del mondo*): The center of the Earth.
- **Line of motion** (original: *linia del moto*): The path along which a weight travels.
- **Proportion** (original: *proportione*): The mathematical relationship between force and weight.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the relationship between the direction of a weight's motion and the force required to move it, concluding that the perpendicular path to the Earth's center is the most efficient. He explores how oblique (slanted) lines of motion increase resistance, requiring a force greater than the weight itself to achieve movement.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, statics, center of gravity, leverage, perpendicular motion, oblique resistance, equilibrium</keywords>

### [Folio 121v]

If a force is applied to the movement of a circle upon its circumference, it will be equal to the power <note>original: "potētia" (potenza). In this context, Leonardo refers to the mechanical advantage or potential force.</note> that would turn it from within, and the circle shall be equal.

<margin>
<note>Geometric diagram of a circle with internal lines and points labeled a, b, c, d, e, f, n, m, r.</note>
</margin>

The circle is of the same distribution from one part as from another; therefore, if we take the center of said circle as the root <note>The "root" or "origin" of its mechanical power.</note> of its power and draw to said center a line through its circumference, that line shall be the root of the power of the force applied to said circumference. And if one applies to said line another line equal to it, in the manner seen within through the other part of that center, then this power shall be equal to said force.

<note>Large geometric diagram in the center of the page featuring a circle with internal chords and intersecting arcs, possibly a projection or study of a sphere.</note>

To define the reason why the circle is part of a ball <note>original: "palla." Leonardo uses this term for a sphere.</note>: when the circle is set in motion circularly around its center, it will turn the said ball moved by the center with it. One will see if, through that center, the ball is turned or if the ball is not equal to that circle.

<margin>
<note>Three diagrams of wheels and mechanical transmission systems. The bottommost one is a large circle with internal radial lines and a central hub.</note>
</margin>

In what way one must give motion to this circle so that its center does not turn.

If the circle turns upon its center, it will not turn the ball; but if the ball is equal to the circle, it will turn it. Consider well how great the power of the inner center is in respect to the force of the said circles and the ball, and how great the power of the center is in respect to the circumference.

## The Theory of the Balance Wheel

If the wheel shall be of uniform weight and its center shall be that of its circle
it will never move by itself unless already one of its parts
be lifted from its weight or indeed increased in weight as is shown
in the balance because the wheel is nothing other than a continuous balance
the arms of which are the spokes <note>original: "raggi," literally rays</note> that go out from the center to [...]
the circumference of its circle and from this it is concluded
that if the arms of the balance be of equal length and of e[...]
qual weight and be loaded with equal weight it shall be impossible that it [...]
will move but if one of its arms shall be longer than the other
or if one be loaded with more weight than the other again the wheel shall be mov[...]
ed and that this is so I am certain with one of the ends of the arm
of the balance being of equal length that one of its heads be loaded
with one pound and the other be empty that it moves from the side of the weight
and if both shall be of equal weight that it will stand still and from th[...]
is it is proved that the wheel being a continuous balance whose arms
are the spokes that go out from its center to the surface of the circle [...]
and if they shall be loaded with equal weight it will stand still and if it be [...]
moved it shall be moved by way of another force and not by itself.

<note>Leonardo uses the "continuous balance" <term>bilancia continua</term> to explain that a wheel is essentially an infinite series of levers. If the weights are balanced around the center, the wheel remains in <term>equilibrium</term>—a state of rest.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explores the fundamental laws of mechanics, arguing that motion requires an external force and demonstrating that a perfectly centered wheel acts as a continuous balance that remains at rest unless its equilibrium is disturbed.</summary>

<keywords>mechanics, law of motion, equilibrium, balance wheel, spokes, weights, levers, physics of rotation</keywords>

<note>Studies of pulleys, levers, and centers of gravity.</note>

<margin>
The principle of a balance <note>original: "libra"</note> is this:

The center of gravity of every body within its own boundaries, and in whatever direction it may turn, always maintains the same distance from its extremities.

<note>A diagram showing a circular mechanism with multiple weights or cord attachments.</note>

# [Folio 130r]

<note>Studies in ballistics and the geometry of solids.</note>

<note>Top diagrams show triangles inscribed in circles and various balance configurations to determine centers of gravity.</note>

If the artillery ball were always of the same substance and of the same round shape, and were fired with the same force, it would be a rare occasion that it did not travel its path for the same length, and it would be a rare occasion that it did not make its direction of the same width. But because it attempts to travel through the air in a straight line and by the shortest path that exists between its end and its beginning, it cannot do so because of the <term>unimità</term> <note>likely meaning the "uniformity" or "oneness" of the air's resistance</note> of the air and because of the <unclear>strength</unclear> of the velocity that the ball acquires...

<note>Central diagrams of truncated cones and pyramidal shapes, used to analyze the distribution of mass.</note>

<margin>
If the motion were not interrupted, the "wind" <note>the air currents or spin</note> of the ball would never vary; and if it did not vary, it would never turn; and if it did not turn, it would always make its path of the same length.
</margin>

<note>A diagram of a rectangular block with lines indicating the central axis of balance.</note>

If half of a weight weighs as much on the right as on the left, its center will be in the middle of its boundaries. But if the weight is always on one same side, it will never come to rest without the torment <note>stress or strain</note> of its support <note>original: "sustentacolo"</note>.

Every hanging heavy body stops below the center of its support, and if it is heavier on one side than the other, it will move until the center of its gravity is in the same perpendicular line with the center of its support.

<note>Vocabulary list: artillery ball, center of gravity, balance, support, perpendicular line, air, motion.</note>

### Description of Drawing
The page is dominated by a fluid, large-scale sketch representing the course of a river system, identified as the Arno in Tuscany. The lines trace the meanders of the main river and several intersecting branches or proposed canal routes. Light cross-hatching and shading are used to suggest topography, such as hills or embankments. Numerous numbers are inscribed along the paths, serving as quantitative data for Leonardo's engineering considerations. The style is typical of his rapid topographical drafts, where technical precision in measurement (the numbers) meets a visionary's eye for the landscape's natural flow. <note>Leonardo often used these sketches to plan the diversion of the Arno to provide Florence with a navigable waterway to the sea or to deprive enemy Pisa of water during wartime.</note>

# f. 23v

Proportion is a certain relationship of things to one another that are of the same kind, such as line to line, surface to surface, or body to body, or time to time, or motion to motion, and <unclear>similar</unclear> <note>Leonardo is defining "magnitude" here, following the Euclidean tradition where only like-quantities can be compared.</note>.
Proportionality is a certain equality of proportions.

Proportion is divided into two parts: namely, into rational and irrational.
Rational is that which can be expressed with numbers, such as 2 to 4 or 4 to 8.
Irrational is that which cannot be <unclear>given</unclear> a number nor expressed by voice, such as the proportion that the side of a square has to its diagonal <note>original: "diametro." Leonardo refers to the "incommensurability" of the diagonal of a square, a classic problem in geometry where the ratio cannot be expressed as a simple fraction.</note>.

### [Left Page]

If you place the tube of the pump <note>original: "tronba" – here referring to a siphon or suction pipe</note> into the water and draw breath with your mouth, the water will rise up through the said tube; and if you stop and do not draw with your mouth, the said water will not move from bottom to top, but will remain at the level of the other water in the basin where it is found.

### [Right Page]

For which reason the weight of the said water cannot move except by force from above or from below; and if the said pump were pierced at the top, the air would enter through the said fissure or hole without any effort, and the water would descend because the weight from above would overcome the weight from below. A vacuum <note>original: "uoto"</note> cannot constrain the air to become thinner nor the water to become thicker, because the air, moved by its own will, moves to fill the vacuum that would be created at the top of the said tube.

<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on atmospheric pressure and the nature of a vacuum, Leonardo now applies these physical principles of air density to the visual arts, specifically developing his theory of "aerial perspective" or the way the atmosphere affects how we see distant objects.</meta>

### [Left Page - Folio 163v]

<note>At the top of the page, there is a faint geometric diagram representing the eye observing objects through horizontal layers of the atmosphere.</note>

<margin>
The air
</margin>

If the air were of a uniform density, the things most remote from the eye would lose as much of their clarity as would be proportional to their distance from the eye.

But because the air is denser the closer it is to the earth, and the higher it rises the thinner and more transparent it becomes, things that are at an equal low altitude and at an equal distance from the eye will appear more blurred and dark if the eye is positioned higher than if the eye were at the same low altitude as those things.

This is proven: let the air be divided into degrees of thinness <note>Leonardo uses "degrees" to describe layers or strata of atmospheric density</note> of which the first is closest to the earth, and the second is above that, and so on, step by step, until the top of the air. Now, if the eye is at **a** and the objects are at an equal distance at **b** and **c**, I say that the eye at **a** will see **b** through thicker air than it will see **c**, because the line **ab** passes through two degrees of thick air and the line **ac** passes through only one degree of thick air.

Furthermore, if the eye is at **d** and the same objects are at **b** and **c**, I say that **b** will be seen through thicker air than **c**, and this happens because the line **db** is more oblique than the line **dc**, and consequently it is longer within the same degree of thick air.

<column-break/>

### [Right Page - Folio 163r]

<note>Only a few lines of text appear at the top of this otherwise blank page.</note>

It is proven by the 4th [proposition] of this [treatise] that the same object will be seen through air of different qualities of <unclear>thicknesses</unclear>...

and this happens because one part of the air is closer to the earth...

<summary>Leonardo explains the principles of aerial perspective, demonstrating how the varying density of atmospheric layers causes distant objects to appear less clear depending on the observer's height and the angle of sight. He concludes that air is densest near the ground, which significantly impacts the visual clarity of objects viewed through it.</summary>

### [Folio 13v]

A river does not flow with its water at a speed equal in every part of itself, even with a consistent volume of water, unless the depth of the bed is the same, the width between the banks is the same, and it possesses the same straightness and the same slope.

And if water of a consistent volume is moved across various slopes, it will not have equal velocity, because that which is on a steeper bed will have a faster flow. Furthermore, if water of a consistent volume and slope is moved through channels of various widths, that which is in the narrower channel will have a faster motion. And again, if water of a consistent volume and slope is moved through channels of the same width but varying depth, that which is in the shallower <note>original: "fondo piu sottile" - literally "thinner bottom," referring to a shallow water column</note> bed will have a faster motion.

<margin>
<note>Diagram of a water channel with a weir/dam at the top right.</note>
If the water has an equal slope and equal width, it will be faster in the middle of its course than at either of its banks.
</margin>

Water that has the same width, slope, and straightness will not be of equal velocity in any of its parts, because the water that is closer to the banks will have a slower motion than that which is in the middle.

Water of a consistent volume, width, and slope will not be of equal velocity throughout its thickness, because the water that is closer to the bottom is of slower motion than that which is at the surface.

---

### [Folio 13r]

Consider the animal body <note>Leonardo often uses the "animal body" or microcosm as a point of comparison for the "body of the earth."</note>; the same motion of the wave occurs in water as in air. For if you throw a ball of water into the sea, it will create a wave just as a stone would, even though water is a fluid body and the stone is solid.

That part of the water wave is of faster motion which is closer to the center of its origin.

<note>Diagrams in the center show circular wave patterns and their expansion.</note>

It is the same for the air to move against a stationary object as it is to move the object against the stationary air. <note>This is a foundational observation of relative motion, crucial to Leonardo's studies of flight.</note>

Consider how the motion of the water wave is of the same nature <note>original: "medesimo atto" - same action or behavior</note> as that of the wave of the air, and of light, and of thunder—even though thunder is not seen.

<margin>
The water wave does not move <insert>forward</insert>, but rather the vibration <term>trepidazione: the oscillating pulse of energy through a medium</term> is moved, which the thrown ball has given to it.
</margin>

The water wave is of two types: one is caused by the wind and the other is caused by a body thrown into it. That which is caused by the wind will be of faster motion than that which is caused by weight.

Air is compressible <note>original: "condensabile"</note> and rarefiable in every part of said air.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the variables affecting the velocity of river currents—such as depth, width, and slope—and theorizes that wave motion in water, air, light, and sound follows the same physical laws of vibration.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, fluid dynamics, wave theory, relative motion, acoustics, atmospheric density, Codex Leicester</keywords>

### Left Page - Left Column

No continuous body <term>continuo: a physical substance that can be infinitely divided</term> shall be divisible into parts that have the same length, body, and surface as its line of incision <note>original: "linea d'inciditione"</note>, because every part is similar to its whole, and its division is almost nothing if, by such division, its own constant quantities were diminished. And if it were possible for a line to be divided into points, that line would be composed of points, which is impossible, as will be stated regarding the line.

Of the proportion of the power <term>potentia: the force or potential energy</term> of weights that have an end of motion compared to weights that have a beginning of motion, and of their velocity.
Motion shall be so much faster as the moved object has in itself more heaviness <note>original: "graveza"</note>.

Because every motion shall be so much slower as its moved object shall be of greater power than its motor <term>motore: the force or agent causing the movement</term>.
And if the motor shall be of lesser power than its moved object, the motion shall never be made, unless there be such a proportion as that of nature, which will be described.

No similarity shall exist between two bodies where one is a mixture of the other, because every mixture shall be dissimilar to its simple elements, and similarly dissimilar to the contrary of itself.

# At this point, shadow meets with light, both of one and the same power.

Pure air will be of an equal clarity, without having within itself any cloud, or rather smoke, or fog. It will be incorporeal <note>meaning without physical substance or body</note>; as much as it is moved, it will be heated and will become thick. It will be of a color that tends toward blue. It will be weak; it will not have the strength to support or sustain any heavy body. It will not be divisible from any other part of that same air.

---

See that you do not place the air between the light and the shadow, because it has no business being there. Between that shadow and that light, there is transparent air. It will be without any color, but it will be of a blue color, and that which is further from the eye will be more blue, and that which is closer to the eye will be less blue.

<note>Small circular diagram with internal lines, likely representing the eye or a celestial body in relation to light propagation.</note>

---

Pure air will be clear between the shadow and the light. It will be without any color, but will be transparent, and will be of an equal clarity. It will be of one and the same power <note>original: "potētia"; referring here to its optical intensity or capacity</note>. It will be of a blue color, and it will be more blue the further it is from the eye, and that will be less blue which is closer to the eye.

---

Pure air will be of a color that tends toward blue. It will be weak; it will not have the strength to support or sustain any heavy body. It will not be divisible from any other part of that same air.

<note>Leonardo discusses the physical and optical properties of air, specifically its transparency, its lack of inherent color except for the blue tint it takes on over distance (aerial perspective), and its interaction with light and shadow. The text emphasizes that air between the light and the shadow is transparent and colorless.</note>

<note>Technical vocabulary: air <term>aria</term>, shadow <term>onbra</term>, light <term>luce</term>, power/potential <term>potentia</term>, blue <term>azurro</term>, eye <term>ochio</term>, transparent <term>trasparēte</term>, cloud/nimbus <term>nembo</term>, smoke <term>fumo</term>, incorporeal <term>incorporea</term>.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physical and optical nature of air, defining it as an incorporeal medium that acquires a blue hue based on its distance from the observer. These notes lay the scientific foundation for "aerial perspective," where distant objects appear bluer and less distinct.</summary>
<keywords>optics, aerial perspective, atmospheric physics, blue sky, light and shadow, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

--- Page 489 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion on the optical properties and transparency of air. This page shifts focus from optics to mechanics and physics, specifically the nature of gravity and the geometry of motion toward the center of the earth.</meta>

To say that the motion of a heavy thing is toward the center of the earth is the same as saying that if you let it fall, it would go by the shortest path to the center of that earth; and if you divided the world in half in any direction, that motion would always follow that division. And the reason is because the center of gravity of every heavy body desires to unite itself with the center of the world <note>Leonardo uses "center of the world" to mean the center of the Earth, following the Aristotelian view that the Earth is the center of the universe</note>.

---

Let **a b** be the weight which, by its motion coming from **a** to **b**, describes the arc **a c b**. I say that said arc is nothing other than a bent straight line; and just as one reaches a determined mark sooner by a straight line than by a curved line, so the weight moves sooner by the straight line than by the curved one. From this it follows that said circumferential motion <term>circumferential motion: movement along the perimeter of a circle</term> must be reduced to a straight line, and once it is reduced, its power will be seen.

---

<margin>
The reason why a weight, if it departed from the straight line tending toward the center of the world and was reduced to a circular line, is nothing other than reducing said straight line into a curved line; and the reason for that curvature must be reduced to a straight line, as is said above; and by this, one recognizes the weakness of motion along an arc.
</margin>

---

Every local motion <term>local motion: the physical movement of an object from one place to another</term> is divided into three parts: of which the first is called direct <note>linear</note>, the second circumferential, and the third is mixed. And the reason for this division is what was said above: because every local motion tends toward the center of the world, and if that motion is direct, it will be of a simple quality; and if it is circumferential, it will be of a mixed quality, because the motion of said circumference joins itself with that direct motion.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the nature of gravity, asserting that all heavy bodies seek the center of the Earth via the shortest path. He argues that circular motion is a "bent" version of linear motion and is inherently "weaker" or less efficient than direct movement.</summary>
<keywords>gravity, center of the world, local motion, circumferential motion, geometry of physics, weight, mechanics</keywords>

Those winds that have diverse natures: let the air of one wind be of heat and the other be of cold, or of dryness or of moisture, or let us say they are of various densities—one being of thin air and the other of thick air. It is shown how, when one wind strikes the other, if it strikes along the line that enters through the centers of these winds, they always depart from a common percussion and go in a straight line to flee the said percussion; and they will be one against the other of the same [force] if they collide directly. And if the motions of the two winds touch along an oblique line, they will result in reflected motions. And when the air is weak, its reflection will be weak; and when the air is of a certain density, its reflection will be so much more powerful. And as the air of one of these winds is of greater velocity than another, so much more will its reflection be powerful within the same air.

If the **bombard** <note>A large-caliber medieval cannon.</note> has a mouth of 1/2 **braccio** <note>A "braccio" (arm) was a common Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> and its fire is another 1/2 braccio in length, and if the said fire is rarefied from an air 400 times more dense than itself, then the said bombard will be filled with 400 half-braccia of said air. This fills the said bombard from a small space of air which is as large as the mouth and 1/2 braccio in height. Wishing, therefore, for such smoke to occupy its place, it took from a small space of air 1/400th of said mouth, and the rest would be <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "uochuo"; Leonardo uses this to describe the space created by extreme expansion or the lack of matter.</note>. Therefore, 399 parts of air would be vacuum, and as much as there is such vacuum, the said air will be 1/400th of said bombard. And if said bombard has a velocity 80 times greater than the said air, then the said air will be 400 times 80 times more than the said air, because as much as the air is more rarefied, so much is it weaker, and as much as the air is more compressed, so much is it stronger. And if you suggest to me that 1/2 braccio of air has to rarefy 800 times from the same air, as the said bombard has a mouth of 1/2 braccio and is 400 times the air, then there are 400 half-braccia of air that have to rarefy 1/2 braccio of air; therefore, said air will be 400 times more rarefied than said air. And if said bombard has a mouth of one braccio and is 800 times the air, then there are 800 half-braccia of air that have to rarefy 1/2 braccio of air; therefore, said air will be 800 times more rarefied than said air. And if said bombard has a mouth of 2 braccia and is 1600 times the air, then there are 1600 half-braccia of air that have to rarefy 1/2 braccio of air; therefore, said air will be 1600 times more rarefied than said air.

### [Folio 43v]

<note>Top left: Diagram of a triangle or pyramid with internal parallel lines, illustrating geometric proportions.</note>

Many people exhaust themselves trying to give the reason for the doubling of the body of a pyramid or cone by means of the doubling of the cube, which seems impossible because, just as two mean proportionals <note>original: "dua medi proporzionali"; in geometry, these are the values needed between two numbers to find the side of a doubled cube.</note> do not fall between the numbers 1 and 2, so they do not fall between 1 and 2 cubes.

<note>Top right: Small diagram of a cube with an elongated section.</note>

Those who wish to double the cube quickly exert such great effort, and thus they struggled until finally they achieved only unity.

<note>Center: A perspective drawing of a cube with lines extending its base, creating a rectangular prism.</note>

For doubling the cube, this method is not true.

<margin>
Send and ensure that the proportion of the pyramid—which results from the doubled substitution that you take crosswise, like the <term>pupa di sesta</term> <note>Literally "doll of the compass," likely a technical term for a specific geometric template or a pivot point.</note> or rather a doubled pyramid—is like the doubling of the other one above, which will serve as equal parts; and as the whole body is doubled, let the other face be equal in <term>r</term> and <term>d</term> and <term>e</term> and <term>s</term> <note>Reference to labeled points in a missing or implied diagram.</note> positions, and the body and thickness.
</margin>

### [Folio 44r]

...means interposed to arrive at a doubled form, regardless of the shape of the natural cube, or rather pyramid or cylinder; and this is because the entire body is doubled by the parallel [line]. It becomes doubled because if the cube or cylinder, whatever it may be, doubles its height, the same body is first <unclear>made</unclear> from the original.

<note>Center right: Diagram of a cube next to a long rectangular block and three horizontal lines representing proportional lengths (likely mean proportionals).</note>

To double the cube with a single <unclear>stroke</unclear> <note>original: "uerso"; can mean direction, line, or method.</note>: this cannot be done because if you make a cube that doubles an equal proportion, it lacks the thickness or the height to truly become a cube.

To double the cube with a single <unclear>parallel</unclear> <unclear>as it is</unclear> tangent to such a direction: this cannot be done because if you provide the doubling according to one proportion, it is lacking in the other two parts.

To double the cube with only two equal joins within the doubling: according to one proportion, it is lacking on the other side.

Many exhaust themselves in giving the reason for doubling the body of a pyramid or cone by doubling the cube or cylinder or whatever body it may be; and to achieve doubling in a single direction, the whole material is crossed in one direction only. Such a body will never result in a rounded, composite, doubled body. Therefore, one should note that the natural cube is doubled through multiple directions and not by one single method alone; and one by one, the smaller cube will be made, one by one from the first.

<summary>Leonardo investigates the geometric challenge of doubling the volume of a cube, pyramid, or cylinder, arguing that doubling only one dimension (height or width) fails to create a proportional solid. He concludes that the "Delian problem" requires finding mean proportionals across multiple dimensions rather than a single linear extension.</summary>
<keywords>geometry, doubling the cube, Delian problem, mean proportionals, pyramid, cylinder, stereometry, proportions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s investigation into the physics of motion and force. While the previous page focused on the static balance of levers and counterweights, these folios transition into dynamics—specifically the "fatigue" or effort required for different types of motion and the mechanics of impact (percussion).</meta>

### [f. 215v - Verso]

Which blow will have the greater percussion <note>impact or striking force</note>: that which falls or consumes its motion along a straight line, or that which consumes it in a curved line? Let the curved motion be of equal length to the straight motion, and of the same weight, and from the same height where such motion had its beginning.

Why curved motion is more laborious than straight motion with the same arc, the same weight, and the same force, will be proven by the 6th [proposition] of this [treatise], which says: curved motion is composed of two motions, of which one is toward the center of the world <note>the center of the Earth, representing gravity</note> and the other is transverse. Motions composed of two simple ones are of as much labor as the simple motions of which they are composed; therefore, curved motion will be of as much labor as the motion toward the center and the transverse motion combined.

The more a curved motion is bent, the greater labor it will be compared to straight motion. This is proven because curved motion is composed of two simple motions, which simple motions will be of more equal labor as the descent and the transverse [components] are more equal. And if one is more powerful than the other, it will be of as much less labor as they are dissimilar. Therefore, as much as there is greater labor in the curved motion, so much less will its blow be at the end of its motion, because as much power is consumed in the motion as is given by the author <note>the source or prime mover</note> of said motion. If, therefore, it is consumed [along the way], less of it will be brought to the percussion.

<note>Geometric diagrams illustrating forces and angles of motion, featuring triangles labeled with letters a, b, c, d, e, m, n, o.</note>

---

### [f. 215r - Recto]

The percussion made by a mobile object against an immobile object of equal resistance will be of as much power as that which is made by the immobile object against the mobile one.

This occurs when the blow falls along a perpendicular line upon the surface of that resistance, and the mobile object is of as much resistance as the power of the blow. And if the mobile object is of greater resistance than the power of the blow, then the immobile object will return a greater blow than the mobile one. And if the immobile object is of lesser resistance than the power of the blow, then the immobile object will return a lesser blow than the power of the blow.

That mobile object will return a greater blow upon the immobile object which, in its motion, has greater weight and greater velocity; and that will be of lesser percussion which moves with lesser weight and lesser velocity. And that will also be of greater percussion which, at its end, has the same velocity and the same thickness as the striking object; for if it has a sharp point, it will penetrate more than strike, and if it has a blunt end, it will strike more than penetrate.

The less resistance the object struck has, the less power the percussion made by that struck object will have upon the object that strikes. Because of this, if you strike with the same blow a sack of feathers and a steel anvil, you will find that the percussion made upon the anvil is much greater than that of the sack of feathers. This arises because the feathers bend and yield to the blow, because their resistance is minimal, and the percussion is consumed over a length of time because the feathers bend inward and do not return resistance to the blow except with their weight, which is little. For the more they bend, the more feathers are added to the resistance, and thus the power of the blow is consumed.

<note>A small geometric diagram at the bottom right corner showing intersecting lines and a triangle.</note>

<summary>Leonardo examines the physics of "labor" in motion, arguing that curved paths dissipate energy more than straight ones, and analyzes how the material properties of an object (like an anvil versus feathers) affect the force of impact.</summary>
<keywords>percussion, resistance, curved motion, straight motion, power, velocity, center of the world, sack of feathers, steel anvil</keywords>

### [Folio 233v]

Knowing how the earth has no soul <note>original: "anima"; Leonardo is clarifying that the Earth is a mechanical system, not a living organism with a spirit</note>, nor does it consume itself

In how the rock rises, which is felt <note>original: "sētito" (sentito); likely a technical term for being subjected to pressure or "perceived" by the surrounding forces</note> by the water that fills with rocks
through long ages, and of that vessel <note>a metaphor for the Earth's crust or a specific geological basin</note> the belly of the

better because of the rock not felt by a water of a vessel sinking to the bottom.
If it sinks into the rocks or the mountains, it lowers because of being felt,
for as much as a water of a vessel sinks to the bottom,
you will see the natural course.

<note>Leonardo argues that the Earth is not a living organism ("non ha anima") and that geological changes are mechanical. He describes how rain washes mud into the sea, turning it into stone over long periods. As mountains lose weight through erosion, they rise, while the weight of the mud on the seabed causes other areas to shift.</note>

### [Left Page (Verso)]

If the <term>visual power</term><note>original: "uirtù uisiua"; the medieval and Renaissance concept of the faculty or force within the eye that enables sight.</note> were a single entity and located in a single point—as my opponent claims—then every object seen through that point would be without proportion of size and would appear as nothing. But because we see that the further an object recedes, the more it diminishes, it is necessary that the <term>convergence of the images</term><note>original: "chonchorso delle spezie"; "species" (images/likenesses) were thought to be physical emissions from objects that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> occurs within a boundary that is **pyramidal**. And if you were to say that the visual power is distributed throughout the entire pupil, then the images entering through it could not converge in a single point; and if they do not converge in a single point, they would not form a pyramid; and if they do not form a pyramid, they would not carry the information of the object which is seen by means of such a pyramid.

<margin>
<note>Diagram showing rays passing through a point and diverging.</note>
</margin>

And if you were to say that the pupil is not entirely the center of the convergence of images, and that the point of convergence is deeper within the visual power, to this it is replied: if it is true that the eye sees by the intersection of rays of every image at a single point—as many say and as it seems <unclear>one</unclear> <unclear>proves</unclear>—it is a necessity that the object seen must appear inverted; and if indeed it does not appear inverted, it is a necessity that this visual power be placed at a point in front of the said intersection of rays, or rather that this visual power receives these images without them intersecting...

<margin>
<note>Diagram of lines 'a', 'b', 'c' converging toward a point labeled 'p'.</note>
</margin>

### [Recto - Right Page]

<note>At the top, several sketches showing projectile impact zones and a mortar firing toward a tower. In the center, a man operates a device near a horizontal trough. Below, a detailed study of a large bombard on a heavy wooden carriage.</note>

If you were inside a fortress during the firing of a <term>bombard</term> <note>original: "bombarda"; an early type of large-caliber cannon or mortar used for throwing heavy stones</note>, and if the bombard were placed upon the walls of the said fortress, if the said bombard were of great weight, it would cause the walls of the said fortress to vibrate. And by the walls vibrating, one of the said walls could crack. For this reason, the said bombard must be placed upon its own structure <note>original: "fortezza"; here meaning a dedicated support or platform</note> which shall be separated from the walls of the city, in such a way that its motion cannot be communicated to the walls. Because if the said bombard were fired once, it would not do great harm; but if the said bombard fired many times, it would cause such vibration to the walls that they would necessarily have to crack. To avoid this, the said bombard must be placed upon its own structure which shall be separated from the walls of the city, so that its motion cannot be communicated to the walls. And this you will do with a space of earth or a space of air, so that the motion cannot be communicated from the walls of the bombard to the walls of the city. And if it should happen that the said bombard were of great weight, it must be made in such a way that its weight does not load the walls of the fortress, but that its load is sustained by wooden timberwork...

the rule of the <term>line-drawers</term> <note>original: "tiralini"; likely referring to instruments for drawing proportional lines or perhaps a specific mechanical component like a drawing-pen or tensioner</note>. And such a rule
shall be for those things that move the force
through the space of the rule of one; [it] shall be the rule
of every part, just as there be the rule .a. .b. and .c.
by the rule .f. .g. it shall be the rule.

The whole part .m. o. [or] .n. p. shall be a part of space;
just as a part of the one shall be the rule
of the other [part] of space, it shall be the rule. And if
the movement be by rule and by space,
let it be that of one part, there be the part of space;
of one, there be the part of space of the other.

<summary>Leonardo defines the mathematical laws of the lever, establishing that force and weight exist in an inverse, reciprocal proportion to their distance from a fulcrum. He attempts to universalize these "rules" of proportion to apply to all mechanical movements and drawing instruments.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, levers, proportional logic, physics, weight and measure, reciprocal proportions, motive force</keywords>

## [Folio 271 verso]

<note>This page contains a dense study on the movement of air, compression, and rarefaction. Leonardo uses the term "rimpingua" (thickens or compresses) and "rinfata" (impacted or packed together) to describe how air molecules interact.</note>

Just as the principle of air which is moved by a force

they strike <unclear>into the other</unclear> and this one into the next, and so the
<unclear>motion</unclear> goes distributing itself through the woods, <unclear>and so</unclear> <unclear>spreading</unclear>

These bellows have made me think whether, by the force of a weight, it could be possible to make one of the bellows reset the other at the same speed with which one of the bellows is pressed by the weight.
</margin>

<note>Small sketch of a circular gear or component in the bottom right.</note>

<summary>This page explores the mechanical engineering of musical instruments, specifically focusing on a design for organ bellows that provides a continuous, uninterrupted flow of air using a system of weights and reciprocal motion. It also includes geometrical studies of circles and notes on the physics of moving weights.</summary>
